chapters.title: Sara
paragraphs: One dark winter day, a little girl with an unusual face was riding slowly along London's broad streets in a cab beside her father. Yellow fog lay so thick and heavy over the city that the street lamps had been lit, and gaslight shone from the shop windows just as it did at night.

Her feet were tucked beneath her, and she leaned into her father, who had an arm around her. As she watched the people passing outside the window, her wide eyes held a strange, thoughtful look that seemed to belong to someone much older.

On so small a girl's face, that expression was unexpected. It would have looked old even on a twelve-year-old, and Sara Crewe was only seven. Yet she was forever dreaming and thinking curious thoughts; she could not remember ever having lived without wondering about grown-ups and the world they inhabited. To her, it felt as though she had already been alive for a very, very long time.

Just now her thoughts were on the journey she had made from Bombay with her father, Captain Crewe. She remembered the great ship, the Lascars moving silently back and forth across it, and the children playing on the hot deck. She remembered, too, the young officers' wives who would coax her into conversation and laugh at the things she told them.

Above all, she was considering how strange it was to be in India's fierce sunshine at one moment, then out in the middle of the sea, and then riding in an unfamiliar carriage through unfamiliar streets, where daylight was as black as night. It puzzled her so much that she pressed a little nearer to her father.
"Papa," she said, her small voice low and mysterious, almost a whisper. "Papa."
Captain Crewe drew her closer and gazed down at her face. "What is it, darling?" he asked. "What is my Sara thinking about?"
"Is this the place?" whispered Sara, nestling even more closely against him. "Is it, papa?"
"Yes, little Sara. This is it. At last we've arrived." She was only seven, but she could hear the sadness in his words.

It felt like years since he had first begun getting her ready for "the place," as she always called it. Her mother had died at her birth, so Sara had neither known her nor felt her absence. Her father, young and handsome and rich and always petting her, seemed to be her one relation in the whole world. They had always been playmates and loved each other's company. She knew he was rich only because people said so when they supposed she could not hear; she had heard them say, too, that she would be rich herself when she grew up. What being rich really meant, she did not entirely understand. Her home had always been a lovely bungalow, full of servants who made salaams to her, addressed her as "Missee Sahib," and let her have her way about everything. She had toys and pets and an ayah who adored her. Little by little, she had come to understand that rich people had these things. Beyond that, she knew nothing about it.

There had been just one worry in her short life: "the place" where she would have to go one day. India's climate was considered very unhealthy for children, and they were sent away as soon as they could be—usually to school in England. Other children had left before her eyes, and she had listened to their parents discussing the letters that came from them. She had always known that her own turn must come. Sometimes her father's accounts of the voyage and the new country made her want to see them, but the knowledge that he could not stay there with her troubled her.
At five she had asked, "Couldn't you come to that place with me, papa? Couldn't you come to school yourself? I'd help you do your lessons."

"But it won't be such a very long stay, little Sara," he had always assured her. "You'll live in a nice house with lots of other little girls, and you'll all play together. I'll send you plenty of books. You'll grow so quickly that it will hardly seem a year before you're big enough and clever enough to come home and look after papa."

That was a prospect she loved. Managing her father's house, riding beside him, taking her place at the head of his table when he gave dinner parties, talking with him and reading his books—nothing in the world could please her more. If reaching that future meant going away to "the place" in England, then she must resolve to go. Other little girls did not interest her very much, but a good supply of books would comfort her. Books were her greatest delight; indeed, she was constantly making up stories about beautiful things and telling them to herself. Sometimes she had shared them with her father, and he had enjoyed them every bit as much as she had.
"Well, papa," she said gently, "since we have arrived, I suppose we must be resigned."

Her old-fashioned words made him laugh, and he kissed her. In truth, he felt nothing like resigned, although he knew he must not let her see it. His curious little Sara had been wonderful company. He thought how lonely he would be, back in India, walking into his bungalow and knowing that no small figure in a white frock would run forward to welcome him. As the cab turned into the large, gloomy square where their destination stood, he held her tight in both arms.
The house was large, gloomy, and built of brick, just like every other house in the row. Its one distinction was a shining brass plate fixed to the front door, bearing these words in black:
MISS MINCHIN,
Select Seminary for Young Ladies.

"Here we are, Sara," Captain Crewe announced, putting as much cheer into his voice as he could. He lifted her down from the cab; together they climbed the steps and rang. Later Sara often thought how exactly the house resembled Miss Minchin. It was respectable, with good furniture, yet everything was ugly. Even the armchairs seemed to have hard bones inside them. Hardness and polish filled the hall; the red cheeks of the moon face on the tall corner clock looked stern beneath their varnish. They were shown into a drawing room with a square-patterned carpet and square chairs. A weighty marble clock rested on an equally weighty marble mantelpiece.
Settling into one of the unyielding mahogany chairs, Sara gave the room one of her swift, observant glances.
"I don't like it, papa," she told him. "Still, I suppose soldiers don't really LIKE going into battle either—even the brave ones."
At that, Captain Crewe burst out laughing. Young and cheerful himself, he found he could never hear enough of Sara's curious remarks.
"Oh, little Sara," he said, "what will become of me without you to say solemn things? Nobody else can be quite so solemn."
"Then why does something solemn make you laugh like that?" Sara wanted to know.

"Because you're so amusing when you say it," he replied, laughing harder. Then he suddenly gathered her into his arms and kissed her fiercely. His laughter stopped at once, and his eyes looked almost as though they were filling with tears.

At that very moment Miss Minchin came in. Sara thought she was remarkably like the house: tall, dreary, respectable, and ugly. Her eyes were large and cold and fishlike; her smile was large and cold and fishlike too. At the sight of Captain Crewe and Sara, that smile widened enormously. The lady who had recommended her school had told her a great many pleasing things about the young soldier. One of them was that he was wealthy and quite ready to spend a very large sum on his little girl.

Taking Sara's hand and stroking it, she said, "Captain Crewe, it will be a great privilege to care for so beautiful and promising a child. Lady Meredith has spoken of her exceptional intelligence. For a school such as mine, a clever child is a real treasure."
Without moving or speaking, Sara kept her gaze on Miss Minchin's face. As usual, an odd thought was passing through her mind.

"Why is she calling me a beautiful child?" she wondered. "I'm not beautiful in the least. Isobel, Colonel Grange's little girl, is beautiful. Her cheeks are rosy, she has dimples, and her long hair is golden. My hair is short and black, and my eyes are green. Besides, I'm thin, and there's nothing fair about me. Hardly any child I've ever seen is as ugly as I am. She's telling a story to begin with."

But Sara was wrong about her ugliness. She looked nothing like Isobel Grange, the regiment's little beauty, yet she possessed a curious charm all her own. Slim and graceful, she was rather tall for seven, with a small face that was intense and appealing. Her thick hair was truly black and curled only at the ends. Her eyes were admittedly a greenish grey, but they were large, remarkable eyes, fringed with long black lashes. Sara might dislike their colour, but plenty of other people liked it very much. Nevertheless, she remained firmly convinced that she was an ugly little girl; Miss Minchin's compliments did nothing at all to lift her spirits.
"If I called her beautiful, I'd be telling a story," she thought, "and I'd know perfectly well it was a story. I think I'm just as ugly as she is, in my own way. Why would she say such a thing?"
With a longer acquaintance, Sara came to understand Miss Minchin's reason. She found that every father and mother who brought a child to the school heard precisely the same compliment.

Sara remained beside her father, listening to his conversation with Miss Minchin. The seminary had been chosen because Lady Meredith had sent both her little girls there, and Captain Crewe placed great trust in her experience. Sara would be what people called "a parlor boarder," with privileges beyond even those such pupils generally received. She would have a pretty bedroom and a sitting room to herself, a pony and carriage, and a maid in place of the ayah who had looked after her in India.

Holding Sara's hand and patting it, Captain Crewe gave his cheerful laugh. "Her education doesn't worry me at all," he said. "Your difficulty will be stopping her from learning too much, too quickly. She sits for ever with that little nose buried in a book. She doesn't read books, Miss Minchin—she devours them, like a small wolf instead of a little girl. She's always hungry for more, and it's grown-up books she wants: huge, thick volumes in French and German as well as English, history, biography, poets, and everything you can imagine. When she's reading too much, pull her away from it. Send her to ride her pony in the Row, or out to buy herself another doll. She ought to spend more time playing with dolls."
"But papa," Sara explained, "if I bought myself a new doll every few days, I'd soon have more dolls than I could love. They ought to be intimate friends. That's what Emily is going to be to me."
Captain Crewe glanced across at Miss Minchin, and she returned his look.
"And who is Emily?" she asked.
Smiling, Captain Crewe said, "You tell her, Sara."
As Sara replied, her green-grey eyes grew very solemn, and tender too.

"She's a doll I don't have yet," she explained. "Papa is going to buy her for me, and we're going out to find her together. I've named her Emily. When papa has gone away, she'll be my friend. I need her so I can talk to her about him."
Miss Minchin's broad, fishlike smile now took on a positively admiring look.
"Such an original child!" she exclaimed. "Such a darling little creature!"
Drawing Sara against him, Captain Crewe said, "Yes, she is a darling little creature. Please look after her very carefully for me, Miss Minchin."

For several days Sara lived with her father at his hotel; she stayed, in fact, right up until his departure for India. Together they visited one big shop after another and bought an extraordinary number of things—far more, indeed, than she could possibly need. But Captain Crewe was an impulsive, innocent young man. Everything his little girl admired, and everything he admired himself, he wanted her to have. Between them they assembled clothes far too splendid for a seven-year-old. There were velvet dresses edged with expensive fur, dresses of lace, dresses with embroidery, hats trailing great soft ostrich feathers, ermine coats and muffs, and boxes of little gloves, handkerchiefs, and silk stockings in enormous quantities. Behind the counters, the courteous young women whispered together. Surely that odd little girl with the big, serious eyes must be a foreign princess at the very least—perhaps an Indian rajah's little daughter.
Eventually they found Emily. But first there were several toy shops to visit and a great many dolls to inspect before she appeared.

"I want her to look as though she isn't really a doll," Sara explained. "When I talk, I want her to seem as though she LISTENS. What's wrong with dolls, papa"—she tilted her head, considering the matter as she spoke—"what's wrong with them is that they never seem to HEAR." So their search took in dolls both large and small, with blue eyes or black ones, with brown curls or golden plaits, some fully dressed and others without any clothes.

While they were studying an undressed doll, Sara said, "You see, if the one I find hasn't any frocks, we could go to a dressmaker and have them made especially for her. They'll fit so much better if she tries them on."

After several disappointments, they chose to continue on foot, looking through the shop windows while the cab followed behind. They passed two or three shops without going inside at all. Then, as they came towards a shop that was actually quite small, Sara gave a sudden start and caught hold of her father's arm.
"Oh, papa!" she exclaimed. "Emily is there!"
Colour rushed into her cheeks. In her green-grey eyes was the look of someone who had unexpectedly caught sight of a beloved and very familiar friend.
"She's been waiting right there for us!" Sara said. "Let's go inside to her."
"Dear me," Captain Crewe replied, "I almost feel we need somebody to make the introductions."
"You must introduce me, and then I'll introduce you," said Sara. "Though I recognized her as soon as I saw her—so perhaps she recognized me as well."

Perhaps Emily really had recognized her. At any rate, when Sara gathered her into her arms, the doll's eyes looked exceedingly intelligent. She was a big doll, though still small enough to carry comfortably. Her golden-brown hair curled naturally and fell all around her like a cloak. Her eyes were a clear, deep grey-blue, shaded by soft, thick lashes—actual eyelashes, rather than lines painted onto her face.
With Emily on her knee, Sara studied her face. "Of course, papa," she said, "of course this is Emily."

They bought Emily, and actually carried her to a shop selling children's clothes, where she was measured for an outfit every bit as fine as Sara's. She, too, received lace frocks, and others in velvet and muslin, along with hats, coats, lovely lace-edged underclothes, gloves, handkerchiefs, and furs.
"I'd like her always to look like a child whose mother takes good care of her," Sara said. "I'm her mother, even though I mean to make her my companion."

Captain Crewe could have taken enormous pleasure in all that shopping if one unhappy thought had not kept pulling at his heart. Every purchase meant that the parting from his dear, curious little companion was drawing nearer.

In the middle of the night he left his bed and stood gazing down at Sara as she slept, holding Emily in her arms. Sara's black hair lay across the pillow, mingling with Emily's golden-brown curls. Each wore a nightgown with lace ruffles, and each had long eyelashes resting against her cheeks and curling upwards. Emily looked so much like a living child that Captain Crewe was thankful she was there. With a deep sigh, he tugged at his moustache, a boyish look on his face.
"Heigh-ho, little Sara!" he murmured to himself. "I don't think you realize how terribly your daddy is going to miss you."

The following day he brought Sara to Miss Minchin's and left her in her care. His ship was sailing the next morning. He told Miss Minchin that his English affairs were managed by his solicitors, Messrs. Barrow & Skipworth. They would provide any advice she needed and settle whatever bills she sent for Sara. He would send his daughter two letters every week, and she must be allowed any pleasure she requested.
"She's a sensible little thing," he explained, "and nothing she asks for is ever anything it would be unsafe to let her have."
Afterwards he went with Sara to her little sitting room for their farewell. She sat on his knee, gripping his coat lapels in her small hands, and studied his face intently for a long time.
Stroking her hair, he asked, "Are you trying to learn me by heart, little Sara?"
"No," she told him. "I know you by heart already. You're inside my heart." They wrapped their arms around one another and kissed as though neither would ever release the other.

As the cab pulled away, Sara sat on her sitting-room floor, her chin resting on her hands, and watched until it vanished around a corner of the square. Beside her sat Emily, watching it go as well. Miss Minchin sent her sister, Miss Amelia, up to discover what the child was doing. When she arrived, the door would not open.
From inside came a curious, courteous little voice. "I've locked the door," it said. "If you please, I would like to be entirely alone."

Miss Amelia was fat and short and lived in considerable awe of her sister. Of the two she was really the kinder, yet she would never go against Miss Minchin. She returned downstairs with a look of something very like alarm.
"Sister, I've never met such a strange, old-fashioned child," she said. "She's locked herself into her room, and there isn't the tiniest sound coming from her."

"That is a great improvement on kicking and screaming, as some children do," replied Miss Minchin. "I thought one so thoroughly spoiled would throw the entire house into an uproar. If any child has ever had everything her own way, this one has."

"I've been unpacking her trunks and putting away her belongings," Miss Amelia said. "I've never seen anything like those clothes—coats trimmed with sable and ermine, and genuine Valenciennes lace on her underclothes. You've seen a few of her things yourself. What DO you make of them?"

"I consider them quite ridiculous," Miss Minchin said sharply. "Still, they will make a very good appearance at the front of the line when we walk the schoolchildren to church on Sundays. She has been outfitted exactly like a little princess."

Upstairs, behind the locked door, Sara and Emily remained on the floor, staring at the corner where the cab had gone out of sight. Captain Crewe, meanwhile, kept looking back, waving and blowing kisses, as though he could not bring himself to stop.

chapters.title: A French Lesson
paragraphs: When Sara came into the schoolroom the following morning, every girl watched her with wide, curious eyes. They had all heard plenty about her already, from Lavinia Herbert, almost thirteen and convinced she was quite grown up, down to four-year-old Lottie Legh, the school's baby. They knew without a doubt that Miss Minchin meant to show her off as a credit to the school. A girl or two had even glimpsed Mariette, her French maid, who had arrived the previous evening. Lavinia had contrived to walk past Sara's open door and catch sight of Mariette unpacking a box delivered late from one of the shops.

"It was packed with petticoats covered in lace frills—rows and rows of them," she whispered to her friend Jessie, bending over her geography book. "I watched her shake them out. Miss Minchin told Miss Amelia, and I heard her, that those clothes were so grand they were ridiculous for a child. My mamma says a child ought to dress simply. She's wearing one of those petticoats this minute. I caught sight of it as she sat down."
Jessie bent over her geography book too. "She's wearing silk stockings!" she whispered. "And such tiny feet! I've never seen feet so small."

Lavinia gave a spiteful sniff. "Oh, that's just how her slippers are shaped. My mamma says a clever shoemaker can make even large feet seem small. I don't find her pretty in the least. What a strange colour her eyes are."

"She isn't pretty in the usual sort of way," Jessie said, sneaking another look across the room. "But you feel like looking at her again. Her eyelashes are amazingly long, though her eyes are practically green."

In her place near Miss Minchin's desk, Sara waited quietly for instructions. All those watching eyes did not embarrass her in the least. Curious herself, she calmly returned the other children's looks. What, she wondered, were they thinking? Did they like Miss Minchin? Did they enjoy their lessons? And did any of them have a papa anything like hers? Earlier that morning she had talked to Emily about her father for a long time.

"Emily, he's out at sea now," she had told her. "You and I must be the very best of friends and tell one another everything. Look at me, Emily. No one has nicer eyes than yours—but how I wish you could talk."

Her head was full of imaginary worlds and curious ideas. One of these was that simply pretending Emily was alive, and could truly hear and understand, might be a great comfort. Mariette dressed her in a dark-blue frock for lessons and fastened a dark-blue ribbon in her hair. Then Sara went over to Emily, seated in a chair of her own, and handed her a book.
"Here's something to read while I'm downstairs," she told her. Noticing Mariette's curious gaze, she turned to explain, with a very serious little face.

"I think dolls can do all sorts of things they keep hidden from us," she said. "Perhaps Emily really knows how to read and speak and walk, but waits until everyone has left the room before she does any of it. It's her secret. After all, if people found out what dolls could do, they'd put them to work. Perhaps the dolls have all promised one another never to tell. While you're here, Emily will only sit and stare. Once you leave, though, she may start reading or walk over to look through the window. If she heard either of us coming back, she'd hurry to her chair, jump up into it, and make believe she'd been sitting there the whole time."

"Comme elle est drole!" Mariette thought, and later, downstairs, she repeated the story to the head housemaid. Already, though, she was growing fond of this unusual little girl, with her clever small face and faultless manners. Other children she had cared for had been far less courteous. Sara was a very fine little person. There was something delightful in the gentle gratitude with which she said, "If you please, Mariette," and "Thank you, Mariette." As Mariette explained to the head housemaid, the child thanked her exactly as she would thank a lady.
"Elle a l'air d'une princesse, cette petite," she said. In fact, her new little mistress pleased her very much indeed, and she was delighted with her position.
A few minutes passed while Sara sat under the other pupils' gaze. Then Miss Minchin gave a dignified tap on her desk to call for attention.

"Young ladies," she announced, "let me introduce your new companion." Every little girl stood beside her seat, and Sara got up too. "I expect you all to make yourselves most agreeable to Miss Crewe. She has travelled a very long way to join us—all the way from India, in fact. When lessons finish, you must get to know one another."
The other pupils made formal bows, and Sara answered with a small curtsy. Then everyone sat down and resumed looking at everyone else.
In her classroom voice, Miss Minchin said, "Sara, come over here to me."
She had lifted a book from her desk and was leafing through it. Sara approached with quiet courtesy.
"Since your papa has hired a French maid to attend you," she began, "I assume he wants you to pay particular attention to studying French."
Sara felt rather uncomfortable.
"I believe he chose her because he—he thought I would like her, Miss Minchin," she replied.

With a faintly sour smile, Miss Minchin said, "I'm afraid you have been a very spoiled little girl. You always suppose things are arranged simply to please you. I believe your papa's intention was for you to learn French."

Had Sara been a little older, or less determined to show perfect politeness to everyone, a few words would have settled the misunderstanding. Instead she felt her cheeks grow hot. Miss Minchin was stern and imposing. She seemed so completely certain that Sara knew no French at all that contradicting her felt almost impolite. In fact, Sara could remember no time when French had seemed unfamiliar. Her father had spoken it to her often, even when she was a baby. Her mother had been French, and Captain Crewe loved her language; so Sara had always heard it around her and had grown up knowing it.
"I—I haven't exactly studied French, but—but—" she started, making a timid effort to explain.

Not knowing how to speak French herself was one of Miss Minchin's most deeply irritating secrets, and she was anxious to keep it hidden. She had no wish to pursue the subject and risk innocent questions from a little pupil who had only just arrived.

"Enough," she replied, tart beneath her politeness. "If you have never learned it, you must start immediately. Monsieur Dufarge, our French master, is due in a few minutes. Take this book and study it while you wait for him."

Her cheeks burning, Sara returned to her place and opened the book. With a solemn face she examined its opening page. To smile would be rude, she knew, and she was determined to avoid rudeness. Yet how strange to be set to study a page explaining that "le pere" was "the father" and "la mere" was "the mother."
Miss Minchin gave her a searching look.
"Sara, you seem rather bad-tempered," she remarked. "I'm sorry that learning French is such an unwelcome prospect."
Deciding to make another attempt, Sara replied, "I like it very much indeed, but—"
"When someone tells you to do something, you mustn't answer 'but,'" Miss Minchin said. "Return your attention to the book."
Sara obeyed. She kept from smiling even at the information that "le fils" was "the son" and "le frere" was "the brother."
"Once Monsieur Dufarge gets here," she thought, "I'll be able to explain it to him."

Monsieur Dufarge appeared soon afterwards. A pleasant, intelligent Frenchman of middle age, he noticed Sara with interest as she made a courteous effort to look completely absorbed in the little phrase book.
"Have you a new pupil for me, madame?" he asked Miss Minchin. "I hope I am that fortunate."

Miss Minchin replied, "Her papa, Captain Crewe, is most eager for her to start learning the language. Unfortunately, she seems to have a childish dislike of it. I'm afraid she shows little willingness to learn."
Turning kindly to Sara, he said, "That makes me sorry, mademoiselle. Perhaps, once our lessons begin, I shall be able to show you how charming a language it is."

Little Sara stood up. She was growing quite desperate, with the feeling that she was almost in disgrace. Raising her large green-grey eyes to Monsieur Dufarge's face, she looked at him with innocent appeal. The moment she spoke, she knew, he would understand. In lovely, fluent French, she gave a simple explanation. Madame had misunderstood her. She had never exactly studied French—not from books—but her papa and other people had always used it when they spoke to her. She had read and written it just as she had English. Her papa loved the language, and she loved it for his sake. Her dear mamma, who had died at her birth, was French. She would gladly learn whatever monsieur cared to teach her. All she had meant to tell madame was that the words in this particular book were already familiar to her. As she said it, she offered him the little phrase book.

At Sara's first words Miss Minchin gave a violent start. She stared over her spectacles, looking almost offended, and went on staring until the explanation ended. Monsieur Dufarge, meanwhile, began to smile with unmistakable delight. That sweet child's voice, speaking his own tongue so naturally and charmingly, made him feel almost at home again. On London's dark, fog-bound days, his native country could seem worlds away. When Sara stopped speaking, he accepted the phrase book with a look bordering on affection. It was Miss Minchin, however, whom he addressed.
"Ah, madame," he said, "I can teach her very little. French is not something she has LEARNED; she is French herself. What an exquisite accent."
Deeply embarrassed, Miss Minchin turned on Sara. "You should have explained that to me," she exclaimed.
"I—I did try," Sara replied. "Perhaps I—I didn't begin in the proper way."

Miss Minchin knew perfectly well that Sara had tried. She knew, too, that the child was not to blame for being given no chance to explain. But the other pupils had been listening, and Lavinia and Jessie were laughing behind their French grammars. The sight filled her with fury.
She rapped sharply on the desk. "Silence, young ladies!" she commanded. "Be silent this instant!"
From that very moment, she began to bear a certain resentment towards her prize pupil.

chapters.title: Ermengarde
paragraphs: That first morning, while Sara sat beside Miss Minchin and the whole schoolroom busily studied her, she soon picked out one little girl of about her own age. The child was gazing hard at her with a pair of pale, rather dull blue eyes. She was plump and did not look the least bit clever, though her mouth had a good-natured pout to it. Her flaxen hair was plaited in a tight pigtail tied off with a ribbon. She had pulled the pigtail round to the front of her neck and was chewing the end of the ribbon, elbows propped on her desk, staring in wonder at the newcomer. When Monsieur Dufarge started speaking to Sara she looked rather alarmed. Then Sara stepped forward, lifted her innocent, pleading eyes to him, and answered him in French without the slightest warning, and the plump girl gave a startled jump and went bright red with astonished awe. For weeks she had cried hopeless tears over trying to remember that "la mere" meant "the mother" and "le pere" meant "the father"—when any sensible person spoke plain English. Now here was a child her own age who not only knew these words perfectly well but clearly knew a great many more, and tossed them into sentences with verbs as though it were nothing at all. It was nearly too much for her.
She stared so hard and chewed her ribbon so fast that she caught the eye of Miss Minchin, who was in a very bad temper just then and swooped down on her at once.
"Miss St. John!" she cried sharply. "What is the meaning of this behavior? Take your elbows off the desk! Get that ribbon out of your mouth! Sit up straight this instant!"

At that Miss St. John jumped again, and when Lavinia and Jessie snickered she turned redder than ever—so red that she looked close to tears in her poor, dull, childish eyes. Sara noticed, and felt so sorry for her that she began to like her and to want to be her friend. She had always been like that: she wanted to leap into any quarrel where somebody was being made to feel wretched.

"If Sara were a boy and had lived a few hundred years ago," her father used to say, "she would have ridden all over the country with her sword drawn, rescuing and defending everyone in trouble. The moment she sees someone in distress, she wants to fight."

So she took a liking to the fat, slow little Miss St. John, and kept glancing across at her all morning. She could see that lessons did not come easily to the girl, and that nobody would ever risk spoiling her by treating her as a star pupil. Her French lesson was pitiful. Her pronunciation made even Monsieur Dufarge smile despite himself, and Lavinia and Jessie and the other luckier girls either giggled or stared at her in amazed contempt. Sara never laughed. She did her best to look as though she hadn't heard when Miss St. John said "le bon pain" as "lee bong pang." She had a fiery little temper of her own, and hearing the snickering and seeing that poor, slow, miserable face made her feel quite fierce.
"It isn't funny, really," she said through clenched teeth, bending over her book. "They shouldn't laugh."

When lessons ended and the girls drew together in little groups to chat, Sara went looking for Miss St. John. She found her slumped rather forlornly in a window seat, walked over, and spoke to her. She only said the sort of thing little girls always say to start a friendship, but there was something warm about Sara, and people always sensed it.
"What's your name?" she asked.

To understand Miss St. John's amazement, you have to remember that a new pupil is, for a little while, something of a mystery. The whole school had talked about this one the night before until everyone fell asleep worn out with excitement and conflicting stories. A new pupil with a carriage and a pony and a maid, and a sea voyage from India to talk about, was not at all an ordinary person to meet.
"My name is Ermengarde St. John," she answered.
"Mine is Sara Crewe," said Sara. "Yours is very pretty. It sounds like something from a storybook."
"Do you like it?" Ermengarde said in a flutter. "I—I like yours."

The great trouble of Miss St. John's life was that she had a clever father. At times it felt to her like a terrible misfortune. When your father knows everything, speaks seven or eight languages, and owns thousands of books he seems to have learned by heart, he usually expects you to know at least what is in your own schoolbooks. He is quite likely to think you should be able to remember a few events from history and write a French exercise. Ermengarde was a heavy disappointment to Mr. St. John. He could not grasp how a child of his could be so plainly and hopelessly dull, and never shine at anything.
"Good heavens!" he had said more than once, staring at her. "Sometimes I think she is as stupid as her Aunt Eliza!"

Her Aunt Eliza had apparently been slow to learn and quick to forget completely whatever she did learn, and Ermengarde was remarkably like her. She was the school's towering dunce, and there was no denying it.
"She must be MADE to learn," her father told Miss Minchin.

So Ermengarde spent most of her life either in disgrace or in tears. She learned things and forgot them, or if she did remember them she didn't understand them. It was only natural, then, that once she had met Sara she would sit and stare at her with deep admiration.
"You can speak French, can't you?" she said respectfully.
Sara climbed onto the window seat, which was big and deep, tucked up her feet, and sat with her arms wrapped around her knees.
"I can speak it because I've heard it all my life," she answered. "You could too, if you'd always heard it."
"Oh, no, I couldn't," said Ermengarde. "I could NEVER speak it!"
"Why not?" Sara asked, curious.
Ermengarde shook her head so hard that her pigtail swung.
"You just heard how I sound," she said. "It's always like that with me. The words simply won't come out of my mouth right. They're so odd."
She paused for a moment, then added in an awed little voice, "You're CLEVER, aren't you?"

Sara looked out the window at the grimy square, where sparrows hopped and chirped along the wet iron railings and the sooty branches of the trees. She thought for a few moments. People had told her very often that she was "clever," and she wondered whether she really was—and IF she was, how it had come about.
"I don't know," she said. "I can't say." Then she saw the gloomy look on the round, chubby face, laughed a little, and changed the subject.
"Would you like to meet Emily?" she asked.
"Who's Emily?" Ermengarde asked, exactly as Miss Minchin had.
"Come up to my room and see," said Sara, holding out her hand.
They hopped down from the window seat together and went upstairs.
"Is it true," Ermengarde whispered as they crossed the hall, "that you have a playroom all to yourself?"

"Yes," Sara answered. "Papa asked Miss Minchin to give me one, because—well, because when I play I make up stories and tell them to myself, and I don't like anyone to overhear. It ruins it if I think someone is listening."
By now they had reached the passage that led to Sara's room, and Ermengarde stopped dead, gaping, quite out of breath.
"You MAKE up stories!" she gasped. "You can do that—as well as speak French? CAN you?"
Sara looked at her in plain surprise.
"Well, anyone can make things up," she said. "Haven't you ever tried?"
She laid her hand on Ermengarde's in warning.
"Let's go to the door very quietly," she whispered, "and then I'll throw it open all at once. Maybe we'll catch her."

She was half laughing, but a look of mysterious hope in her eyes held Ermengarde spellbound, even though she hadn't the faintest idea what it meant, or who it was Sara hoped to "catch," or why. Whatever Sara meant, Ermengarde felt certain it was something wonderfully exciting. So, tingling with expectation, she followed on tiptoe down the passage. They didn't make the slightest sound until they reached the door. Then Sara turned the handle quickly and flung it wide. Inside lay the room, tidy and quiet, with a fire burning softly in the grate and a magnificent doll seated in a chair beside it, seemingly absorbed in a book.
"Oh, she got back to her chair before we could see her!" Sara explained. "Of course, they always do. They're quick as lightning."
Ermengarde looked from Sara to the doll and back again.
"Can she—walk?" she asked, breathless.
"Yes," said Sara. "Well, I think she can. Or at least I PRETEND I think so. And that makes it feel as if it's true. Haven't you ever pretended things?"
"No," said Ermengarde. "Never. I—tell me about it."
This odd new friend had her so enchanted that she actually watched Sara instead of Emily—even though Emily was the loveliest doll she had ever laid eyes on.

"Let's sit down," said Sara, "and I'll tell you. It's so easy that once you start, you can't stop. You just keep doing it forever. And it's wonderful. Emily, you must listen. This is Ermengarde St. John, Emily. Ermengarde, this is Emily. Would you like to hold her?"
"Oh, may I?" said Ermengarde. "May I, really? She's lovely!" And Emily was placed in her arms.
Never in her dull little life had Miss St. John imagined an hour like the one she spent with this peculiar new pupil, before the lunch bell rang and they had to go downstairs.

Sara sat on the hearth rug and told her wonderful things. She sat hunched up, with her green eyes shining and her cheeks glowing. She told stories about the voyage and about India. But what captivated Ermengarde most was her notion of the dolls who walked and talked and did whatever they liked when no humans were in the room, but who had to keep their powers secret, and so darted back to their places "like lightning" whenever people came back in.
"WE couldn't do it," said Sara, in all seriousness. "You see, it's a kind of magic."

Once, as she was telling the story of how she had searched for Emily, Ermengarde watched her face suddenly change. A shadow seemed to cross it and put out the light in her shining eyes. She drew a breath so sharply that it made a funny, sad little sound, then pressed her lips together and held them tight, as if she were determined either to do something or NOT to do it. Ermengarde thought that had Sara been any other little girl, she might have burst into sobs and tears just then. But Sara did not.
"Do you have a—a pain?" Ermengarde ventured.

"Yes," Sara answered, after a silent moment. "But it isn't in my body." Then she added something in a low voice, which she tried hard to keep steady. This is what she said: "Do you love your father more than anything else in the whole wide world?"

Ermengarde's mouth dropped open slightly. She knew that a respectable child at a select seminary could hardly confess that it had never occurred to her that she COULD love her father, or that she would do nearly anything to avoid being left alone with him for ten minutes. She was truly embarrassed.
"I—I hardly ever see him," she stammered. "He's always in the library, reading things."
"I love mine ten times more than anything in the world," Sara said. "That's what my pain is. He's gone away."
She quietly lowered her head onto her small, hunched-up knees and sat very still for a few minutes.
"She's going to cry out loud," thought Ermengarde, frightened.
But Sara did not. Her short black curls tumbled around her ears, and she sat motionless. Then she spoke without lifting her head.

"I promised him I would bear it," she said. "And I will. You have to bear things. Think of what soldiers put up with! Papa is a soldier. If there were a war, he'd have to endure long marches and thirst and maybe terrible wounds. And he would never say a word—not one single word."
Ermengarde could only look at her, but she felt herself starting to adore her. She was so marvelous, and so unlike anyone else.
After a while Sara raised her face and shook back her black curls, with a strange little smile.
"If I keep talking and talking," she said, "and telling you about pretending, I'll bear it better. You don't forget, but you bear it better."
Ermengarde didn't know why a lump rose in her throat and her eyes felt as though tears were gathering in them.

"Lavinia and Jessie are 'best friends,'" she said, rather huskily. "I wish we could be 'best friends.' Would you pick me for yours? You're clever, and I'm the stupidest child in the school, but I—oh, I do like you so much!"
"I'm glad," said Sara. "It makes you thankful when someone likes you. Yes. We'll be friends. And I'll tell you what"—a sudden gleam lit her face—"I can help you with your French lessons."

chapters.title: Lottie
paragraphs: For a different sort of child, the next few years at Miss Minchin's Select Seminary might have been very harmful. Sara was treated like an honoured guest, rather than an ordinary little girl at school. A child already inclined to be conceited and bossy could have become unbearable under so much flattery and indulgence. A lazy one would have learned nothing at all. Miss Minchin secretly disliked Sara, but she understood the world too well to say or do anything that might drive so valuable a pupil away. If Sara wrote to her papa that she was unhappy or uncomfortable, she knew Captain Crewe would take her away immediately. In Miss Minchin's view, constant praise and complete freedom to do as she pleased must make a child love the place that treated her so well. So Sara was praised for learning quickly, for her manners, for being pleasant to the other girls, and for generosity whenever she took sixpence from her well-filled little purse to give a beggar. The most ordinary action was applauded as a virtue. Without her own good nature and clever little mind, she might have become extremely pleased with herself. But that clever mind supplied a great many sensible, truthful observations about herself and her situation. As time passed, she sometimes discussed these with Ermengarde.

"A person's life is full of accidents," she would say. "I've had a lot of happy ones. It just HAPPENED that I enjoyed books and lessons, and remembered what I learned. It just happened that my father was handsome and kind and clever, and could afford everything I wanted. Perhaps I haven't a good temper at all, really. But when you have everything you wish for and everybody treats you kindly, what is there to make you bad-tempered?" She looked very serious. "I don't know how I'll ever discover whether I'm truly a nice child or a horrid one. I might be a HIDEOUS child, and nobody will find out, simply because I never have anything to try me."
Ermengarde answered stolidly, "Nothing tries Lavinia either, and she's quite horrid enough."
Sara considered this, thoughtfully rubbing the very tip of her small nose.

At last she said, "Well, perhaps—perhaps it's because Lavinia is GROWING." Kindly, she had remembered hearing Miss Amelia say that Lavinia was growing so quickly that it seemed to be affecting both her health and her temper.

The truth was that Lavinia was spiteful, and her jealousy of Sara knew no bounds. Before the newcomer arrived, she had considered herself the school's leader. She had secured that position by making herself extremely unpleasant whenever the others refused to follow. She bullied the small children and put on important airs with the girls old enough to be her companions. Rather pretty herself, she had also been the best-dressed pupil in the Select Seminary's procession when they went out two by two. Then came Sara's velvet coats, sable muffs, and drooping ostrich feathers, walking beside Miss Minchin at the front. That had been bitter enough at first. As the months passed, however, it became clear that Sara was another leader—not because she could make herself unpleasant, but because she never did.

Jessie had infuriated her "best friend" with an honest remark. "There's this about Sara Crewe: she never puts on the slightest airs, although you know she could, Lavvie. If I owned all those beautiful things and everyone made that fuss over me, I think I'd have to be a little grand myself. The way Miss Minchin parades her in front of visiting parents is disgusting."

In her most exaggerated Miss Minchin voice, Lavinia mimicked, "'Dear Sara must come into the drawing room and talk to Mrs. Musgrave about India.' 'Dear Sara must speak French to Lady Pitkin. Her accent is so perfect.' Well, at least she didn't get that French from the Seminary. And knowing it doesn't make her clever. She admits herself that she never learned it. She only picked it up from hearing her papa use it all the time. And speaking of her papa, being an Indian officer isn't anything so magnificent."

Jessie answered slowly, "Well, he's killed tigers. The skin in Sara's room came from one he killed himself. That's why she loves it. She lies down on it, pats its head, and speaks to it just as though it were a cat."
"Everything she does is silly," Lavinia snapped. "My mamma says all that pretending of hers is silly. She says she'll turn into an eccentric."

It was true: Sara never put on airs. Friendly by nature, she gladly shared both her possessions and her privileges. The smallest children were used to being scorned and told to move aside by grown-up ladies of ten and twelve. Yet the most envied girl in the school never brought them to tears. There was something motherly about her. If a child fell and grazed a knee, Sara hurried over to pick her up and pat her, or searched her pocket for a bonbon or something else that might comfort her. She did not shove the little ones aside or speak of their age as though it were a disgrace and a stain on their characters.

It must be admitted that on one occasion Lavinia slapped Lottie and called her "a brat." Sara told her sternly, "If you're four, you're four. Next year you'll be five, and the year after you'll be six. And," she added, widening her eyes with a look that convicted the offender, "you need sixteen whole years to get to twenty."
"Dear me, aren't we good at arithmetic!" Lavinia replied. Yet no one could dispute that four and sixteen did make twenty—and even the boldest girls hardly dared to imagine being twenty.

The younger children consequently adored Sara. More than once she gave a tea party in her room for these disregarded little people. They were allowed to play with Emily and use her own tea service, the one with blue flowers on the cups, which held a surprisingly generous amount of weak, very sweet tea. None of them had ever seen a doll's tea set so wonderfully like a real one. From the afternoon of that treat, the entire alphabet class looked upon Sara as both goddess and queen.

Lottie Legh's devotion was so intense that a girl less motherly than Sara might have found it exhausting. Lottie's rather frivolous young papa had sent her away to school because he could think of nothing else to do with her. Her young mother was dead. From the hour she was born, Lottie had been treated like a cherished doll, or an outrageously spoiled pet monkey or lapdog, and she had become a truly alarming little creature. Wanting something made her cry and howl; not wanting something did the same. And since she invariably wanted what she could not have, and objected to what was best for her, her shrill wailing generally rang out from one part of the house or another.

Her most powerful weapon came from a discovery she had somehow made: a very little girl without a mother deserved pity and special attention. Probably she had overheard grown-ups discussing her soon after her mother's death. Whatever the source, she formed the habit of turning that knowledge to very good use.

Sara first took charge of her one morning while passing a sitting room. Inside, both Miss Minchin and Miss Amelia were trying to quiet the furious cries of a child who plainly meant to go on crying. Indeed, the resistance was so determined that Miss Minchin could barely make herself heard without shouting, though she shouted with proper dignity and severity.
"What IS making her cry?" she demanded, almost at a yell.
Sara heard the answer: "Oh—oh—oh! I haven't got any mam—ma-a!"
Miss Amelia shrieked, "Oh, Lottie! Please stop, darling! Don't cry! Please, don't!"
"Oh! Oh! Oh! Oh! Oh!" came Lottie's storm of howls. "Haven't—got—any—mam—ma-a!"
"She deserves a whipping," Miss Minchin declared. "You naughty child, you SHALL have one!"

Lottie's cries grew louder still, and Miss Amelia began crying too. Miss Minchin raised her voice until it was nearly a thunderclap. Then, furious at her own helplessness, she suddenly jumped from her chair and swept out, leaving Miss Amelia to settle the affair.

Out in the hall, Sara had stopped to consider whether she should go in. She and Lottie had lately become friends, and perhaps she could soothe her. When Miss Minchin emerged and saw Sara waiting, she looked distinctly annoyed. She knew that her voice coming through the door could have sounded neither dignified nor kindly.
Trying to arrange an appropriate smile, she exclaimed, "Oh, Sara!"
"I waited because I recognized Lottie," Sara explained. "I thought that perhaps—only perhaps—I could get her to stop crying. May I have a try, Miss Minchin?"

Miss Minchin tightened her lips. "You'll be a clever child if you succeed," she answered. Sara looked a little discouraged by the sharpness, and Miss Minchin noticed. She adopted an approving tone instead. "But then you're clever at everything. I expect you can deal with her. Go in." With that, she walked away.

Inside the room, Sara found Lottie stretched on the floor, shrieking and violently kicking her plump little legs. Miss Amelia bent over her in distress and despair, red-faced and damp with heat. Back in her own nursery, Lottie had always discovered that a fit of screaming and kicking would end in her getting exactly what she demanded. Poor, plump Miss Amelia was trying one approach after another.

One moment she was saying, "Poor darling, I know there's no mamma for you, poor—" Then her tone would change completely. "Lottie, if you go on like this, I'll shake you. Poor little angel! There—! You wicked, bad, hateful child, I'll smack you! I really will!"

Sara approached without a sound. She had no clear idea of what to do, but somewhere inside she felt that it would help to avoid all these wildly different remarks, delivered with such helpless agitation.
She spoke softly. "Miss Amelia, Miss Minchin has said I may try to quiet her. May I try now?"
Miss Amelia turned a hopeless face towards her. "Oh, DO you really think you can manage it?" she gasped.
Still speaking almost in a whisper, Sara replied, "I don't know if I CAN, but I'm willing to try."
With a weary sigh, Miss Amelia struggled up from her knees. Lottie's little fat legs went on kicking just as fiercely.
"If you slip quietly away," Sara told her, "I'll stay here with Lottie."
Miss Amelia's reply was almost a whimper. "Oh, Sara! We've never had a child so dreadful. I can't see how we can keep her here."
Nevertheless, she tiptoed out, enormously grateful to have been given a reason to leave the room.

For a little while Sara remained standing, silently watching the angry, howling child. Then she lowered herself onto the floor at Lottie's side and waited. Apart from those furious shrieks, there was no sound at all. Little Miss Legh had never experienced this before. Her screams usually brought a succession of protests, pleading, orders, and coaxing. To kick and scream while the only person nearby seemed entirely undisturbed was enough to catch her attention. She opened her tightly squeezed, tear-streaming eyes to discover who it was. Only another little girl—but the girl who had Emily and all those lovely possessions. This girl was watching steadily, as if she were simply thinking. After the few seconds it took to establish all this, Lottie felt she ought to start again. Yet the stillness of the room and Sara's curious, attentive face robbed her first renewed howl of much of its energy.
"I—haven't—any—ma—ma—ma-a!" she declared, though with less strength behind it.
Sara's gaze grew steadier still, and something like understanding appeared in her eyes.
"I haven't one either," she replied.

The answer was so unexpected that Lottie was astonished. Her legs actually dropped; she wriggled and lay staring. A fresh idea can quiet a crying child when everything else fails. Besides, Lottie disliked cross Miss Minchin and foolishly indulgent Miss Amelia, while she rather liked Sara, despite hardly knowing her. She was unwilling to surrender her complaint, but her thoughts had wandered away from it. With another wriggle and one sulky sob, she asked, "Where is she?"
For a moment Sara was silent. Having been told that her mamma was in heaven, she had given the subject a great deal of thought. Her ideas about it were not quite the same as other people's.

"She's gone to heaven," she replied. "But I'm certain she comes out to visit me sometimes, even though I can't see her. Your mamma does too. Perhaps they're both watching us this very minute. They might both be here in the room."

Lottie sat straight up and searched the room with her eyes. She was a pretty little thing with curly hair, and her round eyes looked like rain-wet forget-me-nots. Had her mamma watched the previous half-hour, she might have doubted whether such a child was a fitting relation for an angel.

Sara kept talking. To some people her account might have sounded much like a fairy tale. To her own imagination, however, it was so completely real that Lottie found herself listening despite herself. She had heard that her mamma wore a crown and had wings; she had also been shown pictures of ladies in lovely white nightgowns and told they were angels. What Sara described seemed instead a true story of a beautiful country inhabited by real people.

"There are flowers in field after field," she said. As always when a story began, she forgot herself and spoke almost as if dreaming. "Field after field of lilies. A gentle wind passes over them and carries their smell into the air, and everyone breathes it all the time, because that gentle wind never stops. Little children play among the lilies, picking great armfuls, laughing, and weaving little wreaths. The streets shine. Nobody ever gets tired, no matter how far they walk, and they can float wherever they choose. All around the city stand walls of pearl and gold, low enough for people to lean over. They look down at the earth and smile, and send lovely messages to the people below."

Whatever tale Sara had chosen, Lottie would doubtless have stopped crying and listened, spellbound. But this one was undeniably lovelier than most. She edged closer to Sara and swallowed every word until the ending arrived—much too soon. Her disappointment was so great that her lip began to jut out in a threatening way.
"I want to be there," she cried. "Here at school I—I haven't any mamma."
Recognizing the warning, Sara returned from her dream. With a small, coaxing laugh, she took Lottie's chubby hand and drew the child close against her.
"Then I'll be your mamma," she said. "Let's pretend you're my little girl, and we'll make Emily your sister."
All at once, every one of Lottie's dimples appeared.
"Will she really?" she asked.
Sara sprang up. "Yes," she answered. "Come and tell her with me. Afterwards I'll wash your face and brush your hair."

Lottie accepted this quite happily and trotted out of the room and upstairs beside her. She seemed to have forgotten completely that the whole tragedy of the past hour had begun with her refusal to be washed and brushed before lunch, and that Miss Minchin had been summoned to bring her majestic authority to bear.
That was how Sara acquired an adopted daughter.

chapters.title: Becky
paragraphs: Of all Sara's gifts, the greatest was her talent for telling stories and for making everything she described feel like a story, whether it was one or not. It won her even more followers than her luxuries or her title of "the show pupil," and it was the thing Lavinia and some of the other girls envied most, while being drawn to it against their will.

Anyone who has gone to school with a born storyteller knows the magic of it: how the child is followed around and begged in whispers for tales, and how little groups gather and hover at the edges of the favored circle, hoping to be let in to listen. Sara could tell stories, and she loved telling them. When she sat or stood in the middle of a ring of listeners and began inventing marvels, her green eyes grew wide and bright, her cheeks flushed, and without realizing it she began to act out the tale, making it lovely or frightening by raising or lowering her voice, bending and swaying her slender body, and moving her hands dramatically. She forgot she was talking to a circle of children. She saw the fairy folk, or the kings and queens and beautiful ladies whose adventures she was telling, and lived among them. Sometimes when she finished a story she was quite breathless with excitement, and she would press a hand to her thin little chest as it rose and fell quickly, and half laugh at herself.

"When I'm telling it," she would say, "it doesn't feel as if I've only made it up. It feels more real than you are—more real than the schoolroom. I feel as if I were every person in the story, one after another. It's strange."

She had been at Miss Minchin's school for about two years when, on a foggy winter afternoon, she stepped out of her carriage, snugly wrapped in her warmest velvets and furs and looking far grander than she realized. As she crossed the pavement she noticed a grubby little figure on the area steps, craning its neck so that a pair of wide-open eyes could peer at her through the railings. Something in the eagerness and shyness of that smudged face made her look, and when she looked she smiled, because it was her habit to smile at people.

But the owner of the smudged face and wide eyes was plainly afraid she shouldn't have been caught gazing at important pupils. She ducked out of sight like a jack-in-the-box and scurried back into the kitchen, vanishing so suddenly that, had she not been such a poor, forlorn creature, Sara would have laughed in spite of herself. That very evening Sara was sitting in a corner of the schoolroom among a group of listeners, telling one of her stories, when the same figure crept timidly into the room carrying a coal box far too heavy for her and knelt on the hearth rug to build up the fire and sweep the ashes.

She was cleaner than she had been when she peeped through the railings, but she looked just as frightened. She obviously dared not look at the children or seem to be listening. She laid on pieces of coal carefully with her fingers so as not to make any noise, and she moved the fire irons about very softly. But within two minutes Sara could see that she was deeply interested in what was going on, and that she was working slowly in the hope of catching a word here and there. Realizing this, Sara raised her voice and spoke more distinctly.
"The Mermaids swam gently through the crystal-green water, dragging behind them a fishing net woven of deep-sea pearls," she said. "The Princess sat on the white rock and watched them."
The tale was a marvelous one, about a princess whom a Prince Merman loved, and who went to make her home with him in the glittering caverns beneath the waves.

The little drudge at the grate swept the hearth once, then swept it again. When she had done it twice she did it a third time, and as she did, the sound of the story drew her in so completely that she forgot she had no right to be listening at all, and forgot everything else besides. She sank back on her heels where she knelt, and the brush hung loose in her fingers. The storyteller's voice carried on and drew her with it into winding grottoes under the sea, glowing with soft, clear blue light and floored with pure golden sand. Strange sea flowers and grasses swayed around her, and from far away came the faint echo of singing and music.
The hearth brush dropped from her work-roughened hand, and Lavinia Herbert glanced around.
"That girl has been listening," she said.
The guilty girl snatched up her brush and scrambled to her feet. She grabbed the coal box and scuttled from the room like a startled rabbit.
Sara felt her temper flare.
"I knew she was listening," she said. "Why shouldn't she?"
Lavinia tossed her head very elegantly.
"Well," she said, "I don't know whether your mamma would like you telling stories to servant girls, but I know MY mamma wouldn't like ME doing it."
"My mamma!" said Sara, with a strange look. "I don't think she'd mind in the slightest. She knows stories belong to everybody."
"I thought," Lavinia shot back, with grim memory, "that your mamma was dead. How can she know anything?"
"Do you think she DOESN'T know things?" said Sara, in her stern little voice. Sometimes she had a rather stern little voice.

"Sara's mamma knows everything," Lottie piped up. "So does my mamma—except Sara is my mamma at Miss Minchin's—my other one knows everything. The streets are shining, and there are fields and fields of lilies, and everybody picks them. Sara tells me about it when she puts me to bed."
"You wicked thing," said Lavinia, turning on Sara. "Making up fairy tales about heaven."

"There are far more splendid stories in Revelation," Sara replied. "Just go and look! How do you know mine are fairy tales? But I'll tell you this"—and she spoke with a fine flash of very unheavenly temper—"you'll never find out whether they are or not if you aren't kinder to people than you are now. Come along, Lottie." And she marched out of the room, half hoping to see the little servant again somewhere, but when she reached the hall there was no sign of her.
"Who is that little girl who lights the fires?" she asked Mariette that night.
Mariette launched into a torrent of description.

Ah, to be sure, Mademoiselle Sara might well ask! She was a forlorn little creature who had just taken over as scullery maid—though she was a good deal more than a scullery maid, for she did everything else too. She blacked the boots and the grates, hauled heavy coal scuttles up and down the stairs, scrubbed floors, washed windows, and was ordered about by everyone. She was fourteen years old but so stunted that she looked about twelve. Mariette honestly pitied her. She was so timid that if anyone happened to speak to her, her poor frightened eyes seemed ready to leap out of her head.
"What's her name?" asked Sara, who had been sitting at the table with her chin on her hands, listening intently to the whole account.
Her name was Becky. Mariette heard everyone downstairs calling out "Becky, do this" and "Becky, do that" every five minutes of the day.

After Mariette left, Sara sat looking into the fire, thinking about Becky for a long while. She made up a story in which Becky was the mistreated heroine. Becky looked to her as if she had never quite had enough to eat; even her eyes seemed hungry. She hoped she would see her again, but though she glimpsed her several times carrying things up and down the stairs, Becky always seemed to be in such a rush and so afraid of being noticed that it was impossible to speak to her.

But a few weeks later, on another foggy afternoon, Sara walked into her sitting room and found a rather touching sight. In her very own favorite armchair by the bright fire sat Becky, fast asleep—with a coal smudge on her nose and several more on her apron, her shabby little cap hanging half off her head, and an empty coal box on the floor beside her. She was worn out beyond even what her hard-working young body could stand. She had been sent up to tidy the bedrooms for the evening. There were a great many of them, and she had been running about all day. Sara's rooms she had saved for last. They weren't like the other rooms, which were plain and bare, since ordinary pupils were expected to make do with the bare necessities. To the scullery maid, Sara's comfortable sitting room seemed a palace of luxury, though really it was just a pleasant, bright little room. But it held pictures and books and curiosities from India. There was a sofa and the low, soft chair, and Emily sat in a chair of her own, presiding like a goddess, and there was always a glowing fire in a polished grate. Becky left it for the end of her afternoon's work because going in there rested her, and she always hoped to steal a few minutes to sit in the soft chair and look around, and to think about the marvelous good fortune of the child who owned such things, and who went out on cold days in lovely hats and coats that one tried to catch a glimpse of through the area railings.

This afternoon, when she had sat down, the relief to her short, aching legs had been so wonderful that it seemed to soothe her entire body. The warm glow from the fire had crept over her like a spell, until, as she watched the red coals, a slow, tired smile spread over her smudged face, her head nodded forward without her noticing, her eyelids drooped, and she fell sound asleep. She had been in the room only about ten minutes when Sara came in, but she slept as deeply as if she had been, like Sleeping Beauty, dozing for a hundred years. Yet poor Becky didn't look like a Sleeping Beauty at all. She looked only like an ugly, stunted, worn-out little kitchen drudge.
Sara seemed so different from her that she might have come from another world.

This afternoon she had been to her dancing lesson, and the afternoon the dancing master came was quite a grand occasion at the school, though it happened every week. The pupils wore their prettiest dresses, and since Sara danced particularly well she was given special attention, and Mariette was asked to dress her in the lightest, finest things she could find.

Today she had been put into a rose-colored dress, and Mariette had bought real rosebuds and made a wreath for her to wear in her black curls. She had been learning a new, delightful dance in which she skimmed and flew about the room like a big rose-colored butterfly, and the fun and exercise had put a bright, happy glow in her face.
When she came into the room she floated in with a few of her butterfly steps—and there sat Becky, her cap nodding sideways off her head.
"Oh!" cried Sara softly when she saw her. "That poor thing!"

It never crossed her mind to be annoyed at finding her favorite chair taken by the small, grubby figure. In truth, she was quite pleased to find her there. When the mistreated heroine of her story woke up, she could talk to her. She crept quietly up and stood looking down at her. Becky gave a little snore.
"I wish she'd wake up on her own," Sara said. "I don't like to wake her. But Miss Minchin would be furious if she found out. I'll just wait a few minutes."

She perched on the edge of the table and sat swinging her slim, rose-colored legs, wondering what it would be best to do. Miss Amelia might walk in at any moment, and if she did, Becky would certainly be scolded.
"But she's so tired," she thought. "She's so tired!"

A piece of blazing coal settled the question for her right then. It broke off a big lump and dropped onto the fender. Becky started and opened her eyes with a frightened gasp. She hadn't known she'd fallen asleep. She had only sat down for a moment to enjoy the lovely warmth—and now she found herself staring in wild alarm at the wonderful pupil, who sat perched close by like a rose-colored fairy, watching her with interest.

She sprang up and grabbed at her cap. She felt it dangling over her ear and tried frantically to straighten it. Oh, she was in trouble now, and no mistake! To have fallen asleep, bold as brass, in a young lady's chair! She would be thrown out of the house without her wages.
She let out a sound like a great breathless sob.
"Oh, miss! Oh, miss!" she stammered. "I beg yer pardon, miss! Oh, I do, miss!"
Sara hopped down and came right up to her.
"Don't be frightened," she said, just as if she were speaking to a girl like herself. "It doesn't matter one bit."
"I never meant to do it, miss," Becky protested. "It was the warm fire—an' me bein' so tired. It—it WASN'T cheek!"
Sara gave a friendly little laugh and laid a hand on her shoulder.
"You were tired," she said. "You couldn't help it. You're not properly awake yet."

How poor Becky stared! She had never heard such a kind, friendly sound in anyone's voice before. She was used to being ordered about and scolded and having her ears boxed. And here was this girl, in all her rose-colored dancing-day splendor, looking at her as though she weren't guilty at all—as though she had every right to be tired—even to fall asleep! The touch of that soft, slim little hand on her shoulder was the most astonishing thing she had ever known.
"Yer ain't—yer ain't cross, miss?" she gasped. "Yer ain't goin' to go an' tell the missus?"
"No," cried Sara. "Of course I'm not."
The terrible fear in that coal-blackened face made her so sorry that she could hardly stand it. One of her odd thoughts came rushing into her mind. She laid her hand against Becky's cheek.
"Why," she said, "we're just the same—I'm only a little girl like you. It's only an accident that I'm not you, and you're not me!"

Becky understood none of it. Her mind couldn't grasp such astounding ideas, and "an accident" meant to her a calamity in which somebody was run over or fell off a ladder and was carried off to "the 'orspital."
"A' accident, miss," she said, fluttering respectfully. "Is it?"
"Yes," Sara answered, and for a moment she gazed at her dreamily. But then she spoke in a different tone. She had realized that Becky didn't know what she meant.
"Have you finished your work?" she asked. "Do you dare stay here a few minutes?"
Becky was left breathless again.
"Here, miss? Me?"
Sara ran to the door, opened it, and looked out and listened.
"There's nobody about," she explained. "If you've finished the bedrooms, maybe you could stay a tiny while. I thought—perhaps—you might like a piece of cake."

The next ten minutes felt to Becky like some kind of fever dream. Sara opened a cupboard and gave her a thick slice of cake. She seemed delighted when it vanished in hungry bites. She chatted and asked questions and laughed until Becky's fears really did begin to settle, and once or twice she even gathered the courage to ask a question or two of her own, bold as it felt.
"Is that—" she began, gazing longingly at the rose-colored dress, and she said it almost in a whisper. "Is that there your best?"
"It's one of my dancing dresses," said Sara. "I like it. Don't you?"

For a few seconds Becky was nearly speechless with admiration. Then she said, in an awed voice, "Onct I see a princess. I was standin' in the street with the crowd outside Covin' Garden, watchin' the swells go inter the operer. An' there was one everyone stared at most. They was sayin' to each other, 'That's the princess.' She was a growed-up young lady, but pink all over she was—gownd an' cloak, an' flowers an' all. Soon as I seen you sittin' there on the table, miss, I thought of her straight off. You looked just like her."
"I've often thought," said Sara, in her musing voice, "that I'd like to be a princess. I wonder what it feels like. I think I'll start pretending I am one."
Becky gazed at her in admiration and, as before, understood nothing. She watched her with a kind of worship. Before long Sara came out of her thoughts and turned to her with a new question.
"Becky," she said, "weren't you listening to that story?"
"Yes, miss," Becky confessed, alarmed again. "I knowed I hadn't orter, but it was that beautiful I—I couldn't help it."
"I wanted you to listen," said Sara. "When you tell stories, there's nothing you like better than telling them to people who want to hear. I don't know why that is. Would you like to hear the rest?"
Becky lost her breath again.
"Me hear it?" she cried. "Like I was a pupil, miss! All about the Prince—and the little white Mer-babies swimmin' about laughin'—with stars in their hair?"
Sara nodded.

"I'm afraid you haven't time to hear it now," she said. "But if you tell me exactly what time you come to do my rooms, I'll try to be here and tell you a bit every day until it's finished. It's a lovely long one—and I keep adding new pieces to it."
"Then," Becky breathed, devoutly, "I wouldn't mind HOW heavy them coal boxes was—or WHAT the cook done to me, if—if I could have that to think about."
"You can," said Sara. "I'll tell you ALL of it."

When Becky went downstairs, she was no longer the same Becky who had staggered up under the weight of the coal scuttle. She had an extra piece of cake in her pocket, and she had been fed and warmed, but not only by cake and fire. Something else had warmed and fed her, and that something was Sara.
When she was gone, Sara sat on her favorite perch at the end of the table, feet on a chair, elbows on her knees, chin in her hands.

"If I WERE a princess—a REAL princess," she murmured, "I could scatter largess to the people. But even if I'm only a pretend princess, I can invent little things to do for people. Things like this. She was every bit as happy as if it had been largess. I'll pretend that doing things people like is scattering largess. I've scattered largess."

chapters.title: The Diamond Mines
paragraphs: Not long afterward something very exciting happened. Sara found it exciting, and so did the whole school, and for weeks afterward it was the main topic of conversation. In one of his letters Captain Crewe told a fascinating story. A friend who had been at school with him as a boy had turned up in India without warning to visit him. This friend owned a large stretch of land where diamonds had been discovered, and he was busy developing the mines. If everything went as confidently expected, he would come into a fortune so vast it made your head spin to think of it. Because he was fond of his old school friend, he had offered him a chance to share in that enormous wealth by becoming a partner in the venture. That, at least, was what Sara gathered from the letters. Any other business scheme, however grand, would have held little appeal for her or for the schoolroom, but "diamond mines" sounded so much like the Arabian Nights that nobody could stay indifferent. Sara found them enchanting. For Ermengarde and Lottie she painted pictures of winding passages deep inside the earth, where sparkling stones studded the walls and roofs and ceilings, and strange dark men chipped them out with heavy picks. Ermengarde loved the story, and Lottie insisted on hearing it again every evening. Lavinia was nasty about it, and told Jessie she didn't believe diamond mines even existed.
"My mamma has a diamond ring that cost forty pounds," she said. "And it isn't even a big one. If there were mines full of diamonds, people would be so rich it would be absurd."
"Maybe Sara will be so rich she'll be absurd," Jessie giggled.
"She's absurd already, without being rich," Lavinia sniffed.
"I think you hate her," said Jessie.
"No, I don't," Lavinia snapped. "I just don't believe in mines full of diamonds."
"Well, people have to get them from somewhere," said Jessie. "Lavinia," she went on, with a fresh giggle, "do you know what Gertrude says?"
"No, I'm sure I don't, and I don't care if it's more about that eternal Sara."

"Well, it is. One of her 'pretends' is that she's a princess. She plays at it all the time—even in class. She says it helps her learn her lessons better. She wants Ermengarde to be one too, but Ermengarde says she's too fat."
"She IS too fat," said Lavinia. "And Sara is too thin."
Naturally, Jessie giggled again.
"Sara says it has nothing to do with how you look or what you own. It only depends on what you THINK about and what you DO."
"I suppose she thinks she could be a princess even if she were a beggar," said Lavinia. "Let's start calling her Your Royal Highness."

The day's lessons were over, and the girls were sitting by the schoolroom fire, enjoying their favorite part of the day. It was the hour when Miss Minchin and Miss Amelia took tea in their private sitting room. A great deal of talk went on at this time, and a great many secrets changed hands, especially if the younger pupils behaved well and didn't squabble or tear around noisily, which, it must be admitted, they usually did. When they made an uproar, the older girls generally stepped in with scolding and shaking. They were expected to keep order, and if they didn't, Miss Minchin or Miss Amelia might appear and put an end to the fun. Just as Lavinia was speaking, the door opened and Sara came in with Lottie, who always trotted after her everywhere like a puppy.
"There she is, with that horrid child!" Lavinia exclaimed in a whisper. "If she's so fond of her, why doesn't she keep her in her own room? In five minutes she'll be howling about something."

As it happened, Lottie had been seized by a sudden urge to play in the schoolroom and had begged her adopted mother to come along. She joined a group of little ones playing in a corner. Sara curled up in the window seat, opened a book, and began to read. It was about the French Revolution, and she was soon lost in a harrowing picture of the prisoners in the Bastille—men who had spent so many years in dungeons that when their rescuers dragged them out, their long gray hair and beards nearly hid their faces, and they had forgotten there was a world outside at all, and moved like people in a dream.

She was so far from the schoolroom that being yanked back suddenly by one of Lottie's howls was most unpleasant. Nothing was harder for her than keeping her temper when she was disturbed in the middle of a book. People who love books know the surge of irritation that comes over you at such a moment. It is not easy to resist the temptation to be unreasonable and snappish.
"It feels as if someone has hit me," Sara had once told Ermengarde in confidence. "And I want to hit back. I have to think of things quickly to stop myself from saying something bad-tempered."
She had to think quickly now, as she set her book on the window seat and jumped down from her cozy corner.

Lottie had been sliding across the schoolroom floor. After first annoying Lavinia and Jessie with the noise, she had ended up falling and hurting her chubby knee. She was screaming and hopping up and down in a crowd of friends and enemies, who were taking turns coaxing and scolding her.
"Stop this minute, you crybaby! Stop this minute!" Lavinia ordered.
"I'm not a crybaby ... I'm not!" wailed Lottie. "Sara, Sa—ra!"
"If she doesn't stop, Miss Minchin will hear her," cried Jessie. "Lottie, darling, I'll give you a penny!"
"I don't want your penny," sobbed Lottie. She looked down at her chubby knee, saw a drop of blood on it, and burst into tears all over again.
