Sara dashed across the room, knelt down, and put her arms around her.
"Now, Lottie," she said. "Now, Lottie, you PROMISED Sara."
"She said I was a crybaby," Lottie wept.
Sara patted her, but spoke in the calm voice Lottie knew well.
"But if you cry, you will be one, Lottie pet. You PROMISED." Lottie remembered that she had promised, but she would rather raise her voice.
"I haven't got a mamma," she announced. "I haven't—a bit—of a mamma."
"Yes, you have," said Sara cheerfully. "Have you forgotten? Don't you know Sara is your mamma? Don't you want Sara for your mamma?"
Lottie snuggled up to her with a comforted sniff.
"Come and sit in the window seat with me," Sara went on, "and I'll whisper you a story."
"Will you?" Lottie whimpered. "Will you—tell me—about the diamond mines?"
"The diamond mines?" Lavinia burst out. "Nasty, spoiled little thing! I'd like to SLAP her!"

Sara jumped to her feet. We should remember she had been deeply absorbed in the book about the Bastille, and had had to pull herself together fast when she realized she must go and look after her adopted child. She was no angel, and she was not fond of Lavinia.

"Well," she said, with some fire, "I'd like to slap YOU—but I don't want to slap you!" She held herself back. "That is, I both want to slap you—and I'd LIKE to slap you—but I WON'T slap you. We're not little street urchins. We're both old enough to know better."
Here was Lavinia's chance.
"Oh, yes, your royal highness," she said. "We're princesses, I believe. Or at least one of us is. The school ought to be very fashionable now that Miss Minchin has a princess for a pupil."

Sara started toward her. She looked as though she meant to box her ears, and perhaps she did. Her habit of pretending was the joy of her life. She never mentioned it to girls she didn't like. Her new "pretend" about being a princess was close to her heart, and she felt shy and sensitive about it. She had meant it to be something of a secret, and here was Lavinia mocking it in front of nearly the whole school. She felt the blood rush to her face and tingle in her ears. She only just stopped herself. A princess did not fly into rages. Her hand dropped, and she stood perfectly still for a moment. When she spoke, her voice was quiet and steady; she held her head high, and everybody listened.
"It's true," she said. "Sometimes I do pretend I'm a princess. I pretend I'm a princess so that I can try to behave like one."

Lavinia couldn't think of quite the right thing to say. More than once she had found herself unable to come up with a good reply when dealing with Sara. The reason was that the others always seemed, somehow, to be vaguely on her opponent's side. She saw now that they had pricked up their ears with interest. The truth was that they liked princesses, and they all hoped to hear something more definite about this one, so they drew closer to Sara.
Lavinia could come up with only one remark, and it fell rather flat.
"Dear me," she said, "I hope you won't forget us when you come to the throne!"
"I won't," said Sara. She didn't say another word, but stood perfectly still and stared steadily at Lavinia as she watched her take Jessie's arm and turn away.

After this, the girls who were jealous of her called her "Princess Sara" whenever they wanted to be especially scornful, and those who were fond of her used the name among themselves as a term of affection. Nobody ever said "princess" in place of "Sara," but her admirers were delighted by the charm and grandeur of the title. When Miss Minchin heard of it she mentioned it more than once to visiting parents, feeling that it made the place sound like a sort of royal boarding school.

To Becky it seemed the most fitting thing in the world. The friendship that had begun on the foggy afternoon, when she had leaped up in terror from her sleep in the comfortable chair, had ripened and grown, though Miss Minchin and Miss Amelia, it must be said, knew very little about it. They knew Sara was "kind" to the scullery maid, but they knew nothing of the delightful moments stolen at some risk, when the upstairs rooms had been put in order at lightning speed and Becky reached Sara's sitting room and set the heavy coal box down with a sigh of joy. At such times stories were told in installments, and satisfying things were either brought out and eaten or hastily stuffed into pockets to be dealt with at night, when Becky went up to her attic to bed.
"But I has to eat 'em careful, miss," she said once. "'Cos if I leaves crumbs the rats come out to get 'em."
"Rats!" Sara exclaimed in horror. "Are there RATS there?"

"Lots of 'em, miss," Becky answered, quite matter-of-factly. "There's mostly rats an' mice in attics. You gets used to the noise they makes scuttlin' about. I've got so I don't mind 'em as long as they don't run over my piller."
"Ugh!" said Sara.
"You gets used to anythin' after a bit," said Becky. "You has to, miss, if you're born a scullery maid. I'd sooner have rats than cockroaches."
"So would I," said Sara. "I suppose in time you might make friends with a rat, but I don't think I'd ever want to make friends with a cockroach."

Sometimes Becky didn't dare spend more than a few minutes in the bright, warm room, and when that happened only a few words could be exchanged, and a small purchase slipped into the old-fashioned pocket Becky wore under her skirt, tied around her waist with a length of tape. Hunting for filling things to eat that could be packed into a small space gave Sara's life a new interest. When she went out in the carriage or on foot, she eagerly peered into shop windows. The first time it occurred to her to bring home two or three little meat pies, she felt she had made a great discovery. When she showed them to Becky, Becky's eyes positively sparkled.

"Oh, miss!" she murmured. "Them'll be nice an' fillin'. It's fillin'ness that's best. Sponge cake's a 'evenly thing, but it melts away like—if you understand, miss. These'll just STAY in yer stummick."
"Well," Sara said doubtfully, "I don't think it would be good if they stayed forever, but I do believe they'll be satisfying."

They were satisfying—and so were the beef sandwiches from the cook shop—and so were the rolls and Bologna sausage. In time Becky began to lose her hungry, tired feeling, and the coal box no longer felt so unbearably heavy.

However heavy it was, whatever the cook's mood, and however hard the work piled onto her shoulders, she always had the afternoon to look forward to—the chance that Miss Sara might be in her sitting room. In fact, just seeing Miss Sara would have been enough without any meat pies. If there was time for only a few words, they were always friendly, cheerful words that gave you heart; and if there was time for more, there was an installment of a story to hear, or something else you remembered afterward and sometimes lay awake in your attic bed turning over in your mind. Sara was only doing what she unconsciously liked best, since Nature had made her a giver, and she had no idea what she meant to poor Becky, or how marvelous a benefactor she seemed. If Nature has made you a giver, your hands are born open, and so is your heart. There may be times when your hands are empty, but your heart is always full, and you can give from that—warm things, kind things, sweet things—help and comfort and laughter—and sometimes cheerful, kind laughter is the best help of all.

Becky had hardly known what laughter was in all her poor, hard-driven little life. Sara made her laugh, and laughed along with her, and though neither of them quite realized it, the laughter was every bit as "fillin'" as the meat pies.

A few weeks before Sara's eleventh birthday a letter arrived from her father that did not seem to be written in his usual boyish high spirits. He wasn't very well, and he was plainly weighed down by the business of the diamond mines.

"You see, little Sara," he wrote, "your daddy is not a businessman at all, and figures and documents trouble him. He doesn't truly understand them, and all of this seems so enormous. Perhaps if I weren't feverish, I wouldn't lie awake tossing half the night and spend the other half in troubled dreams. If my little missus were here, I dare say she'd give me some solemn, sensible advice. You would, wouldn't you, Little Missus?"
One of his many jokes had been to call her his "little missus," because she had such an old-fashioned air.

He had made wonderful plans for her birthday. Among other things, a new doll had been ordered from Paris, and her wardrobe was to be a marvel of splendid perfection. When Sara had answered his letter asking whether a doll would be an acceptable present, she had been very quaint.

"I'm getting very old," she wrote. "You see, I'll never live to be given another doll. This will be my last doll. There's something solemn about that. If I could write poetry, I'm sure a poem called 'A Last Doll' would be very nice. But I can't write poetry. I've tried, and it made me laugh. It didn't sound a bit like Watts or Coleridge or Shakespeare. Nobody could ever take Emily's place, but I would respect the Last Doll very much, and I'm sure the school would love her. They all like dolls, though some of the big girls—the nearly fifteen ones—pretend they're too grown up."

Captain Crewe had a splitting headache when he read this letter in his bungalow in India. The table in front of him was heaped with papers and letters that alarmed him and filled him with anxious dread, but he laughed as he hadn't laughed in weeks.

"Oh," he said, "she's better fun with every year she lives. God grant this business sorts itself out and lets me run home to see her. What wouldn't I give to have her little arms around my neck this minute! What WOULDN'T I give!"

The birthday was to be celebrated with grand festivities. The schoolroom was to be decorated and there was to be a party. The boxes of presents were to be opened with great ceremony, and a glittering feast was to be laid out in Miss Minchin's private room. When the day came, the whole house was in a whirl of excitement. Nobody quite knew how the morning went by, there was so much to prepare. The schoolroom was being hung with garlands of holly. The desks had been moved out, and red covers had been put on the benches lined up against the walls.

When Sara went into her sitting room that morning, she found a small, squat package on the table, tied up in brown paper. She knew it was a present, and she thought she could guess who it was from. She opened it very tenderly. It was a square pincushion, made of red flannel that wasn't quite clean, and black pins had been stuck carefully into it to spell out the words "Menny hapy returns."
"Oh!" cried Sara, with a warm feeling in her heart. "How much trouble she has taken! I like it so much, it—it makes me feel sad."
But the next moment she was puzzled. Fastened to the underside of the pincushion was a card with the name "Miss Amelia Minchin" written on it in neat letters.
Sara turned it over and over.
"Miss Amelia!" she said to herself. "How CAN it be!"
And at that very moment she heard the door being pushed open carefully, and saw Becky peeping around it.
A happy, affectionate grin was on her face, and she shuffled forward and stood nervously pulling at her fingers.
"Do yer like it, Miss Sara?" she said. "Do yer?"
"Like it?" cried Sara. "You darling Becky, you made it all yourself."
Becky gave a half-sobbing but joyful sniff, and her eyes shone wet with delight.

"It ain't nothin' but flannin, an' the flannin ain't new. But I wanted to give yer somethin', an' I made it of nights. I knowed yer could PRETEND it was satin with diamond pins in. _I_ tried to when I was makin' it. The card, miss," she added, rather doubtfully, "it warn't wrong of me to pick it up out o' the dust-bin, was it? Miss 'Meliar had throwed it away. I hadn't no card o' my own, an' I knowed it wouldn't be a proper presink if I didn't pin a card on—so I pinned Miss 'Meliar's."
Sara rushed at her and hugged her. She couldn't have said, to herself or anyone else, why there was a lump in her throat.
"Oh, Becky!" she cried, with a funny little laugh. "I love you, Becky—I do, I do!"
"Oh, miss!" Becky breathed. "Thank yer kindly, miss, but it ain't good enough for that. The—the flannin wasn't new."

chapters.title: The Diamond Mines Again
paragraphs: When Sara walked into the holly-decked schoolroom that afternoon, she came in at the head of a small procession. Miss Minchin, in her grandest silk dress, led her by the hand. A manservant followed carrying the box that held the Last Doll, a housemaid carried a second box, and Becky brought up the rear with a third, wearing a clean apron and a new cap. Sara would much rather have come in the ordinary way, but Miss Minchin had sent for her and, after a talk in her private sitting room, had made her wishes known.
"This is not an ordinary occasion," she had said. "I do not wish it to be treated as one."
So Sara was ushered in with ceremony, and she felt shy when the big girls stared at her and nudged each other's elbows, and the little ones began to wriggle happily in their seats.
"Silence, young ladies!" said Miss Minchin as a murmur rose. "James, set the box on the table and take off the lid. Emma, put yours on a chair. Becky!" she added suddenly and sharply.

Becky had forgotten herself completely in her excitement and was grinning at Lottie, who was squirming with delighted anticipation. The stern voice startled her so much that she nearly dropped her box, and her frightened, bobbing curtsy of apology was so funny that Lavinia and Jessie tittered.
"You have no business looking at the young ladies," said Miss Minchin. "Remember your place. Set your box down."
Becky obeyed in alarmed haste and quickly backed toward the door.
"You may go," Miss Minchin told the servants with a wave of her hand.

Becky stood aside respectfully so that the senior servants could leave first. She couldn't help casting a longing glance at the box on the table. Something made of blue satin was peeping out between the folds of tissue paper.
"If you please, Miss Minchin," Sara said suddenly, "may Becky stay?"
It was a daring thing to say. Miss Minchin was startled into something like a small jump. Then she raised her eyeglass and stared uneasily at her show pupil.
"Becky!" she exclaimed. "My dearest Sara!"
Sara took a step toward her.
"I'd like her to stay because I know she'll enjoy seeing the presents," she explained. "She's a little girl too, you know."
Miss Minchin was scandalized. She looked from one of them to the other.
"Dear Sara," she said, "Becky is only the scullery maid. Scullery maids—er—are simply not little girls."
It honestly had never occurred to her to think of them that way. Scullery maids were machines for carrying coal scuttles and lighting fires.
"But Becky is," said Sara. "And I know she'd enjoy it. Please let her stay—since it's my birthday."
Miss Minchin answered with great dignity.
"Since you ask it as a birthday favor—she may stay. Rebecca, thank Miss Sara for her great kindness."

Becky had been backing into the corner, twisting the hem of her apron in thrilled suspense. She came forward, bobbing curtsies, and a flash of friendly understanding passed between her eyes and Sara's, while her words tumbled out over each other.

"Oh, if you please, miss! I'm that grateful, miss! I did want to see the doll, miss, I truly did. Thank you, miss. And thank you, ma'am," she added, turning to make a frightened bob to Miss Minchin, "for lettin' me take the liberty."
Miss Minchin waved her hand once more—this time it pointed to the corner over by the door.
"Go and stand over there," she ordered. "Not too near the young ladies."

Becky went to her spot, grinning. She didn't care where she was sent, as long as she had the luck to be inside the room rather than down in the scullery while these delights were going on. She didn't even mind when Miss Minchin cleared her throat ominously and spoke again.
"Now, young ladies, I have a few words to say to you," she announced.
"She's going to make a speech," one of the girls whispered. "I wish it were over."
Sara felt rather uncomfortable. Since this was her party, the speech was probably about her. It is not pleasant to stand in a schoolroom while a speech is made about you.
"You are aware, young ladies," the speech began—for it was a speech—"that dear Sara is eleven years old today."
"DEAR Sara!" Lavinia murmured.

"Several of you have been eleven years old as well, but Sara's birthdays are rather different from other little girls' birthdays. When she is older she will be the heiress to a large fortune, which it will be her duty to spend in a worthy manner."
"The diamond mines," Jessie giggled in a whisper.

Sara didn't hear her, but as she stood with her green-gray eyes fixed steadily on Miss Minchin, she felt herself growing hot. Whenever Miss Minchin talked about money she somehow always hated her—and of course it was disrespectful to hate grown-ups.

"When her dear papa, Captain Crewe, brought her from India and placed her in my care," the speech went on, "he said to me, jokingly, 'I'm afraid she will be very rich, Miss Minchin.' I replied, 'Her education at my seminary, Captain Crewe, will be one that would grace the largest fortune.' Sara has become my most accomplished pupil. Her French and her dancing are a credit to the seminary. Her manners—which have led you to call her Princess Sara—are perfect. She shows her kindness by giving you this afternoon's party. I hope you appreciate her generosity. I want you to show your appreciation by saying aloud, all together, 'Thank you, Sara!'"
The entire schoolroom rose to its feet as it had done on that morning Sara remembered so well.
"Thank you, Sara!" it said, and Lottie, it must be admitted, jumped up and down. Sara looked a little shy for a moment. Then she made a curtsy—and it was a very nice one.
"Thank you," she said, "for coming to my party."

"Very pretty indeed, Sara," Miss Minchin approved. "That is just what a real princess does when the common people applaud her. Lavinia"—and here she was scathing—"the noise you just made sounded extremely like a snort. If you are jealous of your fellow pupil, I beg you to express your feelings in a more ladylike way. Now I'll leave you to enjoy yourselves."

The moment she swept out of the room, the spell her presence always cast over them was broken. The door had barely closed before every seat was empty. The little girls jumped or tumbled out of theirs, and the older ones lost no time in abandoning theirs. There was a rush toward the boxes. Sara had bent over one of them with a delighted face.
"These are books, I can tell," she said.
The little ones broke into a doleful murmur, and Ermengarde looked horrified.
"Your papa sends you books for your birthday?" she exclaimed. "Why, he's just as bad as mine. Don't open them, Sara."

"I like them," Sara laughed, but she turned to the biggest box. When she lifted out the Last Doll, it was so magnificent that the children groaned with joy and actually drew back to gaze at it, breathless with wonder.
"She's nearly as big as Lottie," someone gasped.
Lottie clapped her hands and danced about, giggling.
"She's dressed to go to the theater," said Lavinia. "Look, her cloak has an ermine lining."
"Oh," cried Ermengarde, darting forward, "she's got opera glasses in her hand—blue and gold ones!"
"Here's her trunk," said Sara. "Let's open it and look at her things."

She sat down on the floor and turned the key. The children crowded around her, clamoring, as she lifted out tray after tray and showed what was in them. The schoolroom had never been in such an uproar. There were lace collars and silk stockings and handkerchiefs. There was a jewel case with a necklace and a tiara that looked just like real diamonds. There was a long sealskin coat and muff, and there were ball gowns and walking dresses and dresses for paying calls, and hats and tea gowns and fans. Even Lavinia and Jessie forgot they were too old to care about dolls, and cried out in delight and snatched things up to look at them.

"Suppose," Sara said, standing by the table and putting a large black velvet hat on the calmly smiling owner of all these splendors, "suppose she understands what people say, and feels proud of being admired."
"You're always supposing things," said Lavinia, with a very superior air.
"I know I am," Sara answered, quite undisturbed. "I like it. There's nothing nicer than supposing. It's almost like being a fairy. If you suppose something hard enough, it seems as if it were real."
"Supposing is all very well when you have everything," said Lavinia. "Would you be able to suppose and pretend if you were a beggar with only a garret to live in?"
Sara stopped arranging the Last Doll's ostrich plumes and looked thoughtful.
"I BELIEVE I could," she said. "If you were a beggar, you'd have to suppose and pretend all the time. But it might not be easy."
She often thought afterward how strange it was that just as she finished saying this—at that very moment—Miss Amelia came into the room.

"Sara," she said, "your papa's solicitor, Mr. Barrow, has come to see Miss Minchin. She has to speak with him alone, and the refreshments are laid out in her parlor, so you had all better come and have your feast now, so my sister can have her meeting here in the schoolroom."

Nobody was likely to turn up their nose at refreshments at any hour, and many pairs of eyes gleamed. Miss Amelia got the procession into good order, and then, with Sara at her side leading it, she took the girls away, leaving the Last Doll sitting on a chair with the glories of her wardrobe scattered around her: dresses and coats draped over chair backs, and heaps of lace-frilled petticoats piled on the seats.
Becky, who wasn't expected to join the refreshments, was unwise enough to linger a moment to look at these lovely things—and it really was unwise.

"Go back to your work, Becky," Miss Amelia had said. But Becky had stopped to pick up first a muff and then a coat, reverently, and while she stood gazing at them adoringly she heard Miss Minchin at the doorway. Seized with terror at the thought of being accused of taking liberties, she rashly dived under the table, whose cloth hid her.

Miss Minchin came into the room with a sharp-featured, dried-up little gentleman who looked rather troubled. Miss Minchin herself looked rather troubled too, it must be said, and she was eyeing the dried-up little gentleman with an irritated, puzzled expression.
She sat down with stiff dignity and waved him to a chair.
"Pray be seated, Mr. Barrow," she said.

Mr. Barrow didn't sit down right away. His attention seemed caught by the Last Doll and the things around her. He adjusted his eyeglasses and regarded them with nervous disapproval. The Last Doll herself didn't seem to mind in the least. She simply sat upright and returned his gaze with indifference.
"A hundred pounds," Mr. Barrow remarked curtly. "All costly material, made at a Parisian dressmaker's. He certainly spent money freely, that young man."
Miss Minchin felt offended. This seemed to disparage her best patron, and it was a liberty.
Even solicitors had no right to take liberties.
"I beg your pardon, Mr. Barrow," she said stiffly. "I don't understand."
"Birthday presents," said Mr. Barrow in the same critical tone, "for a child of eleven! Mad extravagance, I call it."
Miss Minchin drew herself up even more stiffly.
"Captain Crewe is a man of fortune," she said. "The diamond mines alone—"
Mr. Barrow wheeled around on her. "Diamond mines!" he burst out. "There aren't any! There never were!"
Miss Minchin actually rose from her chair.
"What!" she cried. "What do you mean?"
"At any rate," Mr. Barrow answered, quite snappishly, "it would have been far better if there never had been."
"Any diamond mines?" Miss Minchin burst out, clutching at the back of a chair, feeling as if a splendid dream were fading away from her.

"Diamond mines spell ruin more often than they spell wealth," said Mr. Barrow. "When a man is in the hands of a very dear friend and is no businessman himself, he would do better to steer clear of that dear friend's diamond mines, or gold mines, or any other kind of mine the dear friend wants his money put into. The late Captain Crewe—"
At this Miss Minchin stopped him with a gasp.
"The LATE Captain Crewe!" she cried. "The LATE! You haven't come to tell me that Captain Crewe is—"

"He's dead, ma'am," Mr. Barrow answered with jerky bluntness. "Died of jungle fever and business troubles together. The fever might not have killed him if the business troubles hadn't driven him half mad, and the business troubles might not have finished him if the fever hadn't helped. Captain Crewe is dead!"
Miss Minchin sank back into her chair. His words filled her with alarm.
"What WERE his business troubles?" she said. "What WERE they?"
"Diamond mines," Mr. Barrow answered, "and dear friends—and ruin."
Miss Minchin lost her breath.
"Ruin!" she gasped.

"Lost every penny. That young man had too much money. The dear friend was obsessed with the diamond mine. He put all his own money into it, and all of Captain Crewe's. Then the dear friend ran off—Captain Crewe was already down with fever when the news came. The shock was too much for him. He died delirious, raving about his little girl—and he didn't leave a penny."

Now Miss Minchin understood, and never in her life had she taken such a blow. Her show pupil and her show patron, swept away from the Select Seminary in one stroke! She felt outraged and robbed, and she blamed Captain Crewe and Sara and Mr. Barrow equally.
"Do you mean to tell me," she cried, "that he left NOTHING! That Sara will have no fortune! That the child is a beggar! That she's been left on my hands as a little pauper instead of an heiress?"
Mr. Barrow was a shrewd businessman, and thought it wise to make clear his own freedom from responsibility without delay.
"She's certainly been left a beggar," he replied. "And she's certainly been left on your hands, ma'am—since she hasn't a relation in the world that we know of."

Miss Minchin lurched forward. She looked as if she meant to throw open the door and rush out to stop the festivities that were going on, joyfully and rather noisily, over the refreshments at that very moment.
"It's monstrous!" she said. "She's in my sitting room right now, dressed in silk gauze and lace petticoats, giving a party at my expense."

"At your expense, madam, if she's giving it at all," said Mr. Barrow calmly. "Barrow & Skipworth are not responsible for anything. There was never a cleaner sweep made of a man's fortune. Captain Crewe died without paying OUR last bill—and it was a large one."
Miss Minchin turned back from the door, more indignant than ever. This was worse than anyone could have dreamed.

"That's what has happened to me!" she cried. "I was always so sure of his payments that I went to all sorts of ridiculous expense for the child. I paid the bills for that ridiculous doll and her ridiculous fantastic wardrobe. The child was to have anything she wanted. She has a carriage and a pony and a maid, and I've paid for every one of them since the last cheque came."

Mr. Barrow plainly had no intention of staying to hear Miss Minchin's grievances now that he had explained his firm's position and set out the bare facts. He felt no particular sympathy for furious boarding-school keepers.
"I'd advise you not to pay for anything more, ma'am," he remarked, "unless you want to make the young lady presents. No one will remember you for it. She hasn't a brass farthing to call her own."
"But what am I to do?" Miss Minchin demanded, as though it were entirely his duty to put the matter right. "What am I to do?"
"There's nothing to be done," said Mr. Barrow, folding up his eyeglasses and slipping them into his pocket. "Captain Crewe is dead. The child is left a pauper. Nobody is responsible for her but you."
"I am not responsible for her, and I refuse to be made responsible!"
Miss Minchin went quite white with rage.
Mr. Barrow turned to go.
"That's no concern of mine, madam," he said, without interest. "Barrow & Skipworth are not responsible. Very sorry this has happened, of course."
"If you think she is going to be foisted on me, you are greatly mistaken," Miss Minchin gasped. "I have been robbed and cheated. I'll turn her out into the street!"
Had she not been so furious, she would have had the sense not to say so much. She saw herself saddled with an extravagantly raised child she had always resented, and she lost all self-control.
Mr. Barrow moved calmly toward the door.
"I wouldn't do that, madam," he remarked. "It wouldn't look well. An unpleasant story to have going around about the establishment. A pupil bundled out penniless and friendless."

He was a clever businessman, and he knew what he was saying. He also knew that Miss Minchin was a businesswoman, shrewd enough to see the truth. She couldn't afford to do anything that would make people call her cruel and hard-hearted.
"Better keep her and put her to use," he added. "She's a clever child, I believe. You can get a good deal out of her as she grows older."
"I'll get a good deal out of her before she grows older!" exclaimed Miss Minchin.
"I'm sure you will, ma'am," said Mr. Barrow, with a faint sinister smile. "I'm sure you will. Good morning!"

He bowed himself out and shut the door, and Miss Minchin, it must be admitted, stood glaring at it for a few moments. What he had said was perfectly true, and she knew it. She had no recourse whatever. Her show pupil had dissolved into nothing, leaving only a friendless, beggared little girl. The money she herself had advanced was lost and could never be recovered.

And as she stood there breathless with her sense of injury, a burst of cheerful voices reached her ears from her own private room, which had actually been given over to the feast. At least she could put a stop to that.
But as she started for the door, Miss Amelia opened it, and when she saw her sister's changed, angry face she stepped back in alarm.
"What IS the matter, sister?" she cried.
Miss Minchin's voice was almost savage as she answered.
"Where is Sara Crewe?"
Miss Amelia was bewildered.
"Sara!" she stammered. "Why, she's with the children in your room, of course."
"Does she have a black frock in her sumptuous wardrobe?" she asked, in bitter irony.
"A black frock?" Miss Amelia stammered again. "A BLACK one?"
"She has frocks of every other color. Has she a black one?"
Miss Amelia began to go pale.
"No—ye-es!" she said. "But it's too short for her. All she has is the old black velvet, and she's outgrown it."
"Go and tell her to take off that preposterous pink silk gauze and put the black one on, whether it's too short or not. She is done with finery!"
Then Miss Amelia began to wring her plump hands and weep.
"Oh, sister!" she sniffed. "Oh, sister! What CAN have happened?"
Miss Minchin did not waste words.
"Captain Crewe is dead," she said. "He died without a penny. That spoiled, pampered, fanciful child has been left on my hands a pauper."
Miss Amelia sank rather heavily into the nearest chair.
"I've spent hundreds of pounds on nonsense for her. And I shall never see a penny of it. Put a stop to this ridiculous party of hers. Go and make her change her frock at once."
"Me?" Miss Amelia panted. "M-must I go and tell her now?"
"This minute!" came the fierce reply. "Don't just sit there gaping like a goose. Go!"

Poor Miss Amelia was used to being called a goose. She knew, in fact, that she was something of a goose, and that it fell to geese to do a great many unpleasant things. It was rather awkward to walk into a room full of delighted children and tell the giver of the feast that she had suddenly turned into a little beggar and must go upstairs and put on an old black frock that was too small for her. But it had to be done. This was clearly not the moment for asking questions.

She rubbed her eyes with her handkerchief until they were quite red. Then she got up and left the room without daring to say another word. When her older sister looked and spoke the way she just had, the wisest thing to do was obey orders without comment. Miss Minchin paced across the room. She was talking aloud to herself without knowing it. Over the past year the story of the diamond mines had suggested all sorts of possibilities to her. Even the owners of seminaries might make fortunes in stocks, with the help of mine owners. And now, instead of looking forward to profits, she was left looking back on losses.

"The Princess Sara, indeed!" she said. "That child has been pampered as though she were a QUEEN." She was sweeping angrily past the corner table as she said it, and the next moment she started at the sound of a loud, sobbing sniff coming from under the cloth.
"What is that!" she exclaimed angrily. The loud, sobbing sniff came again, and she bent down and lifted the hanging folds of the tablecloth.
"How DARE you!" she cried. "How dare you! Come out this instant!"
It was poor Becky who crawled out, her cap knocked sideways and her face red from holding back her tears.
"If you please, 'm—it's me, mum," she explained. "I know I hadn't ought to. But I was lookin' at the doll, mum—an' I was frightened when you come in—an' I slipped under the table."
"You've been there all this time, listening," said Miss Minchin.

"No, mum," Becky protested, bobbing curtsies. "Not listenin'—I thought I could slip out without you noticin', but I couldn't, an' I had to stay. But I didn't listen, mum—I wouldn't for nothin'. But I couldn't help hearin'."
Suddenly it was almost as if she lost all fear of the terrible lady in front of her. She burst into fresh tears.
"Oh, please, 'm," she said. "I dare say you'll give me notice, mum—but I'm so sorry for poor Miss Sara—I'm so sorry!"
"Leave the room!" ordered Miss Minchin.
Becky curtsied again, tears streaming openly down her cheeks.

"Yes, 'm, I will, 'm," she said, trembling. "But oh, I only wanted to ask you: Miss Sara—she's been such a rich young lady, an' waited on hand an' foot, an' whatever will she do now, mum, without no maid? If—if, oh please, would you let me wait on her after I've done my pots an' kettles? I'd do 'em that quick—if you'd let me wait on her now she's poor. Oh," she broke out afresh, "poor little Miss Sara, mum—that was called a princess."

Somehow she made Miss Minchin angrier than ever. That the very scullery maid should line up on the side of this child—whom Miss Minchin now realized more fully than ever she had never liked—was too much. She actually stamped her foot.
"No—certainly not," she said. "She'll wait on herself, and on other people as well. Leave the room this instant, or you'll lose your place."
Becky threw her apron over her head and fled. She ran out of the room and down the steps to the scullery, and there she sat down among her pots and kettles and wept as if her heart would break.
"It's just like the ones in the stories," she wailed. "Them poor princesses that was driven out into the world."
Miss Minchin had never looked so still and hard as she did when Sara came to her a few hours later, in answer to a message she had sent.
Even by then it seemed to Sara that the birthday party had either been a dream, or something that had happened years ago, in the life of some other little girl entirely.

Every sign of the festivities had been swept away. The holly was gone from the schoolroom walls, and the benches and desks were back in their places. Miss Minchin's sitting room looked as it always did—every trace of the feast was gone, and Miss Minchin had changed back into her usual dress. The pupils had been told to put away their party frocks, and having done so they had returned to the schoolroom and huddled in groups, whispering and talking in excitement.
"Tell Sara to come to my room," Miss Minchin had told her sister. "And make it quite clear to her that I will have no crying or unpleasant scenes."

"Sister," Miss Amelia replied, "she's the strangest child I ever saw. She hasn't made any fuss at all. You remember she made none when Captain Crewe went back to India. When I told her what had happened, she just stood perfectly still and looked at me without a sound. Her eyes seemed to grow bigger and bigger, and she turned quite pale. When I finished she kept staring for a few seconds, then her chin began to shake, and she turned and ran out of the room and upstairs. Several of the other children began to cry, but she didn't seem to hear them, or to be aware of anything except what I was saying. It made me feel quite odd not to get an answer. When you tell someone something sudden and strange, you expect them to say SOMETHING, whatever it is."

Nobody but Sara herself ever knew what happened in her room after she ran upstairs and locked the door. She herself hardly remembered anything except pacing up and down, repeating to herself in a voice that didn't seem her own, "My papa is dead! My papa is dead!"
Once she stopped in front of Emily, who sat watching her from her chair, and cried out wildly, "Emily! Do you hear? Do you hear—papa is dead? He died in India—thousands of miles away."

When she came into Miss Minchin's sitting room in answer to her summons, her face was white and her eyes were ringed with dark shadows. Her mouth was set as though she didn't want it to give away what she had suffered and was still suffering. She looked nothing like the rose-colored butterfly child who had flown from one of her treasures to another in the decorated schoolroom. Instead she was a strange, desolate, almost grotesque little figure.

She had put on, without Mariette's help, the discarded black velvet frock. It was too short and too tight, and her slender legs looked long and thin beneath the skimpy skirt. Since she hadn't been able to find a piece of black ribbon, her short, thick black hair hung loose about her face and stood out sharply against its paleness. She held Emily tightly in one arm, and Emily was wrapped in a piece of black cloth.
"Put your doll down," said Miss Minchin. "What do you mean by bringing her here?"
"No," Sara answered. "I won't put her down. She's all I have. My papa gave her to me."

Sara had always made Miss Minchin feel secretly uneasy, and she did so now. She wasn't rude so much as coldly steady, and Miss Minchin found that hard to deal with—perhaps because she knew she was doing something heartless and inhuman.
"You'll have no time for dolls from now on," she said. "You will have to work and improve yourself and make yourself useful."
Sara kept her big, strange eyes fixed on her and said not a word.
"Everything will be very different now," Miss Minchin went on. "I suppose Miss Amelia has explained things to you."
"Yes," answered Sara. "My papa is dead. He left me no money. I'm quite poor."
"You are a beggar," said Miss Minchin, her temper rising as she remembered what all this meant. "It seems you have no relations and no home and nobody to look after you."
For a moment the thin, pale little face twitched, but again Sara said nothing.

"What are you staring at?" Miss Minchin demanded sharply. "Are you so stupid you can't understand? I'm telling you that you are completely alone in the world, with nobody to do anything for you, unless I choose to keep you here out of charity."
"I understand," Sara answered in a low voice, and there was a sound as though she were gulping down something that had risen in her throat. "I understand."
"That doll," cried Miss Minchin, pointing to the splendid birthday gift sitting nearby, "that ridiculous doll with all her nonsensical, extravagant things—I actually paid the bill for her!"
Sara turned her head toward the chair.
"The Last Doll," she said. "The Last Doll." And her sad little voice had an odd sound.
"The Last Doll, indeed!" said Miss Minchin. "And she's mine, not yours. Everything you own is mine."
"Then please take her away from me," said Sara. "I don't want her."

If Sara had cried and sobbed and looked frightened, Miss Minchin might almost have been more patient with her. She was a woman who liked to dominate and feel her power, and as she looked at Sara's pale, steadfast little face and heard her proud little voice, she felt almost as if her authority were being scorned.

"Don't put on grand airs," she said. "The time for that sort of thing is over. You are not a princess anymore. Your carriage and pony will be sent away—your maid will be dismissed. You'll wear your oldest, plainest clothes—your extravagant ones no longer suit your station. You're like Becky—you must work for your living."
To her surprise, a faint gleam came into the child's eyes—a trace of relief.
"May I work?" she said. "If I can work, it won't matter so much. What can I do?"

"You can do whatever you're told," came the answer. "You're a sharp child and you pick things up quickly. If you make yourself useful, I may let you stay here. You speak French well, and you can help with the younger children."
"May I?" Sara exclaimed. "Oh, please let me! I know I can teach them. I like them, and they like me."

"Don't talk nonsense about people liking you," said Miss Minchin. "You'll have to do more than teach the little ones. You'll run errands and help in the kitchen as well as in the schoolroom. If you don't please me, you'll be sent away. Remember that. Now go."
Sara stood still for just a moment, looking at her. In her young soul she was thinking deep, strange thoughts. Then she turned to leave the room.
"Stop!" said Miss Minchin. "Don't you intend to thank me?"
Sara paused, and all the deep, strange thoughts surged up in her breast.
"What for?" she said.
"For my kindness to you," Miss Minchin replied. "For my kindness in giving you a home."
Sara took two or three steps toward her. Her thin little chest rose and fell, and she spoke in a strange, fierce way that was not at all childlike.

"You aren't kind," she said. "You are NOT kind, and it is NOT a home." And she had turned and run out of the room before Miss Minchin could stop her or do anything except stare after her with stony anger.
She climbed the stairs slowly, panting for breath, holding Emily tight against her side.
"I wish she could talk," she said to herself. "If only she could speak—if only she could speak!"

She meant to go to her room and lie down on the tiger skin with her cheek against the great cat's head, and watch the fire and think and think and think. But just before she reached the landing, Miss Amelia came out of the door, shut it behind her, and stood in front of it, looking nervous and awkward. The truth was that she felt secretly ashamed of what she had been told to do.
"You—you're not to go in there," she said.
"Not go in?" Sara exclaimed, and she stepped back.
"That isn't your room now," Miss Amelia answered, reddening a little.
All at once, Sara understood. She realized that this was the start of the change Miss Minchin had spoken of.
"Where is my room?" she asked, hoping very much that her voice wasn't shaking.
"You're to sleep in the attic next to Becky."

Sara knew where it was. Becky had told her about it. She turned and climbed two flights of stairs. The last was narrow, covered with shabby strips of old carpet. She felt as though she were walking away, leaving far behind the world where that other child, who no longer seemed to be herself, had lived. This child, in her short, tight old frock, climbing the stairs to the attic, was an altogether different creature.
When she reached the attic door and opened it, her heart gave a dreary little thump. Then she shut the door, leaned against it, and looked around.

Yes, this was another world. The room had a slanted ceiling and whitewashed walls. The whitewash was dingy and had flaked off in places. There was a rusty grate, an old iron bedstead, and a hard bed covered with a faded quilt. Some pieces of furniture too worn for use downstairs had been sent up. Under the skylight, which showed nothing but an oblong of dull gray sky, stood an old battered red footstool. Sara went over and sat on it. She seldom cried, and she didn't cry now. She laid Emily across her knees, pressed her face down onto her and wrapped her arms around her, and sat there with her little black head resting on the black wrappings, not saying a word, not making a sound.

And as she sat in that silence there came a soft tap at the door—such a low, humble tap that she didn't hear it at first, and wasn't roused until the door was timidly pushed open and a poor tear-streaked face peeped around it. It was Becky's face. Becky had been crying secretly for hours and rubbing her eyes with her kitchen apron until she looked quite strange.
"Oh, miss," she said under her breath. "Might I—would you let me—jest come in?"

Sara lifted her head and looked at her. She tried to begin a smile, and somehow couldn't. Suddenly—and it was all because of the loving sorrow in Becky's streaming eyes—her face looked more like a child's, not so much too old for her years. She held out her hand and gave a small sob.
"Oh, Becky," she said. "I told you we were just the same—only two little girls—just two little girls. You see how true it is. There's no difference now. I'm not a princess anymore."
Becky ran to her, caught her hand, and clasped it to her breast, kneeling beside her and sobbing with love and pain.
"Yes, miss, you are," she cried, her words all broken. "Whatever 'appens to you—whatever—you'd be a princess all the same—an' nothin' couldn't make you nothin' different."

chapters.title: In the Attic
paragraphs: Sara never forgot the first night she spent in her attic. While it passed, she lived through a wild, grown-up sorrow she never spoke of to anyone. There was no one who would have understood. It was good for her, in fact, that as she lay awake in the darkness her mind was forced now and then to notice the strangeness of her surroundings. It was perhaps good for her that her small body reminded her of physical things. If it had not, the anguish in her young mind might have been too great for a child to bear. But really, while the night passed, she barely knew she had a body at all, or remembered anything except one thought.
"My papa is dead!" she kept whispering to herself. "My papa is dead!"

It was only much later that she realized her bed had been so hard that she turned over and over to find a comfortable spot, that the darkness had felt thicker than any she had ever known, and that the wind had howled across the roof among the chimneys like something wailing aloud. Then there was something worse. There were certain scuffling and scratching and squeaking sounds in the walls and behind the baseboards. She knew what they were, because Becky had described them. They were rats and mice, either fighting each other or playing together. Once or twice she even heard sharp little feet skittering across the floor, and afterwards, when she remembered things, she recalled that the first time she heard them she sat straight up in bed, trembling, and then lay down again and pulled the blankets over her head.
The change in her life did not happen gradually. It happened all at once.
"She must begin as she is to go on," Miss Minchin said to Miss Amelia. "She must be taught at once what to expect."

Mariette had left the house the next morning. The glimpse Sara caught of her sitting room, as she passed its open door, showed her that everything had been changed. Her ornaments and luxuries had been taken away, and a bed had been placed in a corner to turn the room into a new pupil's bedroom.
When she went down to breakfast, she saw that her seat at Miss Minchin's side was now occupied by Lavinia, and Miss Minchin spoke to her coldly.

"You will begin your new duties, Sara," she said, "by sitting with the younger children at a smaller table. You must keep them quiet, see that they behave well, and make sure they do not waste their food. You should have been down earlier. Lottie has already spilled her tea."

That was the beginning, and from day to day more duties were piled on her. She taught the younger children French and listened to their other lessons, and these were the lightest of her chores. They found she could be used in countless ways. She could be sent on errands at any time and in any weather. She could be told to do things other people had skipped. The cook and the housemaids took their cue from Miss Minchin, and rather enjoyed bossing around the "young one" who had been fussed over for so long. They were not the best class of servants. They had neither good manners nor good tempers, and it was often convenient to have someone nearby to blame.

During the first month or two, Sara thought that her willingness to do things as well as she could, and her silence under scolding, might soften the people who drove her so hard. In her proud little heart, she wanted them to see that she was trying to earn her keep, not accepting charity. But the time came when she saw that no one was softened at all. The more willing she was to do as she was told, the more bossy and demanding the careless housemaids became, and the more eager the scolding cook was to blame her.

If she had been older, Miss Minchin would have given her the bigger girls to teach and saved money by firing a teacher. But while she still looked like a child, she could be more useful as a sort of higher-ranking errand girl and maid-of-all-work. An ordinary errand boy would not have been so clever and reliable. Sara could be trusted with difficult assignments and complicated messages. She could even go and pay bills, and on top of that she could dust a room well and tidy things up.

Her own lessons became things of the past. She was taught nothing, and only after long, busy days spent running here and there at everyone's orders was she grudgingly allowed to go into the empty schoolroom with a pile of old books and study alone at night.

"If I do not remind myself of the things I have learned, I might forget them," she said to herself. "I am almost a kitchen maid, and if I am a kitchen maid who knows nothing, I shall be like poor Becky. I wonder if I could quite forget, and start dropping my H's, and not remember that Henry the Eighth had six wives."

One of the strangest things about her new life was her changed position among the pupils. Instead of being a sort of small royal personage among them, she no longer seemed to be one of their group at all. She was kept so constantly at work that she rarely had a chance to speak to any of them, and she could not avoid seeing that Miss Minchin preferred her to live a life apart from the schoolroom girls.

"I will not have her forming close friendships and talking to the other children," that lady said. "Girls love a grievance, and if she begins to tell romantic stories about herself, she will become a poor, mistreated heroine, and parents will get the wrong impression. It is better that she live a separate life — one suited to her circumstances. I am giving her a home, and that is more than she has any right to expect from me."

Sara did not expect much, and was far too proud to keep trying to be close with girls who clearly felt awkward and uncertain about her. The truth was that Miss Minchin's pupils were a dull, matter-of-fact group of young people. They were used to being rich and comfortable. As Sara's dresses grew shorter and shabbier and stranger-looking, and as it became plain that she wore shoes with holes in them and was sent out to buy groceries and carry them through the streets in a basket on her arm whenever the cook needed them in a hurry, the girls felt as if, when they spoke to her, they were addressing a lower servant.

"To think she was the girl with the diamond mines," Lavinia commented. "She looks awful. And she's stranger than ever. I never liked her much, but I can't bear that way she has now of looking at people without speaking — just as if she was figuring them out."
"I am," said Sara promptly when she heard about it. "That's what I look at some people for. I like to know about them. I think them over afterwards."

The truth was that she had spared herself trouble several times by keeping an eye on Lavinia, who was quite ready to make mischief, and would have been rather pleased to make some for the former show pupil.

Sara never made any mischief herself, or interfered with anyone. She worked like a drudge. She trudged through wet streets, carrying parcels and baskets. She labored through the little ones' careless French lessons. As she became shabbier and more forlorn-looking, she was told she had better take her meals downstairs. She was treated as if she were nobody's concern, and her heart grew proud and sore — but she never told anyone how she felt.
"Soldiers don't complain," she would say between her small, tight teeth. "I am not going to do it. I will pretend this is part of a war."
But there were hours when her child's heart might almost have broken with loneliness, if it had not been for three people.

The first, it must be admitted, was Becky — just Becky. Throughout that whole first night in the garret, she had felt a vague comfort knowing that on the other side of the wall, where the rats scuffled and squeaked, there was another young human being. And during the nights that followed, the comfort grew. They had little chance to speak to each other during the day. Each had her own tasks, and any attempt at conversation would have been seen as loitering and wasting time. "Don't mind me, miss," Becky whispered the first morning, "if I don't say nothin' polite. Some'un'd be down on us if I did. I means 'please' an' 'thank you' an' 'beg pardon,' but I dassn't take time to say it."

But before daybreak Becky used to slip into Sara's attic, button her dress, and give her whatever help she needed before she went downstairs to light the kitchen fire. And when night came, Sara always heard the humble knock at her door that meant her little servant was ready to help her again if needed. During the first weeks of her grief Sara felt almost too dazed to talk, so some time passed before they saw much of each other or exchanged visits. Becky's heart told her that people in trouble are best left alone.
The second of the trio of comforters was Ermengarde, but odd things happened before Ermengarde found her place.

When Sara's mind seemed to wake up again to the life around her, she realized she had forgotten that an Ermengarde existed in the world. The two had always been friends, but Sara had felt as if she were years older. There was no denying that Ermengarde was as dull as she was affectionate. She clung to Sara in a simple, helpless way. She brought her lessons to Sara to be helped with. She listened to her every word and pestered her with requests for stories. But Ermengarde herself had nothing interesting to say, and she hated books of every kind. She was, in fact, not a person one would remember when caught in the storm of a great trouble, and Sara forgot her.

It had been all the easier to forget her because she had been suddenly called home for a few weeks. When she came back, she did not see Sara for a day or two, and when she met her for the first time, she ran into her coming down a corridor with her arms full of clothes that had to be taken downstairs to be mended. Sara herself had already been taught to mend them. She looked pale and unlike herself, and she was wearing the strange, outgrown dress whose shortness showed so much thin black leg.

Ermengarde was too slow a girl to handle such a moment. She could not think of anything to say. She knew what had happened, but somehow she had never imagined Sara could look like this — so odd and poor and almost like a servant. It made her quite miserable, and she could do nothing but break into a short, hysterical laugh and exclaim — pointlessly, as if without meaning anything — "Oh, Sara, is that you?"

"Yes," answered Sara, and suddenly a strange thought passed through her mind and made her face flush. She held the pile of clothes in her arms, with her chin resting on top of it to keep it steady. Something in the look of her direct, steady eyes made Ermengarde lose her wits even more. She felt as if Sara had turned into a new kind of girl she had never known. Perhaps it was because Sara had suddenly grown poor and had to mend things and work like Becky.
"Oh," she stammered. "How — how are you?"
"I don't know," Sara replied. "How are you?"
"I'm — I'm quite well," said Ermengarde, overwhelmed with shyness. Then suddenly she thought of something to say that seemed more personal. "Are you — are you very unhappy?" she said in a rush.
Then Sara did something unfair. Just at that moment her torn heart swelled inside her, and she felt that if anyone was as stupid as that, one had better get away from her.
"What do you think?" she said. "Do you think I am very happy?" And she marched past her without another word.

In time she realized that if her own misery had not made her forget things, she would have known that poor, dull Ermengarde was not to be blamed for her clumsy, awkward ways. She was always awkward, and the more she felt, the more stupid she tended to be.
But the sudden thought that had flashed through Sara's mind had made her over-sensitive.
"She is like the others," she had thought. "She does not really want to talk to me. She knows no one does."

So for several weeks a wall stood between them. When they met by chance, Sara looked the other way, and Ermengarde felt too stiff and embarrassed to speak. Sometimes they nodded to each other in passing, but there were times when they did not even exchange a greeting.
"If she would rather not talk to me," Sara thought, "I will keep out of her way. Miss Minchin makes that easy enough."

Miss Minchin made it so easy that in the end they barely saw each other at all. During that time, people noticed that Ermengarde was duller than ever, and that she looked listless and unhappy. She used to sit in the window-seat, huddled in a heap, staring out the window without speaking. Once Jessie, who was passing, stopped to look at her curiously.
"What are you crying for, Ermengarde?" she asked.
"I'm not crying," answered Ermengarde, in a muffled, shaky voice.
"You are," said Jessie. "A great big tear just rolled down the bridge of your nose and dropped off the end of it. And there goes another."
"Well," said Ermengarde, "I'm miserable — and no one need interfere." And she turned her plump back, took out her handkerchief, and boldly hid her face in it.

That night, when Sara went up to her attic, she was later than usual. She had been kept at work until after the hour the pupils went to bed, and then she had gone to her lessons in the lonely schoolroom. When she reached the top of the stairs, she was surprised to see a glimmer of light coming from under the attic door.
"Nobody goes there but me," she thought quickly, "but someone has lit a candle."

Someone had indeed lit a candle, and it was not burning in the kitchen candlestick she was supposed to use, but in one of those that belonged in the pupils' bedrooms. The someone was sitting on the battered footstool, dressed in her nightgown and wrapped up in a red shawl. It was Ermengarde.
"Ermengarde!" cried Sara. She was so startled she was almost frightened. "You will get into trouble."
Ermengarde stumbled up from her footstool. She shuffled across the attic in her bedroom slippers, which were too big for her. Her eyes and nose were pink from crying.
"I know I shall — if I'm found out," she said. "But I don't care — I don't care a bit. Oh, Sara, please tell me. What is the matter? Why don't you like me any more?"

Something in her voice made the familiar lump rise in Sara's throat. It was so affectionate and simple — so like the old Ermengarde who had asked her to be "best friends." It sounded as if she had not meant what she had seemed to mean during the past few weeks.
"I do like you," Sara answered. "I thought — you see, everything is different now. I thought you — were different."
Ermengarde opened her wet eyes wide.
"Why, it was you who were different!" she cried. "You didn't want to talk to me. I didn't know what to do. It was you who were different after I came back."
Sara thought for a moment. She saw that she had made a mistake.

"I am different," she explained, "though not in the way you think. Miss Minchin does not want me to talk to the girls. Most of them don't want to talk to me. I thought — perhaps — you didn't either. So I tried to keep out of your way."

"Oh, Sara," Ermengarde almost wailed in her hurt dismay. And then, after one more look, they rushed into each other's arms. It must be admitted that Sara's small black head lay for some minutes on the shoulder covered by the red shawl. When Ermengarde had seemed to abandon her, she had felt horribly lonely.
Afterwards they sat down on the floor together, Sara hugging her knees with her arms, and Ermengarde wrapped up in her shawl. Ermengarde looked at the odd, big-eyed little face adoringly.

"I couldn't bear it any more," she said. "I dare say you could live without me, Sara, but I couldn't live without you. I was nearly dead. So tonight, when I was crying under the bedclothes, I suddenly thought of creeping up here and just begging you to let us be friends again."

"You are nicer than I am," said Sara. "I was too proud to try to make friends. You see, now that hard times have come, they have shown that I am not a nice child. I was afraid they would. Perhaps" — wrinkling her forehead wisely — "that is what they were sent for."
"I don't see any good in them," said Ermengarde stoutly.
"Neither do I — to be honest," admitted Sara, frankly. "But I suppose there might be good in things, even if we don't see it. There might" — doubtfully — "be good in Miss Minchin."
Ermengarde looked round the attic with rather fearful curiosity.
"Sara," she said, "do you think you can bear living here?"
Sara looked round too.
"If I pretend it's quite different, I can," she answered. "Or if I pretend it is a place in a story."
She spoke slowly. Her imagination was beginning to work for her again. It had not worked at all since her troubles had come on her. She had felt as if it had been stunned.
"Other people have lived in worse places. Think of the Count of Monte Cristo in the dungeons of the Chateau d'If. And think of the people in the Bastille!"

"The Bastille," half whispered Ermengarde, watching her and beginning to be fascinated. She remembered stories of the French Revolution which Sara had been able to fix in her mind by telling them dramatically. No one but Sara could have done it.
A familiar glow came into Sara's eyes.

"Yes," she said, hugging her knees, "that will be a good place to pretend about. I am a prisoner in the Bastille. I have been here for years and years — and years — and everybody has forgotten about me. Miss Minchin is the jailer — and Becky" — a sudden new light joining the glow in her eyes — "Becky is the prisoner in the next cell."
She turned to Ermengarde, looking quite like the old Sara.
"I shall pretend that," she said. "And it will be a great comfort."
Ermengarde was at once delighted and awestruck.

"And will you tell me all about it?" she said. "May I creep up here at night, whenever it is safe, and hear the things you have made up during the day? It will feel as if we were more 'best friends' than ever."
"Yes," answered Sara, nodding. "Hard times test people, and mine has tested you and proved how nice you are."

chapters.title: Melchisedec
paragraphs: Lottie made up the third member of the little group. Still small, she knew nothing of adversity and was bewildered by the change in her young adopted mother. She had heard whispers of strange events in Sara's life, but could not understand her altered appearance. Why the old black frock? Why did Sara now enter the schoolroom only to teach, instead of sitting in her honoured place to learn? Among the little children there had been a great deal of whispering when they discovered that Sara had left the rooms where Emily had reigned for so long. What most troubled Lottie was how little Sara would say in answer to questions. At seven, you need a mystery explained very plainly indeed before you can understand it.

On the first morning Sara taught the little French class, Lottie had asked in confidence, "Sara, are you terribly poor now? As poor as a beggar?" Slipping her fat hand into Sara's slender one, she gazed up with round eyes full of tears. "I don't want you to be that poor."
She seemed on the point of tears, and Sara quickly tried to comfort her.
"A beggar hasn't anywhere to live," she answered bravely. "I've still got somewhere to live."
Lottie pressed her. "Where is it? The new girl has your bedroom now, and it doesn't look pretty any more."
"My room is somewhere else now," Sara replied.
"Is it pretty?" Lottie asked. "I'd like to come and look at it."
Sara said, "You must be quiet. Miss Minchin is watching. She'll be angry with me if I let you go on whispering."
She had already learned that anything anyone objected to would be counted as her fault. Children talking, fidgeting, or failing to pay attention—all of it would bring a reprimand upon Sara.

But Lottie was a very determined little person. If Sara would not reveal where she lived, she meant to discover it for herself. She questioned her small friends, lingered near the older girls, and listened to their gossip. With some information they had let slip without noticing, she set off late one afternoon on an exploring expedition. Up she climbed, on staircases she had never known were there, until she arrived at the attic floor. Two doors stood close together. Opening one of them, she found her beloved Sara standing on an old table and looking through a window.

"Sara! Mamma Sara!" she cried in horror. The attic appalled her: it was ugly and empty and seemed cut off from the whole world. Her short legs felt as though they had climbed hundreds of steps to reach it.

Hearing the voice, Sara turned, and now she was the horrified one. What was going to happen? If Lottie burst into tears and someone heard her, both of them were lost. Sara sprang off the table and hurried across to her.
"Please don't cry or make any noise," she begged. "They'll scold me if you do, and they've been scolding me all day. It isn't—it isn't really such a bad room, Lottie."

"Isn't it?" Lottie gasped, biting her lip as she surveyed the place. She was still a spoiled little girl, but she loved her adopted mother enough to try to restrain herself for her sake. Besides, perhaps anywhere Sara lived could somehow prove to be nice. Almost in a whisper, she asked, "Why isn't it bad, Sara?"
Sara held her tightly and attempted a laugh. The warmth of that plump little body brought a kind of comfort. Her day had been difficult, and her eyes were hot from staring out through the window.
"Up here you can see all kinds of things that aren't visible downstairs," she told her.
"What kinds?" Lottie demanded, with the curiosity Sara knew how to awaken even in much older girls.

"Chimneys right beside us, with smoke twisting into wreaths and clouds before it drifts into the sky. Sparrows hopping around and chatting together as though they were people. Other attic windows, where a head might appear at any moment, leaving you to wonder whose it is. Everything feels so high above the ground—almost like being in another world."
"Oh, I want to look!" Lottie cried. "Lift me up to see!"
Sara lifted her onto the old table and climbed up beside her. Together they leaned against the edge of the flat roof window and peered outside.

Unless you have looked out like this yourself, you cannot know how different that world is. Roof slates stretched away to either side, sloping down towards the rain gutters. At home among them, the sparrows hopped and twittered without a trace of fear. On the nearest chimney, two perched together and quarrelled furiously until one pecked his companion and chased him off. The neighbouring garret window remained closed: the house beside theirs was empty.

"I wish there were someone living next door," said Sara. "It's so near that if another little girl had that attic, we could speak through our windows. We could even climb across to visit, if we weren't frightened of falling."

The sky looked so much closer than it did from the street that Lottie was entranced. Here at the attic window, surrounded by chimney pots, the world's goings-on below hardly seemed real. It was difficult even to believe in Miss Minchin, Miss Amelia, and the schoolroom. Wheels rumbling through the square sounded as though they belonged to an entirely separate life.
Nestling into Sara's protective arm, Lottie exclaimed, "Oh, Sara! I like being in this attic—I really like it! It's better than being downstairs!"
"See that sparrow," Sara murmured. "I wish I had a few crumbs I could throw out for him."
Lottie gave a tiny shriek. "I've got some! There's a piece of bun in my pocket. I spent my penny on it yesterday and kept a little bit."

They scattered a few crumbs, and the sparrow started and fluttered off to a nearby chimney. Clearly he was unused to friendly neighbours in attics; food arriving without warning had alarmed him. But Lottie held perfectly still, and Sara made a soft chirping sound, almost like a sparrow herself. He began to understand that what had frightened him was really an offer of hospitality. Tilting his head, he watched the crumbs from his chimney perch, his eyes bright and twinkling. Lottie could hardly bear to stay motionless.
"Is he coming? Do you think he'll come?" she whispered.
Sara whispered back, "His eyes seem to say so. He's trying and trying to decide if it's safe. Yes, he's going to! Look, here he comes!"

Down he flew, hopping towards the crumbs, then pausing a few inches short of them. Again he tilted his head, as though calculating the possibility that Sara and Lottie were really large cats ready to spring. At last his heart assured him they were kinder than they appeared. Hop by hop, he came closer. With a peck as quick as lightning, he snatched the largest crumb and flew with it to the far side of his chimney.
"Now he KNOWS it's safe," said Sara. "He'll return to fetch the rest."

Return he did, bringing a friend. That friend went off and fetched a relation, and the whole party enjoyed a substantial meal, twittering, chattering, and exclaiming over it. Now and then they paused, cocked their heads, and inspected Sara and Lottie. Lottie's delight swept away her first horrified impression of the attic. When Sara lifted her down from the table, bringing her back, so to speak, to earthly matters, she could show her all sorts of lovely things about the room that she herself would never have imagined were there.

"It's so small, and so far above everything else," she explained, "that it almost feels like a nest in a tree. And what a funny sloping ceiling. Look—at this end you can barely stand upright. When morning begins, I can stay in bed and see straight into the sky through the flat window overhead. It's a square of light. On a day that's going to be sunny, little pink clouds drift past, so close I feel I might touch them. When it rains, the drops keep pattering as if they were saying something pleasant. At night, when the stars come out, you can lie there counting how many fit inside that square. There are so many. And see that tiny rusty grate in the corner. Imagine it polished, with a fire burning inside—wouldn't that be lovely? You see, it really is a beautiful little room."

Holding Lottie's hand, she moved about the tiny room. Her gestures pointed out the beauties she was persuading herself to see, and Lottie saw them too. Whatever picture Sara drew in words, Lottie could always believe it.

"Imagine a thick, soft Indian rug, blue, covering the floor," she continued. "Over there could be a cosy little sofa with cushions for curling up on. Above it, a bookshelf low enough for you to reach the books without getting up. In front of the fire we could have a fur rug, and on the walls there could be hangings to hide the whitewash, and pictures. The pictures would need to be small, but they could still be beautiful. There could be a lamp under a deep rose-coloured shade, and a table in the centre with everything for tea. A little round copper kettle could sing on the hob. Even the bed could change completely: soft inside, with a lovely silk coverlet over it. How beautiful it might be. Perhaps we could coax the sparrows into becoming such good friends that they'd tap on the window with their beaks and ask us to let them in."
Lottie cried, "Oh, Sara! How I'd love to live up here!"

At last Sara persuaded her to return downstairs and saw her safely on her way. Back in the attic, she stood in the centre and looked around. The spell of the lovely pictures she had made for Lottie had faded. Under its shabby quilt, the bed was hard. The whitewashed walls were broken in patches; the floor lay bare and cold. The grate was damaged and rusty, and the only place to sit was a battered footstool leaning sideways on its broken leg. Sara sank onto it for a few minutes and lowered her head into her hands. Somehow Lottie's visit, and her departure, made everything worse—perhaps as prisoners feel still more lonely after their visitors have come and gone, leaving them behind.
"How lonely it is," she said. "Sometimes nowhere in the world could be lonelier."

As she sat there in that position, a small sound nearby caught her attention. She raised her head to find its source. A more nervous child would have jumped from that battered footstool immediately, for a large rat was sitting back on his hindquarters, sniffing with interest. Some crumbs from Lottie's bun had fallen onto the floor, and their smell had tempted him out of his hole.

His curious appearance fascinated Sara: he looked so like a dwarf or gnome with grey whiskers. His bright eyes met hers as though asking a question. He seemed so uncertain that one of Sara's strange little thoughts came to her.

"Being a rat must be rather difficult," she reflected. "No one likes you. Everyone jumps and runs and screams, 'Oh, a horrid rat!' I wouldn't enjoy people jumping and screaming, 'Oh, a horrid Sara!' as soon as they caught sight of me. Or putting out traps for me and making them look like dinner. How different it is for a sparrow. But when this rat was made, nobody asked whether being a rat was what he wanted. No one said, 'Wouldn't you rather be a sparrow?'"

Sara had remained so still that the rat was beginning to feel braver. He was terribly afraid of her, but perhaps, like the sparrow, he had a heart that could tell him she was not the kind of creature that pounced. And he was very hungry. Inside the wall were his wife and many children; for days they had been having dreadful luck. He had left the little ones crying bitterly. A few crumbs seemed worth a considerable risk, and he carefully lowered himself onto all four feet.
"Come along," Sara told him. "I'm no trap. Have the crumbs, you poor thing! People imprisoned in the Bastille used to befriend rats. Why shouldn't I be friends with you?"

I cannot say how animals understand such things, but understand them they certainly do. Perhaps there is a language without words, known to everything in the world. Perhaps a hidden soul lives in everything and can speak to another soul without the smallest sound. Whatever the explanation, from that instant the rat understood that he was safe, rat though he was. The young human sitting on the red footstool would not leap up and frighten him with piercing cries. She would not hurl heavy things at him, which might crush him where they fell or leave him limping as he scrambled home to his hole. He was, in fact, a very nice rat with no wish to hurt anybody. Standing upright and sniffing, with his bright eyes on Sara, he had hoped she would realize that, instead of hating him at once as an enemy. When the mysterious voice that uses no words assured him that she would understand, he moved gently towards the crumbs and started eating. Now and again he looked up at Sara, just as the sparrows had. There was something so apologetic in his expression that it touched her heart.

She sat watching him without making the slightest movement. Among the crumbs lay one much larger piece—hardly a crumb at all, really. He plainly longed for it, but it was close to the footstool, and some of his shyness remained.
"I think he'd like to take that home to his family in the wall," Sara thought. "Perhaps he'll fetch it if I keep perfectly still."

So intent was she that she barely let herself breathe. The rat edged nearer, ate some smaller crumbs, and paused to sniff delicately, casting a sideways look at the child on the footstool. Then, with a sudden boldness much like the sparrow's, he dashed at the piece of bun. No sooner had he seized it than he ran to the wall, slipped through a crack in the skirting board, and disappeared.
"I was sure it was for his children," Sara said. "I really think we could become friends."

About a week later, Ermengarde found one of her rare safe opportunities to creep up to the attic. She tapped lightly with her fingertips, but Sara took two or three minutes to answer. At first the room was so silent that Ermengarde wondered whether she might be asleep. Then, to her astonishment, she heard a quiet little laugh and Sara's voice coaxing somebody.
"There you are!" she heard Sara say. "Take it home with you, Melchisedec! Off you go to your wife!"
A moment later Sara opened the door. Ermengarde stood on the threshold, staring at her with frightened eyes.
"Sara, who—who ARE you speaking to?" she gasped.
Sara carefully drew her inside, with a look of mingled pleasure and amusement.
"First you must promise you won't be frightened or give even the tiniest scream," she replied. "Otherwise I can't tell you."

Ermengarde almost screamed then and there, but held herself back. She searched the attic with her eyes and could see nobody. Yet Sara had unmistakably been speaking TO somebody. Ghosts came into her mind.
"Is it—is it something frightening?" she asked in a timid voice.
"Some people find them frightening," Sara answered. "I did myself at first, but I don't any more."
Trembling, Ermengarde asked, "Was it—a ghost?"
Sara laughed. "No, it was my rat."
In a single leap Ermengarde landed in the centre of the small, shabby bed. She drew her feet beneath her nightgown and red shawl. No scream came, but she gasped in terror.
Under her breath she cried, "Oh! Oh! A rat! A rat!"
"I thought you might be afraid," said Sara. "But there's no need. I'm teaching him to be tame. He really recognizes me, and when I call, he comes out. Are you too frightened to have a look at him?"

In truth, as the days passed, scraps carried upstairs from the kitchen had helped their unusual friendship grow. Sara had gradually stopped remembering that the shy little creature she was getting to know was, after all, only a rat.

At first Ermengarde could do nothing but curl into a frightened heap on the bed, keeping her feet well tucked away. Gradually, though, Sara's calm little face and her account of Melchisedec's first visit stirred her curiosity. She leaned over the bedside and watched Sara cross the room and kneel beside the hole in the skirting board.
"He—he isn't going to dash out and leap onto the bed, is he?" she asked.
"No," Sara assured her. "His manners are as good as ours. He's exactly like a person. Watch him now!"

A soft whistle came from her lips, so quiet and coaxing that only perfect silence could have made it audible. She repeated it several times, wholly absorbed.
