To Ermengarde, she seemed to be casting a spell. At length, apparently answering the summons, a grey-whiskered head with bright eyes peered out of the hole. Sara let the crumbs in her hand fall to the floor. Melchisedec emerged without a sound and ate them. One larger piece he picked up and carried home with an air of brisk efficiency.

"That one's for his wife and children, you see," Sara explained. "He's very kind. He keeps only the little crumbs for himself. Whenever he goes home, I hear his family squeaking happily. I can tell three different sorts of squeak: the children's, Mrs. Melchisedec's, and Melchisedec's own."
A laugh escaped Ermengarde.
"Oh, Sara!" she exclaimed. "You really ARE strange—but you're nice."

"I know I'm strange," Sara agreed happily, "and I do TRY to be nice." She passed her small brown paw across her forehead, looking puzzled and tender. "Papa was always laughing at me, and I liked him doing it. He thought I was strange, but he enjoyed my make-believe. I—I can't stop inventing things. Without that, I don't think I could live." She broke off to look around the attic, then added softly, "Certainly not here. I couldn't live here."
As always, Ermengarde listened with interest. "When you describe things," she said, "it's as if they become real. The way you speak of Melchisedec makes him sound like a person."

"But he IS a person," Sara replied. "He feels hunger and fear just like us. He has a wife and children. Who can say he doesn't have thoughts the way we do? His eyes look like a person's eyes to me. That's the reason I named him."
She settled on the floor, clasping her knees in the way she liked best.
"Besides, he's a rat from the Bastille, sent here to befriend me," she added. "There's always a scrap of bread the cook has discarded, and that's quite enough to keep him fed."
Ermengarde asked eagerly, "Is this still the Bastille? Do you pretend you're in the Bastille all the time?"
"Almost all the time," Sara said. "Now and then I try to imagine some different place. Usually the Bastille is easiest, especially in cold weather."
Just then a noise startled Ermengarde so badly that she nearly sprang off the bed. It sounded like two separate knocks against the wall.
"What's making that noise?" she exclaimed.
Rising from the floor, Sara replied with considerable drama:
"The prisoner in the cell beside mine is knocking."
"Becky!" exclaimed Ermengarde in delight.
"Yes," Sara replied. "Listen. Two knocks say, 'Prisoner, are you there?'"
She gave three answering taps against the wall herself.
"And that says, 'Yes, I am here, and all is well.'"
From Becky's side came four taps in reply.
Sara interpreted them: "Those say, 'Then, fellow-sufferer, we will sleep in peace. Good night.'"
Ermengarde's whole face shone with pleasure.
"Oh, Sara!" she whispered happily. "It's just like being in a story!"
"It IS a story," Sara answered. "EVERYTHING'S a story. You're one, and I'm one, and Miss Minchin is a story too."

Sitting down again, she talked on until Ermengarde forgot that she, too, was something of an escaped prisoner. Sara finally had to remind her that she could not spend the entire night in the Bastille: she must slip silently downstairs and steal back into the bed she had left empty.

chapters.title: The Indian Gentleman
paragraphs: But journeys to the attic were risky for Ermengarde and Lottie. Neither could be certain of finding Sara there, and they could almost never be sure that Miss Amelia would not come inspecting the bedrooms after the girls were meant to be asleep. Their visits were therefore few, and Sara's life grew strange and solitary. Downstairs she was even lonelier than in her attic. There was nobody to talk to. Sent on errands, she would walk the streets with a basket or parcel, a forlorn little figure trying to keep her hat on in the wind or feeling the rain work its way through her shoes. The hurrying crowds only seemed to deepen her isolation. In the days of Princess Sara, when she drove in her brougham or went walking with Mariette, people had often turned to watch the bright, eager face and the striking coats and hats. A happy child, beautifully looked after, naturally draws the eye. Poorly dressed, shabby children are neither unusual nor pretty enough to make passers-by turn and smile. These days nobody looked at Sara. As she hurried along the busy pavements, it seemed nobody even saw her. She had begun growing rapidly, and only the plainest remnants of her old wardrobe were left to clothe her. She knew how peculiar she must look. Everything valuable had been sold or otherwise disposed of; she was expected to keep wearing what remained as long as she could get into it at all. Now and then, passing a shop window with a mirror, the glimpse of herself almost made her laugh aloud. At other times it brought the colour to her face, and she bit her lip and looked away.

In the evenings, lighted windows offered glimpses of warm rooms. Sara entertained herself by inventing lives for the people she saw gathered around tables or sitting beside fires. Catching these glimpses before the shutters closed always interested her. In her own way, she had become well acquainted with several households in Miss Minchin's square. Her favourite was the Large Family. The name described their numbers rather than their size, since most of them were quite small. There were eight children, a round, rosy mother, a round, rosy father, a round, rosy grandmother, and more servants than she could count. The children were always doing something. Comfortable-looking nurses took them walking or wheeled them out in perambulators; sometimes they went for a drive with their mamma. In the evening they flew to the door to welcome their papa, kissing him, dancing around him, pulling off his overcoat, and hunting through its pockets for parcels. Or they crowded the nursery windows, peering out, jostling one another, and laughing. There was always some pleasant activity perfectly suited to a large family's tastes. Sara had grown very fond of them and borrowed wonderfully romantic names from books to give them. When she was not calling them the Large Family, she called them the Montmorencys. The plump, fair baby in the lace cap became Ethelberta Beauchamp Montmorency; the next baby was Violet Cholmondeley Montmorency. The little boy with the round legs, only just able to toddle, was Sydney Cecil Vivian Montmorency. After him came Lilian Evangeline Maud Marion, Rosalind Gladys, Guy Clarence, Veronica Eustacia, and Claude Harold Hector.
Something rather funny happened one evening—although, from another point of view, there was perhaps nothing funny about it at all.

Several Montmorencys were clearly off to a children's party. As Sara approached their door, they were crossing to the carriage waiting beside the pavement. Veronica Eustacia and Rosalind Gladys, wearing white lace dresses with beautiful sashes, had just climbed inside. Five-year-old Guy Clarence came next. He was such a lovely little boy, with rosy cheeks, blue eyes, and a dear round head covered in curls, that Sara quite forgot both her basket and her shabby cloak. Indeed, she forgot everything except her wish to look at him a little longer. She stopped and watched.

It was Christmas, and the Large Family had been hearing story after story about poor children. These children had no mammas and papas to fill stockings or take them to the pantomime; they were cold and hungry, with too little to wear. In every story, a kind person would notice them—sometimes a tender-hearted little boy or girl—and give them money or splendid presents, or bring them home to a beautiful dinner. That very afternoon one such tale had made Guy Clarence cry. Ever since, he had longed to find a poor child and present her with a particular sixpence of his own, thus securing her comfort for the rest of her life. Surely a whole sixpence would make her rich for ever. Now, crossing the red carpet laid over the pavement between the front door and the carriage, he had that very coin in the pocket of his extremely short man-o-war trousers. Just as Rosalind Gladys climbed in and bounced on the seat to feel its springy cushions, he noticed Sara. In her worn dress and hat, her old basket over her arm, she stood on the wet pavement looking hungrily at him.

He supposed her hungry eyes meant she had gone without food for a long time. He could not know that she longed for the warmth and happiness of his home, reflected in his rosy face, or that she ached to gather him into her arms and kiss him. All he saw were large eyes, a thin face, thin legs, poor clothes, and an ordinary basket. Reaching into his pocket, he found the sixpence and approached her with kindly purpose.
"Here you are, poor little girl," he told her. "I've got a sixpence here, and it's for you."

Sara started. Suddenly she understood: she looked exactly like the poor children who, in her happier days, had stood on the pavement watching her step down from her brougham. Many times she had given those children pennies. Her face flushed, then turned pale. For one instant, accepting that dear little sixpence seemed impossible.
"Oh, no!" she replied. "No, thank you—really, I mustn't accept it!"

There was so little of the ordinary street child in her voice, and such good breeding in her manner, that Veronica Eustacia, whose actual name was Janet, and Rosalind Gladys, really Nora, bent forward to hear her.
Guy Clarence, however, had no intention of letting anyone frustrate his kindness. He pressed the sixpence into her palm.
"You must have it, poor little girl!" he declared firmly. "It will buy you something to eat. It's an entire sixpence!"

His face held such openhearted kindness, and he seemed so certain to be miserably disappointed by a refusal, that Sara knew she must accept. Pride carried that far would become cruelty. So she really did put her pride in her pocket, although, it must be confessed, her cheeks were burning.

"Thank you," she said. "You are a kind, kind little darling thing." He clambered happily into the carriage, and she walked on, doing her best to smile. Her breath caught, however, and a mist shone in her eyes. She had known she looked shabby and odd. Until that moment, she had not realized she could be mistaken for a beggar.
As the Large Family drove off, the children in the carriage began an eager, excited discussion.
Janet exclaimed in alarm, "Oh, Donald"—Guy Clarence's real name—"why did you give that little girl your sixpence? I'm quite sure she isn't a beggar!"
"Her voice wasn't a beggar's voice!" Nora cried. "And really, her face didn't look like one either!"
"And she never asked for anything," Janet added. "I was terribly worried you'd make her angry. People don't like being mistaken for beggars when that isn't what they are, you know."

A little troubled but holding his ground, Donald replied, "She wasn't cross. She laughed a tiny bit, and she called me a kind, kind little darling thing. And I was!" he insisted. "I gave her my whole sixpence."
Janet looked at Nora, and Nora looked back.
"No beggar girl would say a thing like that," Janet concluded. "She'd have said, 'Thank yer kindly, little gentleman—thank yer, sir,' and maybe dipped a curtsy as well."

Sara did not know it, but from then on the Large Family took as deep an interest in her as she took in them. When she passed, faces appeared at the nursery windows. Around the fire, they talked about her again and again.
"She does some sort of servant's work at the seminary," Janet said. "I don't think she has anyone of her own. I think she's an orphan. But however shabby her clothes are, she's certainly no beggar."

After that, the whole family called her "The-little-girl-who-is-not-a-beggar." Naturally, this was a rather lengthy name, and when the smallest children hurried through it, it sometimes sounded extremely funny.

Sara managed to pierce the sixpence and thread it onto an old narrow ribbon, which she wore around her neck. Her love for the Large Family grew, just as her love grew for anything to which she could give it. Becky became dearer to her every day. She began looking forward to the two mornings each week when she went into the schoolroom to teach French to the youngest girls. Her little pupils adored her and competed to stand beside her, slipping their small hands into hers. Their closeness nourished her hungry heart. The sparrows grew so friendly that she had only to climb onto the table, lean her head and shoulders through the attic window, and chirp. Almost at once there would be fluttering wings and answering calls, and a small flock of dingy city birds would settle on the slates to converse with her and feast on the scattered crumbs. Melchisedec's trust had grown so complete that he sometimes brought Mrs. Melchisedec along, and occasionally a child or two as well. Sara would talk to him; somehow, his expression made it seem that he understood every word.

A rather strange feeling about Emily had taken shape in Sara's mind. The doll sat there always, silently witnessing everything, and one moment of terrible loneliness had started the feeling. Sara longed to believe—or pretend to believe—that Emily could understand and sympathize. She could not bear to admit that her only companion was incapable of feeling or hearing anything. Sometimes she placed Emily on a chair and sat opposite on the old red footstool. She would stare and invent things about her until her own eyes widened with something close to fear. This happened especially at night, in the deep quiet, when the only attic sounds were occasional scurries and squeaks from Melchisedec's family inside the wall. In one of her make-believes, Emily was a good witch, able to protect her. At times, after staring until her imagination was stretched to its furthest point, Sara asked questions and ALMOST felt certain that an answer would come at any moment. No answer ever did.

Trying to comfort herself, Sara said, "But when it comes to answering, I don't say much myself. If I can help it, I don't answer at all. When someone insults you, nothing works better than silence—just looking at them and THINKING. Miss Minchin goes white with fury when I do that. Miss Amelia looks scared, and the other girls do too. If you refuse to lose your temper, people realize you're stronger than they are. You have enough strength to keep your anger inside, while they haven't, and out come foolish things they regret saying afterwards. Anger is stronger than almost anything, except whatever helps you control it—that's stronger still. Keeping quiet with your enemies is a good thing. I hardly ever answer mine. Perhaps Emily is more like me than I am myself. She may prefer not to answer even her friends. She keeps everything inside her heart."

She tried to find satisfaction in these arguments, but it was difficult. There were long, exhausting days of being sent first here, then there, sometimes far through wind, cold, and rain. She would return hungry and wet, only to be sent straight out again: nobody cared to remember that she was a child, whose slender legs could ache and whose little body could be chilled. Her thanks were harsh words and cold, contemptuous glances. Sometimes the cook was coarse and insulting, Miss Minchin was in her foulest mood, and the other girls sneered together at Sara's worn clothes. After such days, imagination could not always soothe that hurt, proud, lonely heart. Emily merely sat stiffly on her old chair, staring, and Sara could not always find comfort in pretending.

On one of those nights, she reached the attic cold and hungry, with a storm raging inside her. Emily's gaze seemed so empty, her sawdust arms and legs so incapable of expression, that Sara's self-control broke completely. There was only Emily—nobody else in all the world. And Emily simply sat.
At first she said, "Soon I shall die."
Emily only looked on.

The poor child trembled. "I can't stand it," she said. "I know I'm going to die. I'm freezing and wet and dying of hunger. Today I've walked a thousand miles, and all they've done from morning to night is scold. Because I couldn't find the last thing the cook sent me to buy, they refused to give me supper. My worn-out shoes made me slip into the mud, and some men laughed at me. Look—I'm covered in mud still. And they laughed. Can you hear me?"

She stared into the glass eyes and that satisfied, untroubled face. Suddenly a heartbroken sort of fury swept through her. With one fierce little hand she knocked Emily from the chair and burst into violent sobs—Sara, who never cried at all.

"You're only a DOLL!" she cried. "Only a doll—doll—doll! Nothing matters to you. There's nothing inside you but sawdust. You've never had a heart, and nothing could ever make you feel anything. You're a DOLL!" On the floor Emily's legs were folded disgracefully back over her head, and the tip of her nose had acquired a flat patch. Yet she remained calm, almost dignified. Sara buried her face in her arms. Inside the wall, the rats began scrambling and squealing, biting and fighting one another. Melchisedec was disciplining some members of his family.

Little by little the sobbing subsided. Breaking down was so foreign to Sara that her own behaviour surprised her. Eventually she lifted her face and looked towards Emily, who appeared to be peering around the bend of one leg. Somehow there now seemed to be a glassy-eyed sympathy in that gaze. Sara stooped to lift her. Remorse came over her, and she even allowed herself a tiny smile at her own foolishness.

With a resigned sigh she said, "Being a doll isn't your fault, any more than Lavinia and Jessie can help having no sense. We're not all made the same. Perhaps you do the best that sawdust can." She kissed Emily, shook out and straightened her clothes, and restored her to the chair.

Sara had been longing for somebody to move into the empty house beside them. It was the attic window, so close to her own, that made her wish it. How pleasant it would be if one day that window were propped open and somebody's head and shoulders appeared through its square opening.
"If the face seemed friendly," she thought, "I could start with 'Good morning,' and then anything might happen. Though, of course, nobody but the lower servants is really likely to sleep up there."

One morning, coming back around the square after errands at the grocer's, the butcher's, and the baker's, she saw something delightful. While she had been away for rather a long time, a furniture van had pulled up outside the house next door. The front doors stood wide open, and men in shirtsleeves carried heavy parcels and furniture in and out.
"Someone's taken it!" she said. "Someone really HAS! Oh, please let a nice head appear in that attic window!"

She almost wished she could join the idlers on the pavement, who had gathered to watch the unloading. A look at the furniture, she thought, might allow her to guess something about the people who owned it.

"Miss Minchin's chairs and tables are exactly like her," she reflected. "Even though I was so little then, I remember noticing it the instant I met her. Afterwards I told papa, and he laughed and agreed. The Large Family must have plump, comfortable sofas and armchairs. I can see that their wallpaper, with its red flowers, is just like them—warm and cheerful, kind-looking and happy."

Later she was sent to the greengrocer for parsley. As she came up the area steps from the basement, her heart suddenly quickened with recognition. Several pieces from the van stood on the pavement: a lovely table of intricately worked teakwood, chairs, and a screen dressed in rich Oriental embroidery. Looking at them filled her with a strange homesickness. In India she had seen things so much like these. Among the possessions Miss Minchin had taken away was a carved teakwood desk sent to her by her father.
"Such beautiful things," she said. "They seem as though they should belong to somebody nice. Everything looks quite grand. I imagine the family must be rich."

Throughout the day one van arrived, was emptied, and made way for the next. Sara happened several times to be in a position to see the furniture going inside. Soon it was clear that her guess about the newcomers' wealth had been correct. Everything was handsome and costly, and much of it Oriental. From the vans came magnificent rugs, hangings, and ornaments, many pictures, and enough books to furnish a library. Among the objects was a splendid image of the god Buddha, housed in a superb shrine.

Sara thought, "Somebody in that family MUST have lived in India. They've grown used to Indian things and love having them. I AM pleased. Even if no head ever comes out of the attic window, I'll feel they're friends of mine."

That evening, while fetching the cook's milk—there seemed no odd job she was not expected to perform—Sara saw something that made the new household more intriguing still. The handsome, rosy father of the Large Family crossed the square quite casually and ran up the next house's steps. He moved as though perfectly at home, expecting to use those steps many times in the future. He remained inside for a long while, coming out repeatedly to instruct the workmen with the air of someone fully entitled to do so. Clearly he knew the new arrivals intimately in some way and was managing things on their behalf.
"If children are moving in," Sara mused, "the Large Family children are certain to visit and play. And just for fun, they MIGHT climb all the way to the attic."
When work was over that night, Becky visited her fellow prisoner, bringing some news with her.

"There's a Nindian gentleman movin' in next door, miss," she reported. "Can't say if he's a black gentleman, but he's a Nindian one, sure enough. He's rich as anything, an' sick, an' the Large Family gentleman does his lawyerin'. He's had terrible troubles, an' they've made him poorly an' downhearted. He worships idols, miss. A heathen, he is, bowin' to wood an' stone. I saw them carryin' in an idol for him to worship. Someone ought to give him a tract. A penny'll buy you one."
Sara gave a small laugh.
"I don't think that idol is there for him to worship," she said. "People sometimes keep them simply because they're interesting to look at. Papa owned a beautiful one, and he never worshipped it."

Becky, however, rather preferred the idea that their neighbour was "an 'eathen." It seemed much more romantic than an ordinary gentleman attending church with his prayer book. That evening she talked for a long time about what he might be like, and about his wife, if there was a wife, and his children, if there were children. Sara could see her secret hope: that the whole family would be black and wear turbans, and, most exciting of all, that they would all be "'eathens" like their father.
"Never had heathens livin' next door to me before, miss," she said. "I'd like to find out how they go about things."

Several weeks passed before she learned the answer. The new resident, it turned out, had neither a wife nor children. Alone in the world, without any family at all, he was plainly broken in health and deeply unhappy.

One day a carriage stopped outside the house. The footman climbed down from the box to open its door. First out came the father of the Large Family, followed by a uniformed nurse. Two men-servants then came down the front steps to help their master. When they lifted him from the carriage, Sara saw a man with a worn, suffering face and a body like a skeleton, swathed in furs. They carried him up the steps while the Large Family's father accompanied him, visibly anxious. Soon afterwards another carriage arrived, bringing a doctor, who went inside, evidently to attend the sick man.
Later, during French, Lottie whispered, "Sara, the gentleman next door is so yellow. Is he a Chinee, do you think? Our geography says Chinee men are yellow."
"He isn't Chinese," Sara whispered in reply. "He's terribly ill. Get on with your exercise, Lottie. 'Non, monsieur. Je n'ai pas le canif de mon oncle.'"
That was how the story of the Indian gentleman began.

chapters.title: Ram Dass
paragraphs: Even the square sometimes had beautiful sunsets, though from below you saw only pieces of them between chimney stacks and above the roofs. From the kitchen windows the sunset itself was invisible. You could only guess at it from the warmth spreading over the bricks, a brief rose or yellow colour in the air, or a sudden blaze reflected from some distant pane. There was one place, however, where all its splendour lay open: red and golden clouds piled in the west, purple masses rimmed with dazzling light, little woolly clouds flushed pink. When the wind blew, these last rushed across the blue like flocks of pink doves. The place to see it all, and to feel you were breathing cleaner air at the same time, was naturally the attic window. Whenever the square began to glow as if enchanted, looking wonderful despite its soot-black trees and railings, Sara knew the sky was doing something remarkable. If she could possibly leave the kitchen without being missed or summoned back, she slipped away and crept up all the stairs. She climbed onto the old table and leaned her head and body as far through the window as she could. Once there, she always took a deep breath and gazed about. The whole sky and world seemed to belong to her alone. No one ever appeared at the neighbouring attics. Usually their skylights were shut, but even when they stood open for air, nobody came near. Sara would remain there, sometimes lifting her face to the blue overhead, so close and friendly, like a lovely arched ceiling. At other times she watched the west and its transformations: clouds dissolving, drifting, or waiting quietly to turn pink, crimson, snowy white, purple, or soft dove-grey. They formed islands, or great mountains around lakes of deep turquoise-blue, liquid amber, and chrysoprase-green. Dark headlands sometimes reached into strange, forgotten seas; narrow stretches of marvellous country linked one marvellous country to another. There seemed places to run, to climb, to stand waiting for whatever might appear next—until everything melted and you might float away yourself. That, at least, was how Sara saw it. Nothing had ever looked more beautiful to her than these sights from the old table, with half her body through the skylight and sparrows twittering softly on the slates in the evening light. Whenever these wonders unfolded, she always thought their voices grew especially quiet and gentle.

A few days after the Indian gentleman arrived at his new home, just such a sunset appeared. Luckily the afternoon's kitchen work was finished, and no one had told Sara to run an errand or undertake another task. Slipping away upstairs was easier than usual.

She climbed onto the table to look out. What a moment it was. Molten gold flooded the west, like a magnificent tide sweeping across the world. The air glowed a deep, rich yellow, against which birds crossing over the rooftops appeared perfectly black.
Sara murmured to herself, "This is a Splendid one. It almost frightens me, as if something extraordinary were about to happen. That's always how the Splendid ones make me feel."

A sound only a few yards away made her turn abruptly. It was a peculiar, squeaky chatter, coming from the next attic's window. Somebody else had climbed up to watch the sunset. A head and part of a body rose through the skylight, but they belonged to neither a little girl nor a housemaid. The striking figure was wrapped in white, with a dark face, bright eyes, and a white turban: an Indian man-servant. "A Lascar," Sara thought at once. In his arms, held with evident affection, was a small monkey. It snuggled against his chest, chattering, and it was the source of the sound she had heard.

As she turned towards him, he turned towards her. Her first thought was how sad and homesick his dark face appeared. She felt certain he had come upstairs for a glimpse of the sun, having seen so little of it in England that he longed for it. For a moment she watched with interest, then smiled at him across the roof. She had learned what comfort a smile could give, even a stranger's.

Plainly her smile pleased him. His expression changed completely. In his answering smile, his teeth shone so white that it seemed a lamp had been lit within his dark face. That friendly look in Sara's eyes could do a great deal for people who were weary or unhappy.

Perhaps he relaxed his grip on the monkey while making his greeting. The little creature was mischievous, always eager for an adventure, and the sight of a little girl probably excited him. Suddenly he wriggled free, leapt onto the slates, raced chattering across them, and sprang onto Sara's shoulder. From there he jumped straight into her attic. Sara laughed in delight, but knew he must be returned to his master—if the Lascar was his master. How was she to manage it? Would he allow her to pick him up? Or would he misbehave, evade her, perhaps escape across the rooftops and become lost? That must not happen. He might belong to the Indian gentleman, and perhaps the poor sick man loved him.

She turned back to the Lascar, thankful that some of the Hindustani she had learned while living with her father remained in her memory. She could explain herself to him. Using his own language, she spoke.
"Can I catch him, do you think?" she asked.

She had never, she thought, seen a face show such astonishment and joy as his did at the sound of those familiar words. To the poor man, it was as though his gods had intervened and the little voice's kindness came straight from heaven. Sara immediately recognized that he was used to European children. Respectful thanks poured from him. He was Missee Sahib's servant. The monkey was good and would never bite, but catching him was unfortunately another matter. He darted like lightning from place to place. Disobedient he might be, but he was not wicked. Ram Dass knew him like his own child. Sometimes the creature would obey Ram Dass, though not always. If Missee Sahib permitted it, Ram Dass could come across the roof himself, enter through her window, and retrieve the unworthy little animal. Yet he clearly feared she might consider this a serious liberty and refuse him entry.
Sara, however, agreed to let him come immediately.
"Are you able to cross?" she asked.
He replied, "In no time at all."
"Please come, then," she said. "He's racing all around the room, from one side to the other, as if he's scared."

Ram Dass slid out of his window and crossed to Sara's with the light, sure steps of someone who had spent his life walking roofs. He slipped through the opening and landed noiselessly. Turning to Sara, he made another salaam. At the sight of him the monkey gave a small shriek. Ram Dass quickly closed the skylight as a precaution and began the pursuit. It did not last long. The monkey kept it going for a few minutes, seemingly for his own amusement, then jumped chattering onto Ram Dass's shoulder. There he stayed, still chattering, one strange little skinny arm clasped around the man's neck.

Ram Dass thanked Sara with profound gratitude. She had noticed how swiftly his Indian eyes had surveyed the attic's bare, shabby condition. Nevertheless, he addressed her like a rajah's little daughter and behaved as though he had noticed nothing. After recovering the monkey, he did not presume to linger beyond a few moments. Those moments he spent bowing deeply in further thanks for her kindness. Stroking the monkey, he explained that this little wicked one was really less wicked than he appeared. His master was ill, and the creature sometimes entertained him. Losing his favourite would have made him very sad. With one final salaam, Ram Dass climbed through the skylight and crossed the slates as nimbly as the monkey had done before him.

After he left, Sara stood in the centre of the attic, thinking of everything his face and behaviour had brought back. His Indian dress and deeply respectful manner stirred memories of her whole past. How strange to remember that only a few years earlier she—the drudge whom the cook had insulted scarcely an hour ago—had been surrounded by people who treated her exactly as Ram Dass had. They made salaams as she passed; when she spoke, they bowed until their foreheads almost met the ground. They had been her servants and her slaves. It seemed like something dreamed. Now it was over and could never return. Certainly there appeared no possible way for anything to change. She understood the future Miss Minchin had planned for her. Until she was old enough to be a proper teacher, she must serve as errand girl and servant, while somehow retaining everything she knew and mysteriously acquiring still more knowledge. Most evenings were supposed to be devoted to study. At irregular intervals she was examined, knowing that any failure to make the expected progress would earn a severe rebuke. In fact, Miss Minchin understood that Sara's eagerness to learn made teachers unnecessary. Provide books, and she would devour them, ending by knowing them by heart. In a few years she could be relied on to teach a considerable range of subjects. Then her drudgery would simply move into the schoolroom from the other rooms of the house. They would have to supply more respectable clothes, but would certainly choose plain, ugly ones that somehow still made her look like a servant. That seemed the whole future awaiting her. For several minutes she stood motionless, considering it.
Then a familiar thought returned, bringing colour to her cheeks and a spark to her eyes. She drew her thin little frame upright and raised her head.

"Whatever happens, one thing can't be changed," she said. "Even a princess wearing rags can remain a princess inside. In cloth of gold it would be easy. The real triumph is staying a princess all the time when nobody knows that's what you are. Think of Marie Antoinette in prison, with her throne lost, wearing nothing but a black dress. Her hair had turned white, and people insulted her and called her Widow Capet. She seemed far more a queen then than in the happy days when everything around her was magnificent. That's when I like her best. All those howling crowds couldn't frighten her. Even when they cut off her head, she was stronger than they were."

By now this was an old thought, not a new one. It had comforted Sara through many bitter days. She would move about the house wearing an expression Miss Minchin could neither understand nor tolerate, as though the child inhabited some private life that raised her above the rest of the world. Rude and sour remarks seemed scarcely to reach her; if she heard them, they seemed to leave her quite unmoved. Sometimes, in the middle of a harsh, bullying speech, Miss Minchin found those quiet, unchildlike eyes resting on her with what looked like a proud smile inside them. She had no idea that Sara was thinking:

"You have no idea you're speaking to a princess like this. If I wanted, a wave of my hand could send you to execution. I'm sparing you only because I'm a princess, and you're a poor, foolish, unkind, vulgar old creature who doesn't know any better."

Nothing else interested and amused her quite so much. Odd and fanciful though the notion was, it gave her comfort and did her good. While she held onto it, the spite and rudeness around her could not turn her spiteful and rude in return.
"A princess has to be courteous," she reminded herself.
So when the servants copied their mistress's tone, speaking insolently and ordering her about, Sara kept her head high. She answered with a curious politeness that often left them staring.

Sometimes the cook chuckled over it. "That young one's got more airs and graces than if she'd come out of Buckingham Palace," she said. "She makes me lose my temper often enough, but I will give her this: her manners never leave her. 'If you please, cook'; 'Will you be so kind, cook?' 'I beg your pardon, cook'; 'May I trouble you, cook?' She scatters them round the kitchen as if they cost nothing."

The morning after meeting Ram Dass and his monkey, Sara was in the classroom with her small pupils. Their lesson over, she gathered the French exercise books together. As she worked, she thought of the tasks royal people in disguise had been made to perform. There was Alfred the Great, burning cakes and having his ears boxed by the neat-herd's wife. How terrified the woman must have been on discovering what she had done. Suppose Miss Minchin discovered that she, Sara, with her toes nearly poking out of her boots, was a princess—a real princess! That thought brought precisely the expression to Sara's eyes that Miss Minchin hated most. She would not tolerate it. Standing close by and suddenly furious, she rushed at Sara and boxed her ears, exactly as the neat-herd's wife had struck King Alfred. Sara started, shocked awake from her dream. Catching her breath, she remained still for a second. Then, before she knew she was going to, she gave a little laugh.
"You bold, insolent child, what is there to laugh at?" Miss Minchin demanded.
With her cheeks red and stinging from the blows, Sara needed a few seconds to regain enough control to remind herself that she was a princess.
She replied, "I was thinking."
Miss Minchin said, "Ask my pardon at once."
For one second, Sara paused before answering her.
"If laughing was rude, I'll ask your pardon for that," she said at last. "But I won't apologize for having thoughts."
"What thoughts?" demanded Miss Minchin. "How dare you think at all? Tell me what you were thinking."

Jessie giggled; she and Lavinia nudged one another. All around the room girls raised their heads from their books to listen. They always found Miss Minchin's attacks on Sara rather interesting. Sara invariably said something curious and never appeared remotely frightened. She was not frightened now either, although her ears were scarlet where they had been struck and her eyes shone like stars.
With grand courtesy Sara answered, "I was thinking that you didn't realize what it was you were doing."
Miss Minchin almost gasped for breath. "I didn't realize what I was doing?"

"Yes," Sara replied. "I was imagining what would happen if you boxed my ears and I turned out to be a princess—what I'd do to you. And I thought that, if I were one, nothing I said or did would make you dare to strike me. Then I thought how astonished and afraid you'd be if you suddenly discovered—"

The imagined future was so vivid to her that even Miss Minchin felt the force of her manner. For a moment, that narrow mind, so lacking in imagination, almost believed there must be some actual power behind such open fearlessness.
"What?" she demanded. "Discovered what, exactly?"
Sara said, "That I was a real princess and could do anything at all—anything I wanted."
Every eye in the room opened as wide as it could. Lavinia bent forward in her seat for a better look.
Breathless, Miss Minchin cried, "Go straight to your room, this instant! Out of the classroom! Young ladies, get back to your lessons!"
Sara gave a small bow.
"If my laughter was impolite, please excuse it," she said. She left Miss Minchin struggling to contain her fury while the other girls whispered behind their books.
Jessie burst out, "Did you look at her? Did you notice that strange expression? It wouldn't surprise me one bit if she turned out to be somebody. Just imagine if she did!"

chapters.title: The Other Side of the Wall
paragraphs: Living in a row of houses, you can find yourself wondering what people are saying and doing just beyond the wall of your own room. Sara enjoyed imagining the lives concealed on the other side of the wall between the Select Seminary and the Indian gentleman's house. His study, she knew, adjoined the schoolroom. She hoped the wall was thick enough to keep the noise the girls sometimes made after lessons from troubling him.

"I'm getting very fond of him," she told Ermengarde. "I wouldn't want him bothered. I've adopted him as a friend. You can do that without ever talking to someone, you know. You watch them and think of them and feel sorry for them, until they're almost part of your family. Sometimes, when the doctor comes twice in one day, I get quite worried."

Ermengarde considered this. "I've hardly any relations, and I'm glad," she said. "I don't like the ones I do have. My two aunts keep saying, 'Dear me, Ermengarde! You are very fat. You shouldn't eat sweets.' And my uncle is always putting questions to me: 'When did Edward the Third ascend the throne?' or 'Who died of a surfeit of lampreys?'"
Sara began to laugh.
"Someone you don't speak to can't question you like that," she said. "But even if you knew him very well, I'm certain the Indian gentleman wouldn't. I really am fond of him."

She had grown attached to the Large Family because they seemed so happy; the Indian gentleman drew her affection because he seemed so unhappy. Clearly he was still recovering from a very serious illness. Down in the kitchen, where the servants mysteriously knew everything, his condition was much discussed. He was not actually Indian, but an Englishman who had lived in India. Terrible misfortunes had once threatened his entire fortune, convincing him he was ruined and disgraced for ever. The shock had nearly killed him with brain fever. His health had remained broken ever since, although his luck had turned and everything he owned had been restored. Mines had been at the root of his trouble and danger.
"Diamond mines, what's more!" the cook declared, glancing sideways at Sara. "No savings of mine are ever goin' near a mine, especially not a diamond one. We've all learned a thing or two about THEM."
Sara thought, "He must have felt what papa felt. He fell ill the way papa did. Only he didn't die."

Her heart went out to him more strongly than ever. Sometimes she was almost pleased to be sent on an evening errand: perhaps the curtains next door would still be open, allowing her to look into that warm room and see her adopted friend. If the street was empty, she occasionally stopped, held the iron railings, and wished him good night as though he could hear.

She imagined, "Even if you can't hear me, perhaps you can FEEL it. Perhaps kind thoughts find a way through doors and windows and walls to reach people. Maybe you feel warmer and more comforted without knowing why, while I'm outside in the cold wishing you health and happiness again." In an earnest little whisper she would say, "I'm so sorry for you. I wish there were a 'Little Missus' to make a fuss of you, as I did for papa when his head ached. I'd like to be your 'Little Missus' myself, you poor dear! Good night, good night. God bless you!"

Afterwards she went on her way comforted, and feeling a little warmer herself. Her sympathy was so powerful that it seemed it MUST somehow reach the lonely man in the armchair by his fire. He was almost always wrapped in a large dressing gown, almost always supporting his forehead with one hand as he stared hopelessly into the flames. To Sara he looked like someone with a present burden on his mind, rather than someone whose troubles were all behind him.

"It always looks as though something is hurting him NOW," she thought. "But his money has come back, and in time he'll recover from the brain fever. Why does he still look that way? I wonder whether something else is wrong."

If another trouble existed, one that even the servants had not heard about, she felt certain the Large Family's father knew of it. This was the man she called Mr. Montmorency. He visited often. Mrs. Montmorency and all the small Montmorencys called as well, though less frequently. The Indian gentleman seemed especially attached to the two older girls, Janet and Nora, who had been so distressed when little Donald offered Sara his sixpence. Indeed, he had a very tender feeling for children in general, and for little girls in particular. Janet and Nora returned his affection. They eagerly awaited the afternoons when they could cross the square to pay him their quiet, well-mannered visits. Since he was an invalid, these visits had to be exceptionally well behaved.
Janet said, "Poor thing, he tells us we make him feel happier. We try to do it very quietly."

Janet was the family's leader and kept the others in line. She judged when it was appropriate to invite stories about India, and she noticed when the Indian gentleman grew tired. Then she would take everyone quietly away and tell Ram Dass to attend him. They loved Ram Dass. He could have provided endless stories himself, if only he spoke a language besides Hindustani. The Indian gentleman was really called Mr. Carrisford. Janet told him how they had met the little-girl-who-was-not-a-beggar, and he was greatly interested. His interest deepened when Ram Dass described the monkey's rooftop adventure. Ram Dass gave him a vivid account of that desolate attic: the naked floor, the broken plaster, the empty, rusty grate, and the narrow, hard bed.

After hearing this, he said to the Large Family's father, "Carmichael, I wonder how many attics around this square are just like hers. How many miserable little servant girls lie on beds like that while I turn restlessly on down pillows, burdened and troubled by money most of which isn't even mine."

Mr. Carmichael answered brightly, "My dear fellow, the sooner you stop torturing yourself, the better for your health. Even with all the riches of all the Indies, you couldn't put every hardship in the world to rights. Suppose you furnished every attic in this square: there would still be all the attics in every other square and street awaiting your attention. That's how it is!"
Staring into the glowing bed of coals inside the grate, Mr. Carrisford sat biting his fingernails.

After a silence he said slowly, "Do you suppose the other child—the one who is never out of my thoughts—could be living like that? Could she POSSIBLY have fallen into the same state as that poor little creature next door?"
Mr. Carmichael watched his friend with an uneasy expression. Nothing, he knew, could be worse for the man's health and reason than dwelling on this particular subject in this particular way.

He replied reassuringly, "If the girl at Madame Pascal's school in Paris was the child we're looking for, she seems to have gone to people with the means to look after her. Their little daughter had died, and they adopted this girl because she'd been their daughter's dearest companion. They had no other children. Madame Pascal described them as very wealthy Russians."
Mr. Carrisford exclaimed, "And that wretched woman couldn't even say where they'd taken her!"
Mr. Carmichael gave a shrug.

"She was a worldly, calculating Frenchwoman. Clearly she was delighted to have the child taken off her hands so conveniently, once her father's death left her without a penny. Women like that don't concern themselves with what becomes of children who might be an expense. Apparently the adoptive parents went away without leaving any clue to their whereabouts."
"But your word is 'IF'—if she was the child we're seeking. You keep saying 'if.' We don't know for certain. The name wasn't quite the same."

"Madame Pascal said the name as though it were Carew, not Crewe. That could simply have been her pronunciation. The details of the case were strikingly alike: an English officer in India had enrolled his motherless daughter there, then died suddenly after losing his money." Mr. Carmichael paused, apparently struck by another thought. "Are you SURE the girl was sent to Paris? Was Paris definitely where the school was?"

Carrisford burst out with restless bitterness, "My dear fellow, there's nothing I'm SURE about. I never met the mother or the child. Ralph Crewe and I were devoted friends as boys, but from our school days until we met again in India, we hadn't seen one another. The magnificent promise of those mines absorbed me completely, and it absorbed him too. It was all so enormous, so dazzling, that we nearly lost our heads. Whenever we met, we talked of scarcely anything else. I knew only that his daughter had gone away to school somewhere. Now I can't even remember HOW I learned that much."
Agitation was taking hold of him. Memories of those past disasters always had this effect upon his still-weakened brain.
Mr. Carmichael kept an anxious eye on him. Some questions were unavoidable, but they must be asked gently and with great care.
"Still, something gave you reason to believe the school WAS in Paris?"
"Yes," he replied. "The mother was French, and I'd heard she wanted her daughter educated in Paris. I naturally supposed that was where the child would be."
Mr. Carmichael agreed, "Yes, that does seem very likely indeed."
The Indian gentleman bent forward, bringing a long, wasted hand down against the table.

"Carmichael, I MUST find her," he said. "If she's living, she must be somewhere. And if she has neither friends nor money, I'm the one to blame. How can a man recover his nerve with that weighing on him? The mines' sudden turn of fortune has brought our wildest dreams to life, yet poor Crewe's little girl might be begging on a street!"
"No, no. Try to keep calm," Carmichael urged. "Remember what comfort there is in knowing you have a fortune ready to give her the moment she's found."

Carrisford groaned in fretful misery. "Why couldn't I be man enough to hold firm when things went wrong? I think I might have managed it if only my own money had been at stake, instead of other people's too. Poor Crewe invested every penny he possessed. He trusted me—he LOVED me. And he went to his grave believing I'd ruined him. Me, Tom Carrisford, who'd played cricket beside him at Eton. He must have thought me the blackest villain!"
"You mustn't blame yourself so harshly."

"It's not the threatened failure of the investment I blame myself for. It's my cowardice. I fled like a cheat and a thief because I couldn't bear to face my best friend and say I'd destroyed both him and his child."
The kindly father of the Large Family laid a comforting hand on his friend's shoulder.

"You fled because the strain of that mental torment had broken you," he said. "You were already half delirious. Otherwise you would have remained to fight it through. Remember, only two days after leaving, you were in hospital, strapped to a bed and raving with brain fever. Don't forget that."
Carrisford lowered his forehead into both hands.

"Good God! Yes," he said. "Fear and horror had made me mad. For weeks I hadn't slept. That night, as I stumbled out of the house, the very air seemed alive with hideous things making faces at me and mocking me."
"That alone explains it," Mr. Carmichael replied. "How could anyone about to fall into brain fever be capable of sound judgment!"
Still bowed, Carrisford shook his head.

"By the time consciousness returned, poor Crewe was already dead and buried. My memory seemed quite gone. Months and months passed before I remembered the child. Even when I began to recall that she existed, everything was blurred, as though under a haze."
He paused, rubbing his brow. "Sometimes, trying to remember, I still feel that haze. Surely at some point Crewe told me the name of her school. He must have mentioned it, don't you think?"
"Perhaps he never gave you precise details. You don't seem even to have learned what her actual name was."

"He had a curious pet name he'd made up: his 'Little Missus.' That was what he called her. But those accursed mines crowded everything else out of our minds. They were all we discussed. If he ever named the school, I forgot it—forgot it. And now I'll never get it back."

"Come now," Carmichael said. "We'll find her in the end. We'll go on looking for Madame Pascal's kindly Russians. She had a vague recollection of their living in Moscow. That's a clue we can follow. I'll travel to Moscow."

"If I could travel, I'd come too," said Carrisford. "Instead I sit here in furs, gazing at the fire. In those flames I seem to see Crewe's cheerful young face looking back at me, as though asking something. Sometimes he comes into my dreams. He stands in front of me and puts the same question into words, always the same. Can you imagine what he asks, Carmichael?"
Mr. Carmichael's reply came in a somewhat lowered voice.
"Not precisely," he replied.

"Every time he says, 'Tom, old man—Tom—where is the Little Missus?'" Seizing Carmichael's hand, he held it tight. "I must have an answer for him—I must! Help me find her," he pleaded. "Please help me."
Beyond the dividing wall, Sara sat up in her garret, talking to Melchisedec as he ate the supper he had come out to find.

"Melchisedec, being a princess has been difficult today," she told him. "More difficult than it usually is. The colder it gets, and the muddier the streets become, the harder it is. Lavinia laughed at my dirty skirt when we passed in the hall. In a flash I knew what I could say back, and I only just managed to stop it. Princesses can't sneer at people in return. But sometimes you have to bite your tongue to keep quiet. I bit mine. It's been such a cold afternoon, Melchisedec. And now the night is cold too."
Then, quite abruptly, she bent her dark head into her arms, as she so often did when there was nobody with her.
"Oh, papa," she whispered, "it feels so very long ago that I was your 'Little Missus'!"
Such were the events of that day on either side of the wall.

chapters.title: One of the Populace
paragraphs: That winter was miserable. On some errand days Sara had to tramp through snow; worse were the days when it thawed into muddy slush. At other times the fog lay so thick that street lamps burned from morning to night. London looked just as it had on that afternoon years earlier, when Sara had ridden through its streets curled up in the cab beside her father's shoulder. In such weather the Large Family's windows seemed wonderfully welcoming and snug, and the Indian gentleman's study glowed with rich colours and warmth. The attic, by contrast, was dreary beyond description. There seemed to be no sunrises or sunsets any more, and hardly a star. Low clouds covered the skylight, grey or mud-brown, or pouring rain. Even without a particularly heavy fog, daylight had gone by four in the afternoon. Sara needed a candle whenever she had to fetch something from her room. The kitchen women were miserable, which sharpened their tempers still further. They worked Becky like a little slave.

One night Becky crept into the attic and told Sara hoarsely, "If it wasn't for you, miss—for you an' the Bastille an' me bein' the prisoner next door—I think I'd die. It's gettin' real, isn't it? Every day the missus is more like the head jailer. I can almost see those big keys you say she's got. Cook's one of the jailers under her. Please tell me more, miss. Tell me about the underground passage we've dug beneath the walls."

Shivering, Sara answered, "I'll give you a warmer story. Bring your coverlet and wrap yourself up. I'll use mine, and we'll sit close together on the bed. I'll tell you about the tropical forest where the Indian gentleman's monkey lived. When he's on the table by the window, gazing at the street with that sorrowful face, I'm always sure he's remembering the forest where he swung by his tail from coconut trees. I wonder who captured him. And did he leave a family who counted on him to bring them coconuts?"
"That does sound warmer, miss," Becky said gratefully. "Though somehow even the Bastille warms me up a bit when you're tellin' me about it."

"That's because it gives you something else to think about," Sara explained. She wrapped herself so thoroughly that only her little dark face peeped out. "I've noticed how it works. When your body is miserable, you have to set your mind to thinking of something different."
Looking at her admiringly, Becky asked with some hesitation, "Can you manage that, miss?"
For a moment Sara drew her brows together.

"Sometimes yes, sometimes no," she answered bravely. "But when I CAN, I feel all right. I think we could always manage it if we practised enough. Lately I've been practising a great deal, and it's getting easier. When everything's dreadful—perfectly dreadful—I concentrate as hard as I possibly can on being a princess. I tell myself, 'I am a princess, and I am a fairy one, and because I am a fairy nothing can hurt me or make me uncomfortable.'" She laughed. "You can't imagine how it helps you forget."

There was no shortage of chances to direct her thoughts elsewhere, or of tests to discover whether she truly was a princess. But among the hardest came one terrible day that she often thought afterwards would stay with her, never entirely fading from memory however many years passed.

Rain had fallen for days. The streets were cold and slushy, filled with dreary chilly mist; sticky London mud lay everywhere beneath a shroud of fog and drizzle. Naturally, there were many long, wearisome errands—there always were in weather like that. Again and again Sara was sent out, until the damp had worked right through her shabby clothes. The ridiculous old feathers in her pitiful hat drooped more absurdly than ever. Her worn-down shoes were so saturated that they could take in no more water. Miss Minchin had also decided to punish her by withholding dinner. Cold, hungry, and exhausted, she began to look pinched about the face. Occasionally a kind passer-by glanced at her with sudden pity, but Sara never noticed. She hurried along, struggling to occupy her mind with something else. The need was desperate. With all her remaining strength she tried to "pretend" and "suppose." Yet this time it was harder than it had ever been. Once or twice the effort seemed almost to increase her hunger and cold instead of easing them. Still, she persisted stubbornly. Muddy water squelched through her broken shoes, and the wind tugged as though trying to tear off her thin jacket. As she walked she held a silent conversation with herself, neither speaking aloud nor moving her lips.

"Suppose my clothes were dry," she imagined. "Suppose I had sound shoes, a thick long coat, merino stockings, and an umbrella without holes. And suppose—just suppose—that beside a bakery selling hot buns I found sixpence with no owner. SUPPOSE I did: I'd go straight inside and buy six buns, the very hottest, and eat every one without pausing."
Sometimes the world allows remarkably strange things to happen.

What happened to Sara was certainly strange. Just as those thoughts were passing through her mind, she needed to cross the road. The mud was so deep that crossing was almost wading. She chose each step carefully, though it did little to keep her clean. But watching her steps meant watching her feet and the muddy ground. As she reached the pavement, something glittered in the gutter. It truly was silver: a tiny coin, trampled by countless feet, with just enough spirit remaining to give a faint shine. Not sixpence, but almost the next best thing—a fourpenny piece.
An instant later she held it in her cold, red-and-blue little hand.
"Oh," she gasped, "it really happened! It's true!"

Then, believe it or not, she looked directly at the shop in front of her. It was a bakery. A cheerful, plump, motherly woman with rosy cheeks was setting a tray in the window: delicious buns newly drawn from the oven, hot, round, and glossy, studded with currants.
For a few seconds Sara almost fainted. The surprise, the sight of those buns, and the lovely smell of warm bread rising from the baker's cellar window were nearly too much.

She knew there was no reason not to spend the coin. It had plainly lain in the mud a while. Among the crowds that pushed and jostled past all day, its owner had vanished beyond any hope of finding them.

Still feeling faint, she told herself, "But first I'll ask the woman in the bakery whether she's lost anything." She crossed the pavement and set one wet foot on the doorstep. There, a sight made her stop.

A small figure sat there, even more wretched than Sara. It was scarcely more than a heap of rags, with little bare feet showing, red and muddy, because the girl kept trying to cover them and the rags were too short. Above the bundle rose a tangle of uncombed hair and a dirty face with great hollow eyes, full of hunger.
The instant Sara saw those eyes she recognized their hunger, and pity rose in her.
With a small sigh she thought, "Here is one of the populace, and she's even hungrier than I am."

The child, this "one of the populace," looked up at Sara and edged aside to let her through. Giving way to everyone was a familiar duty. She knew a policeman, if he happened to spot her, would simply order her to "move on."
Tightening her fingers around the fourpenny piece, Sara stood undecided for a moment. Then she addressed the girl.
"Do you feel hungry?" she asked.
The girl shifted herself and her bundle of rags again.
"Don't I just," she rasped. "You bet I am."
Sara asked, "Have you had nothing for dinner?"
"No dinner," came the still-hoarser answer, with another shuffle. "No breakfast neither. No supper. Nothin' at all."
Sara asked, "Since when?"
"Can't say. Had nothin' today, nowhere. Kept askin' and askin'."
The sight alone made Sara feel hungrier and fainter. Yet her strange little thoughts were working inside her head. Heartsick though she was, she went on speaking silently to herself.

"If I'm a princess—if I'm one—when princesses were poor and forced from their thrones, they always shared with the populace when they found someone poorer and hungrier than themselves. They always did. Each bun costs a penny. With sixpence I could have eaten six. This won't give either of us enough. But something is better than nothing."
She told the little beggar, "Wait here a moment."
Inside, the shop was warm and full of delicious smells. The woman was about to add another batch of hot buns to the window display.
Sara held out her poor little coin. "Please, have you lost a silver fourpence?" she asked. "A fourpenny piece like this?"
The woman examined the coin, then the child: the earnest little face and the bedraggled clothes that had once been fine.
"Goodness, no," she replied. "Was it you who found it?"
"Yes, down in the gutter," Sara answered.
"Then it's yours to keep," the woman said. "It might have lain there a week. Heaven knows whose it was—you certainly can't find out."
"I realize that," replied Sara, "but I thought I ought to ask you first."
Puzzlement, interest, and kindness mingled in the woman's face. "There aren't many who'd ask," she said.
Noticing Sara's eyes turn towards the buns, she added, "Would you like to buy something?"
"Please may I have four buns," Sara said, "the ones that cost a penny each?"
At the window, the woman began filling a paper bag with buns.
Sara counted six going into the bag.
"I only asked for four, please," she pointed out. "Fourpence is all I have."
The woman gave her kindly look. "The extra two are makeweight—I'll throw them in. You'll find time to eat them, I expect. Aren't you hungry?"
Sara's eyes filled with a mist.

"Yes, very hungry," she replied. "I'm most grateful for your kindness, and—" She had meant to explain that a child outside was even hungrier than she was. At that moment, however, two or three customers entered together, each apparently in a great hurry. All Sara could do was thank the woman once more and leave.

The beggar girl remained curled up at the corner of the step. Her filthy, wet rags made her look dreadful. She stared blankly ahead, her expression dulled by suffering. Suddenly Sara saw her drag the back of a rough, blackened hand across her eyes. Tears had forced themselves beneath her lids, apparently surprising her, and she was wiping them away. She muttered under her breath.
Opening the paper bag, Sara pulled out a hot bun. Already its warmth had begun to take the chill from her own hands.
She placed it in the girl's rag-covered lap. "Look, it's lovely and hot," she said. "Eat it; it'll help with the hunger."
The girl gave a start and stared up at her, almost frightened by this astonishing turn of luck. Then she seized the bun and stuffed it into her mouth in enormous, wolf-like bites.
In hoarse, frantic delight she cried, "Oh, my! Oh, my! OH my!" Sara could hear it clearly.
From the bag Sara drew three further buns and set them down.
Something terrible sounded in that hoarse voice, so ravenously hungry.
"Her hunger is worse than mine," Sara told herself. "She's starving." Her hand shook as she laid down the fourth bun. Then she said, "I'm not starving," and added the fifth.

As Sara turned away, the little savage of London went on snatching and devouring. Her ravenous hunger left no room for thanks, even had anyone taught her manners, which nobody had. She was simply a poor little wild creature.
Sara said, "Good-bye."

From across the road she glanced back. With a bun in each hand, the child had paused halfway through a mouthful to watch her. Sara nodded gently. After another long, curious stare, the girl jerked her tangled head in reply. Until Sara disappeared, she took no further bite and did not even finish the mouthful already begun.
Just then, the woman in the bakery glanced through her window.
"Well, I never!" she exclaimed. "She's handed those buns to a beggar child! And it wasn't for lack of wanting them herself. Dear me, she looked hungry enough. I'd like to know what made her do that."
For a few moments she remained behind the glass, thinking. Curiosity finally won. She went to the doorway to question the child on the step.
"Who gave you your buns?" she asked. The child pointed with her head towards Sara, now disappearing in the distance.
The woman asked, "What did she tell you?"
The rough voice replied, "Wanted to know if I was hungry."
"And what was your answer?"
"Told her I was."
"So she went into the shop, bought the buns, and brought them out for you?"
The girl nodded back.
"How many buns?"
"Five."
The woman stood considering that.
Quietly she said, "Only one left for herself, then. She could have eaten all six, too. I could tell by looking at her eyes."
She watched the bedraggled little figure far down the street. Her usually comfortable mind felt more unsettled than it had for a long time.
"I wish she hadn't hurried off," she said. "Bless me, I'd have given her a dozen." Then she turned back to the girl.
"Do you still feel hungry?" she asked.
"Always hungry, me," the girl replied. "Only it's not quite so bad now."
Holding the shop door wide, the woman said, "Come inside with me."
The child rose and shuffled through. An invitation into warmth, into a place full of bread, seemed impossible to believe. She had no idea what would happen next. She hardly cared.

Pointing towards the fire in the small back room, the woman said, "Warm yourself there. And listen: whenever you're desperate for some bread, come here and ask. For that little girl's sake, bless me if I won't give you some."
The bun she had kept gave Sara a little comfort. At least it was still very hot, and better than an empty stomach. As she walked she tore off tiny pieces, eating slowly so they would last.
"Imagine it's a magic bun," she said, "with every bite equal to a whole dinner. If I carried on eating at this rate, I'd be having far too much."

By the time she came to the square containing the Select Seminary, darkness had fallen and all the houses were lit. The blinds were still open in the room where she so often saw the Large Family. At this hour she frequently found the man she called Mr. Montmorency in a big chair, surrounded by a swarm of children. They talked and laughed, perched on his knees or the chair's arms, or leaned against him. Tonight they swarmed around him as usual, but he was standing. A considerable bustle was underway. Someone was evidently leaving on a journey, and that someone was Mr. Montmorency. Outside waited a brougham with a large portmanteau strapped to it. The children danced, chattered, and clung to their father. Their pretty, rosy mother stood close by, talking as if settling last-minute questions. Sara stopped briefly to watch the smaller children lifted for kisses, and their father bend to kiss the older ones too.
"Will he be gone for long, I wonder?" she thought. "That's quite a large portmanteau. Oh dear, they'll miss him so much! I'll miss him too, though he doesn't even know I exist."
Remembering the sixpence, she moved on when the front door opened. But she saw the traveller emerge against the warm light of the hall, with the older children still clustered close.
Janet, the little girl, asked, "Will there be snow all over Moscow? And ice everywhere?"
Another called, "Will you ride in a drosky? Are you going to see the Czar?"

Laughing, he promised, "I'll tell you everything in my letters. And I'll send pictures of muzhiks and other things. Inside with you now. It's a horrible wet night. I'd far rather stay here with you than set off for Moscow. Good night! Good night, my duckies! God bless you!" He hurried down the steps and sprang into the brougham.
Bouncing on the doormat, Guy Clarence shouted, "When you find the little girl, tell her we send our love."
Then the children went inside and closed the door.

On their way back to the room, Janet asked Nora, "Did you notice the little-girl-who-is-not-a-beggar going past? She looked cold and soaked, and I saw her glance back over her shoulder at us. Mamma says her clothes always seem to have been given away by someone very rich, someone who parted with them only because they'd grown too shabby to wear. That school sends her on errands on the very worst days and nights."
Feeling faint and unsteady, Sara crossed to the area steps leading down to Miss Minchin's basement.
She wondered, "Who is that little girl—the one he's setting out to find?"

Dragging her basket, which now felt terribly heavy indeed, she went down the area steps. Meanwhile the Large Family's father drove swiftly towards the station to catch the train that would carry him to Moscow, where he would do everything he could to trace Captain Crewe's lost little daughter.

chapters.title: What Melchisedec Heard and Saw
paragraphs: That same afternoon, during Sara's absence, something unusual took place in the attic. Melchisedec alone witnessed it. So frightened and bewildered was he that he scurried home to his hole and hid. There he actually shook and trembled, peering out with furtive caution to discover what was happening.

Since Sara's departure early that morning, the attic had been silent except for rain tapping on the roof slates and skylight. Melchisedec had found it rather boring. When even the rain stopped and the silence became complete, he decided to venture out and investigate, although experience told him Sara would not be back for a while. He wandered, sniffing, and had just discovered a completely unexpected crumb, unaccountably left over from his previous meal, when a noise on the roof caught his attention. Heart beating fast, he stood perfectly still, listening. Something seemed to be moving up there. It came towards the skylight and reached it. Mysteriously, the skylight began to open. A dark face looked down into the attic, and another face appeared behind it. Both watched with careful interest. Two men were outside, quietly preparing to climb through the opening. They were Ram Dass and the Indian gentleman's young secretary, though Melchisedec naturally knew nothing of that. All he knew was that men were violating the attic's quiet privacy. As the dark-faced one lowered himself through the window with such effortless skill that he made no sound, the rat turned and raced for his hole. He was terrified. He had stopped being afraid of Sara: she threw only crumbs and made only soft, low, coaxing whistles. Strange men, however, were dangerous company. Crouched flat just inside his home, he could barely manage to look through the crack with one bright, anxious eye. I cannot say how much of their talk he understood. Even if he had understood every word, he would probably still have been thoroughly puzzled.
Young and lightly built, the secretary followed through the skylight as quietly as Ram Dass. He caught one last glimpse of Melchisedec's tail disappearing.
In a whisper he asked Ram Dass, "Was that a rat?"
Ram Dass whispered back, "A rat, yes, Sahib. A great many live inside these walls."
"Ugh!" said the young man. "How is the child not frightened out of her wits by them?"
Ram Dass moved his hands in a gesture and gave a respectful smile. Though Sara had spoken to him only once, he stood there as someone who knew her intimately and could explain her nature.

"Sahib, this child befriends everything," he replied. "She differs from other children. Often I see her without her seeing me. Many nights I cross the slates to make sure she is safe. From my window I watch when she has no idea I am nearby. On that table she stands gazing at the sky, as though it has words for her. When she calls, the sparrows answer. Loneliness has led her to feed and tame the rat. The poor slave who works in this house seeks comfort here. A little child visits secretly, and an older one who adores her would listen for ever if allowed. Crossing the roof, I have seen it all. The mistress here is a wicked woman and treats her like a pariah. Yet she carries herself like a child with royal blood in her veins!"
"You've learned a great deal about her, it seems," remarked the secretary.

"I know the life she leads each day," Ram Dass answered. "I know when she leaves and returns, what makes her sad, and her few poor pleasures. I know her hunger and her cold. I know the nights she studies alone over her books until midnight, and the times her hidden friends creep in and make her happy, as children can be happy even in poverty. Their coming lets her whisper, laugh, and talk. If illness came to her, I should know that too, and if it could be managed I would come to tend her."
"You're certain nobody else comes anywhere near this place, and that she won't return to catch us? Finding us in her room would frighten her and ruin Sahib Carrisford's plan."
Without a sound, Ram Dass went over and stationed himself beside the door.
"Only she comes up here, Sahib," he assured him. "She went out carrying her basket and may be absent for hours. Here by the door I will hear footsteps before they reach the final staircase."
From his breast pocket the secretary drew a pencil and a writing tablet.
"Listen carefully," he told him. Then he began a slow, quiet circuit of the miserable little attic, making quick notes as he examined its contents.
He started with the narrow bed, testing the mattress with his hand and giving an exclamation.

"Hard as stone," he said. "One day while she's away we'll have to change this. Bringing a mattress across will need a special trip; tonight won't be possible." He turned back the bedclothes and inspected the single thin pillow.

"A grubby, worn coverlet, a thin blanket, patched and ragged sheets," he observed. "What a bed to put a child in, especially in a supposedly respectable house!" His eyes moved to the rusty fireplace. "That grate hasn't held a fire in a very long time."
"Not once in all the time I have watched it," Ram Dass replied. "This house's mistress does not consider that anyone besides herself might feel cold."
Writing rapidly, the secretary filled his tablet. He looked up, tore away one sheet, and tucked it into his breast pocket.
"An unusual way to go about things," he remarked. "Whose idea was it?"
Ram Dass bowed with modest, almost apologetic deference.

"The first idea was mine, Sahib, though only a fancy," he admitted. "I am fond of the little one. We are lonely, both of us. She tells her secret friends the visions she imagines. One night, feeling sad myself, I lay by the open skylight and listened. She described how this wretched room might look if it were comfortable. As she spoke she seemed to see it, and the words made her warmer and happier. Then she imagined this plan. Next day the Sahib was ill and miserable, and I repeated it to entertain him. It was only a dream then, yet it pleased him. Hearing what the child did amused him. He grew interested and began asking questions. At last the idea of turning her visions into actual things became a pleasure to him."

"Do you really think you can manage it while she's asleep? What if she wakes?" the secretary asked. Whatever this scheme was, it had plainly caught his imagination and pleased him as much as it had Sahib Carrisford.

Ram Dass answered, "My feet can be as quiet as velvet. Children sleep deeply, even unhappy children. Many times I could have entered at night without making her turn her head on the pillow. If the other bearer hands everything through the skylight, I can arrange it all without waking her. She will open her eyes and believe a magician has visited."
His smile suggested a heart growing warm beneath the white robe, and the secretary returned it.
"Like something from the Arabian Nights," he said. "Only an Oriental could have dreamed this up. A plan like that doesn't belong among London's fogs."

Their visit was short, much to Melchisedec's relief. Probably understanding none of their words, he found their whispering and movements threatening. The young secretary appeared interested in every detail. His notes covered the floor, fireplace, damaged footstool, old table, and walls. He repeatedly ran his hand over the last, looking especially pleased to discover old nails driven in here and there.
"They'll do for hanging things," he said.
A mysterious smile crossed Ram Dass's face.

"Yesterday I came while she was away," he explained. "I brought small, sharp nails that press into plaster without hammering. Wherever I might need one, I put it in. Many are now waiting in the walls."
Standing still, the Indian gentleman's secretary surveyed the room once more and slipped his tablet back into his pocket.
"That should be enough notes. We can leave now," he said. "Sahib Carrisford has a generous heart. What a terrible pity he still hasn't found that missing child."
"Finding her would bring back his strength," said Ram Dass. "Perhaps his God will yet guide her to him."

They climbed out as silently as they had entered. Only when Melchisedec was absolutely certain they had gone did relief take hold. A few minutes later he judged it safe to leave his hole and scuffle about again. After all, even such terrifying human beings might have carried crumbs in their pockets and accidentally dropped one or two on the floor.

chapters.title: The Magic
paragraphs: When Sara had passed the house next door, she had seen Ram Dass closing the shutters, and she had caught a glimpse of this room too.
"It is a long time since I saw a nice place from the inside," was the thought that crossed her mind.
There was the usual bright fire glowing in the fireplace, and the Indian gentleman was sitting in front of it. His head was resting in his hand, and he looked as lonely and unhappy as ever.
"Poor man!" said Sara. "I wonder what you are supposing."
And this was what he was "supposing" at that very moment.

"Suppose," he was thinking, "suppose—even if Carmichael traces the people to Moscow—the little girl they took from Madame Pascal's school in Paris is NOT the one we are searching for. Suppose she turns out to be quite a different child. What steps shall I take next?"
When Sara went into the house, she met Miss Minchin, who had come downstairs to scold the cook.
"Where have you wasted your time?" she demanded. "You have been out for hours."
"It was so wet and muddy," Sara answered. "It was hard to walk, because my shoes were so bad and kept slipping."
