"Was he," she said, glancing toward the closed library door, "was HE the wicked friend? Oh, do tell me!"
Mrs. Carmichael was crying as she kissed her again. She felt Sara ought to be kissed very often, since she had gone so long without it.

"He wasn't wicked, my dear," she answered. "He didn't really lose your papa's money. He only thought he had, and because he loved your papa so much, his grief made him so ill that for a time he wasn't in his right mind. He nearly died of brain fever, and long before he began to recover, your poor papa was dead."
"And he didn't know where to find me," Sara murmured. "And I was so near." Somehow she couldn't forget that she had been so near.

"He believed you were at school in France," Mrs. Carmichael explained. "And he was constantly misled by false clues. He's searched for you everywhere. When he saw you go by, looking so sad and neglected, it never entered his head that you were his friend's poor child, but because you were a little girl too, he felt sorry for you and wanted to make you happier. So he told Ram Dass to climb in at your attic window and try to make you comfortable."
Sara gave a start of joy, and her whole expression changed.
"Did Ram Dass bring the things?" she cried. "Did he tell Ram Dass to do it? Did he make the dream that came true?"
"Yes, my dear—yes! He is kind and good, and he felt sorry for you, for the sake of little lost Sara Crewe."
The library door opened and Mr. Carmichael appeared, beckoning Sara to him.
"Mr. Carrisford is better already," he said. "He wants you to come to him."
Sara didn't wait. When the Indian gentleman looked at her as she came in, he saw that her whole face was glowing.
She went and stood in front of his chair, her hands clasped against her breast.
"You sent the things to me," she said, in a joyful, trembling little voice, "the beautiful, beautiful things? YOU sent them!"

"Yes, poor dear child, I did," he answered. He was weak and worn down by long illness and trouble, but he looked at her with the look she remembered in her father's eyes—that look of loving her and wanting to take her in his arms. It made her kneel down beside him, just as she used to kneel by her father when they were the dearest friends and sweethearts in the world.
"Then you're my friend," she said. "You're my friend!" And she laid her face on his thin hand and kissed it again and again.
"The man will be himself again in three weeks," Mr. Carmichael said quietly to his wife. "Just look at his face already."

And indeed he did look changed. Here was his "Little Missus," and already he had new things to think about and plan. First of all, there was Miss Minchin. She had to be seen and told about the change in her pupil's fortunes.
Sara was not to go back to the seminary at all. The Indian gentleman was quite determined on that point. She must stay where she was, and Mr. Carmichael would go and see Miss Minchin himself.
"I'm glad I don't have to go back," said Sara. "She'll be very angry. She doesn't like me, though perhaps that's my fault, because I don't like her."

But oddly enough, Miss Minchin saved Mr. Carmichael the trouble of calling on her by coming in search of her pupil herself. She had wanted Sara for something and, on asking about her, had heard an astonishing thing. One of the housemaids had seen her slip out of the area with something hidden under her cloak, and had also seen her go up the steps next door and enter the house.
"What can she mean!" Miss Minchin cried to Miss Amelia.
"I'm sure I don't know, sister," Miss Amelia answered. "Unless she's made friends with him because he's lived in India."

"It would be just like her to push herself on him and try to win his sympathy in some such impertinent way," said Miss Minchin. "She must have been in that house for two hours. I won't allow such presumption. I shall go and look into the matter, and apologize for her intrusion."
Sara was sitting on a footstool close to Mr. Carrisford's knee, listening to some of the many things he felt he had to explain to her, when Ram Dass announced the visitor.
Sara stood up involuntarily and turned rather pale, but Mr. Carrisford saw that she stood quietly and showed none of the usual signs of a frightened child.
Miss Minchin swept into the room with stern dignity. She was dressed correctly and well, and was stiffly, rigidly polite.
"I'm sorry to disturb Mr. Carrisford," she said, "but I have explanations to make. I am Miss Minchin, the proprietress of the Young Ladies' Seminary next door."
The Indian gentleman studied her for a moment in silence. He was a man with a rather hot temper by nature, and he did not want it to get the better of him.
"So you are Miss Minchin?" he said.
"I am, sir."
"In that case," the Indian gentleman replied, "you've come at just the right time. My solicitor, Mr. Carmichael, was about to go and see you."
Mr. Carmichael gave a slight bow, and Miss Minchin glanced in amazement from him to Mr. Carrisford.

"Your solicitor!" she said. "I don't understand. I have come here out of duty. I have just discovered that you've been imposed upon by the forwardness of one of my pupils—a charity pupil. I came to explain that she intruded without my knowledge." She turned on Sara. "Go home at once," she commanded indignantly. "You will be severely punished. Go home at once."
The Indian gentleman drew Sara to his side and patted her hand.
"She isn't going."
Miss Minchin felt rather as though she must be losing her senses.
"Not going!" she repeated.
"No," said Mr. Carrisford. "She isn't going home—if you give your house that name. From now on her home will be with me."
Miss Minchin fell back in amazed indignation.
"With YOU! With YOU, sir! What does this mean?"

"Kindly explain the matter, Carmichael," said the Indian gentleman, "and get it over with as quickly as possible." And he made Sara sit down again and held her hands in his—another habit of her papa's.
Then Mr. Carmichael explained—in the quiet, even, steady manner of a man who knew his subject and all its legal consequences, which Miss Minchin, as a businesswoman, understood, and did not enjoy.

"Mr. Carrisford, madam," he said, "was an intimate friend of the late Captain Crewe. He was his partner in certain large investments. The fortune Captain Crewe believed he had lost has been recovered, and is now in Mr. Carrisford's hands."
"The fortune!" cried Miss Minchin, and she actually lost color as she said it. "Sara's fortune!"
"It WILL be Sara's fortune," replied Mr. Carmichael rather coldly. "In fact, it's Sara's fortune now. Certain developments have increased it enormously. The diamond mines have redeemed themselves."
"The diamond mines!" Miss Minchin gasped. If this was true, she felt, nothing so dreadful had happened to her since the day she was born.

"The diamond mines," Mr. Carmichael repeated, and he couldn't resist adding, with a rather sly, un-lawyerlike smile, "There aren't many princesses, Miss Minchin, who are richer than your little charity pupil, Sara Crewe, will be. Mr. Carrisford has been searching for her for nearly two years. He has found her at last, and he means to keep her."

After that he asked Miss Minchin to sit down while he explained matters to her fully, and he went into as much detail as was needed to make it perfectly clear that Sara's future was secure, that what had seemed lost would be restored to her tenfold, and also that in Mr. Carrisford she had a guardian as well as a friend.
Miss Minchin was not a clever woman, and in her excitement she was foolish enough to make one desperate attempt to win back what she could not help seeing she had lost through her own worldly folly.
"He found her in my care," she protested. "I've done everything for her. If it weren't for me she'd have starved in the streets."
At this the Indian gentleman lost his temper.
"As for starving in the streets," he said, "she might have starved more comfortably there than in your attic."

"Captain Crewe left her in my charge," Miss Minchin argued. "She must return to it until she comes of age. She can be a parlor boarder again. She must finish her education. The law will take my side."

"Come, come, Miss Minchin," Mr. Carmichael interrupted, "the law will do nothing of the kind. If Sara herself wishes to go back to you, I daresay Mr. Carrisford would not forbid it. But that is up to Sara."

"Then," said Miss Minchin, "I appeal to Sara. Perhaps I haven't spoiled you," she said awkwardly to the little girl, "but you know your papa was pleased with your progress. And—ahem—I have always been fond of you."
Sara's green-gray eyes fixed on her with the quiet, clear look that Miss Minchin particularly disliked.
"Have YOU, Miss Minchin?" she said. "I never knew that."
Miss Minchin reddened and drew herself up.

"You ought to have known," she said. "But children, unfortunately, never know what's best for them. Amelia and I always said you were the cleverest child in the school. Won't you do your duty to your poor papa and come home with me?"

Sara took a step toward her and stood still. She was thinking of the day she had been told she belonged to nobody and was in danger of being turned out into the street. She was thinking of the cold, hungry hours she had spent alone in the attic with Emily and Melchisedec. She looked Miss Minchin steadily in the face.
"You know why I won't go home with you, Miss Minchin," she said. "You know perfectly well."
A hot flush rose in Miss Minchin's hard, angry face.
"You will never see your friends again," she began. "I'll see to it that Ermengarde and Lottie are kept away—"
Mr. Carmichael cut her off with polite firmness.

"Excuse me," he said. "She will see anyone she likes. The parents of Miss Crewe's schoolmates are hardly likely to refuse her invitations to visit her at her guardian's house. Mr. Carrisford will see to that."

It must be admitted that even Miss Minchin flinched. This was worse than the eccentric bachelor uncle who might have a peppery temper and take offense at the way his niece had been treated. A woman with a sordid mind could easily believe that most people wouldn't refuse to let their children stay friends with a little heiress to diamond mines. And if Mr. Carrisford chose to tell certain of her patrons how unhappy Sara Crewe had been made, a great many unpleasant things could happen.

"You haven't taken on an easy charge," she said to the Indian gentleman as she turned to leave the room. "You'll find that out very soon. The child is neither truthful nor grateful. I suppose," she added, to Sara, "that you feel you're a princess again now."
Sara looked down and flushed a little, because she thought her cherished fancy might not be easy for strangers—even nice ones—to understand at first.
"I—TRIED not to be anything else," she answered in a low voice. "Even when I was coldest and hungriest—I tried not to be."
"Well, now there will be no need to try," said Miss Minchin acidly, as Ram Dass salaamed her out of the room.

She went home and, going to her sitting room, sent for Miss Amelia at once. She shut herself up with her for the rest of the afternoon, and poor Miss Amelia, it must be admitted, went through more than one bad quarter of an hour. She shed a good many tears and mopped her eyes a great deal. One of her unfortunate remarks nearly made her sister snap her head clean off, but it ended in an unusual way.

"I'm not as clever as you, sister," she said, "and I'm always afraid to say things to you for fear of making you angry. Perhaps if I weren't so timid it would be better for the school and for both of us. I must say, I've often thought it would have been better if you'd been less hard on Sara Crewe and seen to it that she was decently dressed and more comfortable. I KNOW she was worked too hard for a child her age, and I know she was only half fed—"
"How dare you say such a thing!" cried Miss Minchin.

"I don't know how I dare," Miss Amelia answered with a sort of reckless courage, "but now that I've begun, I may as well finish, whatever happens to me. That child was clever and good—and she'd have repaid you for any kindness you'd shown her. But you never showed her any. The truth is, she was too clever for you, and you always disliked her for it. She used to see right through us both—"
"Amelia!" her furious elder sister gasped, looking as though she would box her ears and knock her cap off, as she had so often done to Becky.
But Miss Amelia's disappointment had made her hysterical enough that she didn't care what happened next.

"She did! She did!" she cried. "She saw through us both. She saw that you were a hard-hearted, worldly woman, and I was a weak fool, and that we were both vulgar and mean enough to grovel on our knees for her money and treat her badly once it was taken from her—though she behaved like a little princess even when she was a beggar. She did—she did—like a little princess!" And her hysterics overcame the poor woman, and she began to laugh and cry at the same time, rocking herself back and forth.

"And now you've lost her," she cried wildly. "And some other school will get her and her money, and if she were like any other child she'd tell how she was treated, and all our pupils would be taken away and we'd be ruined. And it serves us right. But it serves you right more than it does me, for you are a hard woman, Maria Minchin, you're a hard, selfish, worldly woman!"

And she was in danger of making so much noise with her hysterical choking and gurgling that her sister had to go to her and use smelling salts and sal volatile to calm her, instead of pouring out her indignation at such audacity.

And from then on, it may be mentioned, the elder Miss Minchin actually began to stand a little in awe of a sister who, for all her foolish look, was evidently not quite so foolish as she looked, and might therefore burst out and speak truths people didn't want to hear.

That evening, when the pupils had gathered around the schoolroom fire as they did every night before bed, Ermengarde came in with a letter in her hand and an odd expression on her round face. It was odd because it was an expression of delighted excitement mixed with the kind of amazement that comes from a shock just received.
"What IS the matter?" two or three voices cried at once.

"Does it have anything to do with the row that's been going on?" Lavinia asked eagerly. "There's been such a row in Miss Minchin's room. Miss Amelia has had something like hysterics and had to go to bed."
Ermengarde answered them slowly, as if she were half stunned.
"I've just had this letter from Sara," she said, holding it out so they could see how long it was.
"From Sara!" Every voice joined in the exclamation.
"Where is she?" Jessie almost shrieked.
"Next door," said Ermengarde, "with the Indian gentleman."
"Where? Where is she? Has she been sent away? Does Miss Minchin know about it? Was that what the row was about? Why did she write to you? Tell us! Tell us!"
There was a perfect babel, and Lottie began to cry plaintively.
Ermengarde answered slowly, as if she were half lost in what seemed, at that moment, the most important and self-explanatory thing of all.
"There WERE diamond mines," she said stoutly. "There WERE!" Open mouths and wide eyes confronted her.
"They were real," she hurried on. "It was all a mistake about them. Something went wrong for a while, and Mr. Carrisford thought they were ruined—"
"Who is Mr. Carrisford?" Jessie shouted.

"The Indian gentleman. And Captain Crewe thought so too—and he died, and Mr. Carrisford had brain fever and ran away, and HE nearly died. And he didn't know where Sara was. And it turned out there were millions and millions of diamonds in the mines, and half of them belong to Sara, and they belonged to her when she was living in the attic with nobody but Melchisedec for a friend, and the cook ordering her about. And Mr. Carrisford found her this afternoon and has taken her to his home—and she's never coming back—and she'll be more of a princess than she ever was—a hundred and fifty thousand times more. And I'm going to see her tomorrow afternoon. So there!"

Even Miss Minchin herself could hardly have controlled the uproar after this, and although she heard the noise, she didn't try. She was in no mood to face anything more than she was already facing in her room, with Miss Amelia weeping in bed. She knew the news had somehow seeped through the walls, and that every servant and every child would go to bed talking of it.

So until nearly midnight the entire seminary, sensing somehow that all the rules were set aside, crowded around Ermengarde in the schoolroom and heard the letter read and read again, a letter containing a story every bit as wonderful as any Sara herself had ever invented, with the amazing charm of having happened to Sara herself and the mysterious Indian gentleman in the very next house.

Becky, who had heard it as well, managed to slip upstairs earlier than usual. She wanted to get away from people and go and look at the little magic room once more. She didn't know what would become of it. It was hardly likely to be left to Miss Minchin. It would be taken away, and the attic would be bare and empty again. Glad as she was for Sara's sake, she climbed the last flight of stairs with a lump in her throat and tears blurring her sight. There would be no fire tonight, no rosy lamp, no supper, and no princess sitting in the glow, reading or telling stories—no princess!
She choked down a sob as she pushed open the attic door, and then she broke into a low cry.
The lamp was flushing the room with light, the fire was blazing, the supper was waiting—and Ram Dass stood there smiling into her startled face.

"Missee sahib remembered," he said. "She told the sahib everything. She wished you to know the good fortune that has come to her. Behold, a letter on the tray. She has written it. She did not wish you to go to sleep unhappy. The sahib commands you to come to him tomorrow. You are to be the attendant of missee sahib. Tonight I take these things back over the roof."
And having said this with a beaming face, he made a small salaam and slipped through the skylight with a nimble silence of movement that showed Becky how easily he had done it before.

chapters.title: Anne
paragraphs: The Large Family's nursery had never known such happiness. Nobody had imagined the pleasures that friendship with the little-girl-who-was-not-a-beggar could bring. Her adventures and suffering alone made her a treasure. Everyone begged to hear, again and again, the account of what had happened to her. From a seat beside a warm fire in a large, glowing room, listening to descriptions of an attic's cold could be quite delightful. Indeed, it must be confessed that they rather loved the attic. Its bareness and chill dwindled into insignificance whenever Melchisedec entered the tale, along with the sparrows and all that you could see by climbing onto the table and putting your head and shoulders through the skylight.

Naturally, their favourite was the tale of the banquet and the dream that turned out to be real. Sara first related it the day after she was found. Several children from the Large Family came to tea. As they sat or curled on the hearthrug, she told it in her own fashion, while the Indian gentleman watched and listened. When the story ended, she lifted her eyes to him and rested a hand on his knee.
"That's how it happened to me," she said. "Uncle Tom, will you tell us your part now?" He had asked her always to call him "Uncle Tom." "I haven't heard it yet, and it must be lovely."

So he described his lonely days, ill, bored, and irritable, and how Ram Dass had tried to divert him by telling him about the people passing outside. One child passed more often than anyone. She began to interest him, perhaps partly because another little girl occupied so much of his thoughts. Another reason was Ram Dass's account of following the monkey into the attic. He had spoken of its bleak appearance and of the child's manner, which suggested someone not accustomed to the class of life lived by drudges and servants. Little by little, Ram Dass discovered how miserable her existence was. He also learned how easy it was to cross the few yards of roofing to her skylight. Everything else had begun with that discovery.

One day he said, "Sahib, while the child is running an errand, I could cross the roof and light her fire. Imagine her returning cold and soaked and finding flames waiting for her. She would believe a magician had been at work."

The fanciful idea brought a smile to Mr. Carrisford's unhappy face. Ram Dass, delighted by that response, expanded his scheme, explaining how easily many other improvements could be made. His pleasure and inventiveness were almost a child's. Planning and preparing gave purpose and interest to days that otherwise would have dragged painfully by. On the night the banquet failed, every package stood ready in Ram Dass's attic. He kept watch with the person who was to assist him, his companion just as eager for this curious adventure. Ram Dass had been stretched along the slates, peering through the skylight, when the feast came to its disastrous end. He waited until he was certain Sara had fallen deeply into exhausted sleep. Then he entered with a dark lantern, while his helper stayed outside passing objects through. At the faintest movement from Sara, he shut the lantern's slide and lay flat on the floor. The children learned all this and many more exciting details by asking a thousand questions.
Sara said, "How glad I am. How GLAD I am that my secret friend was you!"

No two people ever became closer friends. Somehow they suited one another wonderfully. The Indian gentleman had never enjoyed anyone's company quite as much as Sara's. Within a month, just as Mr. Carmichael had predicted, he was a changed man. Life continually amused and interested him. Even the wealth he had thought an intolerable burden began giving him genuine pleasure. There were so many lovely things he could arrange for Sara. They shared a little joke about his being a magician, and devising surprises for her was one of his delights. Beautiful new flowers appeared in her room; curious small presents waited beneath pillows. One evening, while they were together, a heavy paw scratched at the door. Sara went to investigate and found a magnificent great dog—a Russian boarhound. Around his neck was a splendid collar of gold and silver, engraved with the words, "I am Boris; I serve the Princess Sara."

To the Indian gentleman, no memory was dearer than that of the little princess dressed in rags. Afternoons spent in happy gatherings with the Large Family, or with Ermengarde and Lottie, were wonderful. Yet the quiet hours when he and Sara read or talked together alone had a charm of their own, and many interesting things happened during them.
One evening Mr. Carrisford raised his eyes from his book. Sara had not moved for a while; she was sitting gazing steadily into the flames.
He asked, "What are you 'supposing' now, Sara?"
Colour bright in her cheeks, Sara lifted her head.
"I WAS supposing something," she replied. "I remembered that hungry day and a child I met."
A note of sadness entered the Indian gentleman's voice. "There were so many hungry days, though. Which one were you remembering?"
"I'd forgotten you hadn't heard," Sara said. "The day my dream came true—that one."

She then described the bakery, the fourpence she had found in the wet mud, and the little girl whose hunger was worse than hers. Her telling was simple and as brief as she could make it. Somehow, though, the Indian gentleman felt obliged to cover his eyes with one hand and stare down at the carpet.
When she had finished, she added, "I was supposing a sort of plan. There's something I'd like to do."
Mr. Carrisford spoke softly. "What is it, princess? Whatever it is you want to do, you may."

Sara hesitated a little. "I wondered—since you say I have so much money—whether I could visit the woman who sells the buns. Could I ask her, whenever hungry children sit on her steps or stare through her window, especially on those awful days, to invite them inside and give them something to eat? Then she could send me the bills. Would I be allowed to do that?"
"Tomorrow morning you shall arrange it," the Indian gentleman promised.
"Thank you," Sara replied. "You see, I've felt that hunger myself. And it's terribly hard when you can't even make it disappear by PRETENDING."
"Yes, my dear, yes," the Indian gentleman said. "It must be terribly hard. Try to put it behind you. Come down to the footstool by my knee, and remember only that you're a princess."

Smiling, Sara answered, "Yes, and I can give the populace bread and buns." She settled on the stool. The Indian gentleman—another name he sometimes liked her to use for him—drew her small dark head against his knee and gently stroked her hair.

The following morning Miss Minchin looked out and saw perhaps the very sights she most disliked. Her neighbour's carriage, drawn by tall horses, stopped outside his door. The Indian gentleman came down the steps with a small figure beside him, warmly wrapped in luxurious soft furs. Miss Minchin knew that little figure well; it brought back earlier days. Behind came someone equally familiar and particularly irritating to behold: Becky. As a delighted attendant, she now always escorted her young mistress to the carriage, carrying her belongings and wraps. Already Becky's face had grown round and pink.
A little later the carriage stopped at the bakery. Strangely enough, its passengers stepped out just as the bun-woman was again placing a tray of steaming-hot buns in the window.
The woman turned when Sara entered the shop. Leaving the tray of buns, she came behind the counter and looked at her intently for a moment. Then recognition lit up her kindly face.
"I do believe I've seen you before, miss," she said. "But then again—"
"You have," Sara answered. "You once let me have six buns for fourpence, and—"

"Five of them went to that beggar girl," the woman interrupted. "I haven't forgotten. At first I couldn't understand it." Turning towards the Indian gentleman, she continued, "Begging your pardon, sir, but few young people notice hunger in a face the way she did. I've thought about it often." To Sara she added, "Forgive me speaking so freely, miss, but you're looking rosier now, and—well—better than you did on that—that—"
"I am better, thank you," Sara assured her. "Much happier, too. And I've come because there's something I'd like you to do for me."
"Me, miss!" said the bun-woman, beaming. "Well, bless you! Of course, miss. What is it you want me to do?"
Leaning against the counter, Sara then explained her little scheme: the terrible weather, the hungry waifs, and the buns they could be given.
Watching her closely, the woman listened in open astonishment.

When she had heard everything, she repeated, "Well, bless me! I'd be delighted to do it. I'm a working woman and can't spare much myself, with so much suffering everywhere you look. But, if you'll pardon me, I've given away plenty of bread since that rainy afternoon just because I kept thinking of you. So cold and wet you were, and looking so hungry, yet handing out your hot buns as if you were a princess."
The words brought an involuntary smile to the Indian gentleman's face. Sara smiled slightly too, remembering her own thoughts as she had placed the buns on the ravenous child's ragged lap.
"She seemed so terribly hungry," she said. "Even more hungry than I was."
"Starving, she was," the woman replied. "Since then she's told me many times how she sat outside in the wet, feeling as though a wolf were tearing at her poor little insides."
Sara exclaimed, "Oh, you've met her again since that day? Can you tell me where she is?"

Her smile kinder than ever, the woman said, "Indeed I can, miss. She's right in the back room there, and she's been here a month. She's turning into a decent, willing girl. Given the life she's had, you'd hardly credit what a help she is, both in the shop and in my kitchen."

She went to the little back parlour's door and called. A moment later a girl followed her out and took her place behind the counter. It really was the beggar child, clean now, neatly dressed, looking as though she had not suffered hunger for a long time. She was shy, but her face was pleasant now that she was no longer a savage. That wildness had left her eyes. She recognized Sara instantly and stood gazing as though she could never take in enough of her.

The woman explained, "I said she could come here when she needed food. When she came, I'd find small jobs for her. She was willing, I discovered, and little by little I grew fond of her. In the end I gave her a place and a home. She helps me, behaves herself, and she's as grateful as any girl could be. Anne is her name. She hasn't another."
For several moments the girls simply faced one another. Then Sara drew a hand from her muff and offered it across the counter. Anne clasped it, and the two looked directly into each other's eyes.

"I'm so pleased," Sara said. "And an idea has just come to me. Maybe Mrs. Brown would let you hand out the bread and buns to the other children. You might like being the one to do it, since you know what being hungry feels like too."
The girl replied, "Yes, miss."

Somehow Sara felt that she understood Anne, though Anne said so little. She only stood motionless, gazing after Sara as she left the shop with the Indian gentleman, climbed into the carriage beside him, and drove away.
